items.title: Must-Know Algorithms (Trace by Hand)
items.text:
• FCFS, SJF, SRTF, RR, Priority — calculate wait/turnaround
  • Banker's Algorithm — safety check, request granting
  • Producer-Consumer — semaphore setup, wait/signal order
  • Readers-Writers — read_count logic
  • Peterson's Algorithm — 2-process mutual exclusion
  • Dining Philosophers — 3 deadlock-free solutions
  • Page Replacement — FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Clock

items.title: Must-Know Concepts
items.text:
• Process vs Thread, PCB vs TCB
  • User/Kernel mode, system calls, interrupts
  • Context switch components
  • Race condition, critical section, 3 requirements
  • Spinlock vs mutex vs semaphore
  • Priority inversion + inheritance
  • Memory hierarchy, caching principle
  • MLFQ aging/demotion/promotion
  • COW fork(), virtual memory, demand paging
  • TLB, EAT calculation
  • NUMA, memory locality

items.title: Code-Level Understanding
items.text:
• fork()/exec()/wait() flow
  • pthread_create/join/mutex_lock/cond_wait
  • sem_wait/sem_post for producer-consumer, readers-writers
  • Signal handlers with sigaction()
  • mmap() for memory-mapped files
  • sched_setaffinity() for CPU pinning
  • Banker's algorithm trace

items.title: Study Strategy
items.text:
1. Read topics in order — each builds on previous
  2. Draw diagrams — scheduling Gantt charts, memory layouts, RAGs, state transitions
  3. Trace examples by hand — don't just read solutions
  4. Write small C programs — fork, threads, mutex, semaphores, signals
  5. Connect concepts — how does MLFQ use aging? How does priority inheritance fix inversion?
  6. Ask "what if?" — quantum too small? No aging? Wait/signal reversed?

items.title: Topic 1: OS Introduction & Computer System Organization
items.text: Source: Lecture 1 + Textbook Ch. 1 (Silberschatz Ch. 1-2, Stallings Ch. 1-2, Stevens & Rago Ch. 1)

items.title: 1.1 What is an Operating System?
items.text:
Definition (Silberschatz): "An operating system is a program that acts as an intermediary between a user of a computer and the computer hardware."

Two Views: | View | Role | |------|------| | User View | Convenience, ease of use, performance | | System View | Resource Allocator (CPU, memory, I/O) + Control Program (prevent errors, control I/O) |

Kernel: "The one program running at all times on the computer" — everything else is system programs or applications.

items.title: 1.2 Computer System Organization (4 Components)
items.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Users                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│    Application Programs             │  ← Compilers, browsers, DBs, games
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│         Operating System            │  ← Resource allocator + control
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│           Hardware                  │  ← CPU, Memory, I/O Devices
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Hardware Components: - CPU(s): General-purpose + special-purpose (GPU, disk controller, NIC) - Memory: RAM (volatile), ROM/EEPROM (firmware) - I/O Devices: Disk, keyboard, mouse, network, display - System Bus: Connects CPU, memory, device controllers - Memory Controller: Synchronizes access to shared memory

items.title: 1.3 System Boot Process
items.text: Step Description 1. Power On / Reset CPU PC → firmware address (ROM/EEPROM) 2. Bootstrap Program First code to run; initializes CPU, devices, memory; locates & loads kernel 3. Kernel Initialization Sets up system services, interrupt vectors, starts init process 4. Init Process First user process (init or systemd, PID 1); waits for login/daemons

items.title: 1.4 Interrupt-Driven Operation
items.text: Modern OS is interrupt-driven — sits idle waiting for events.

items.title: Interrupt Classification
items.text:
Interrupt Event
    ├── Hardware Interrupt
    │     ├── Polling (CPU queries devices)
    │     └── Vectored (hardware provides offset → Interrupt Vector Table → ISR)
    └── Software Interrupt (Trap/Exception)
          ├── Error (divide by zero, invalid memory access → SIGSEGV)
          └── System Call (user requests OS service)

items.title: Interrupt Handling Lifecycle
items.text:
1. Generation — IRQ from device or trap instruction
  2. Processor Response — Halts current thread at instruction boundary
  3. State Preservation — Saves PC, PSW, registers to kernel stack
  4. Dispatching — Vectored (via IVT) or Polling
  5. Handler Execution — ISR runs (e.g., read keyboard buffer)
  6. State Restoration — Restore registers/PC, resume interrupted thread

Key Insight: Interrupts enable multiprogramming — CPU switches to another process while I/O completes.

items.title: 1.5 Storage Hierarchy
items.text: Level Technology Speed Capacity Volatility Cost/Byte Registers CPU internal Fastest Smallest Volatile Highest Cache (L1/L2/L3) SRAM Very Fast Small Volatile High Main Memory (RAM) DRAM Fast Medium Volatile Medium SSD / NVRAM Flash Fast Large Non-volatile Medium Hard Disk (HDD) Magnetic Slow Very Large Non-volatile Low Tape / Optical Magnetic/Optical Slowest Huge Non-volatile Lowest

items.title: Caching Principle
items.text:
1. Copy data from slower → faster storage temporarily
  2. Cache Hit → read from fast cache
  3. Cache Miss → fetch from slow storage, populate cache
  4. Replacement policies: LRU, FIFO, etc.

items.title: DMA (Direct Memory Access)
items.text:
• Problem: Interrupt per byte wastes CPU for high-speed devices
  • Solution: DMA controller transfers blocks directly between device buffer ↔ memory
  • Result: Only one interrupt per block; CPU executes user code concurrently

items.title: I/O Modes
items.text: Mode Behavior Synchronous (Blocking) CPU waits for I/O completion; one request at a time Asynchronous (Non-blocking) CPU continues immediately; checks completion later

items.title: 1.7 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. OS = Resource Allocator + Control Program (Silberschatz §1.2.1)
  2. Kernel = the one program running at all times (Silberschatz §1.2.1)
  3. Interrupts = OS's nervous system (Silberschatz §1.5)
  4. Storage hierarchy trades speed vs capacity vs cost (Silberschatz §1.4)
  5. DMA offloads bulk data movement from CPU (Silberschatz §1.7.3)
  6. Boot: Firmware → Bootstrap → Kernel → Init (PID 1)

items.title: 1.8 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer What are the two main roles of an OS from system view? Resource Allocator + Control Program What is the kernel? The one program running at all times How does vectored interrupt differ from polling? Hardware provides offset into IVT; polling = CPU queries each device What happens during DMA transfer? Device ↔ memory directly; 1 interrupt/block; CPU free Why is storage organized hierarchically? Trade-off: speed ↑, cost ↑, capacity ↓, volatility ↑ as you go up

items.title: 1.9 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns (from prep file)
items.text:
• Q13: Dual-mode operation — mode bit (0=kernel, 1=user) checked by hardware on every instruction
  • Q14: Interrupt vs Trap — interrupt = async (hardware), trap = sync (syscall, division by zero)
  • Q15: System call parameters too large for registers → stored in memory block, address passed in register
  • Q18: Symmetric cluster + SAN → local semaphores invisible across nodes → need DLM (Distributed Lock Manager)

items.title: Need for OS
items.text: Without OS, application developers would need direct hardware knowledge to access hardware — OS provides user-friendly environment to develop/execute programs without hardware expertise.

items.title: OS Goals
items.text:
• Execute user programs and make solving user problems easier
  • Make computer system convenient to use
  • Use computer hardware efficiently
  • Manage resources: Memory, Processor(s), I/O Devices
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: Why Study OS?
items.text:
• Almost all code runs on top of an OS — understanding OS is crucial for efficient, effective, secure programming
  • Understanding OS fundamentals is essential for all computer practitioners

path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: Four Components (Abstract View)
items.text:
1. Hardware — CPU, memory, I/O devices; provides basic computing resources
  2. Operating System — Controls and coordinates hardware use among applications/users
  3. Application Programs — Define how system resources solve user problems (compilers, browsers, DBs, games)
  4. Users — People, machines, other computers
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: What Operating Systems Do
items.text:
User View: Convenience, ease of use, good performance; don't care about resource utilization

System View: - Resource Allocator — Manages all resources, decides between conflicting requests for efficient/fair use - Control Program — Controls program execution to prevent errors and improper computer use

items.text:

  • Must know how to load OS kernel and start executing it
  • Locates and loads OS kernel into memory
  • First process created is init (PID 1), waits for events

items.title: 1.6 I/O Structure
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: Device Controller
items.text:
• Each device controller manages a specific device type
  • Has local buffer storage and special-purpose registers
  • Responsible for moving data between peripheral devices
  • Device driver provides uniform interface between controller and kernel
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: I/O Operation Modes
items.text: Mode Behavior Synchronous (Blocking) CPU waits for I/O completion; one request at a time; wait instruction idles CPU until interrupt Asynchronous (Non-blocking) CPU continues immediately; system call allows waiting for I/O; device-status table tracks device state
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.title: I/O Flow
items.text:
1. I/O from device to local buffer of controller
  2. CPU moves data between main memory and local buffers
  3. Device controller informs CPU of completion via interrupt
  4. Device-status table tracks type, address, state of each I/O device
path: Topic 1 (Detailed): OS Introduction & Computer System Organization

items.text:

  • Hard Disks: Rigid platters with magnetic material; tracks → sectors; disk controller manages logical interaction
  • SSD: Faster than HDD, non-volatile

items.title: Caching Principle Details
items.text:
• Performed at many levels: hardware, OS, software
  • Information copied from slower to faster storage temporarily
  • Cache checked first; if hit → fast; if miss → copy to cache
  • Cache smaller than storage being cached
  • Cache management: size and replacement policy

items.title: Topic 2: Computer Architecture & OS Operations
items.text: Source: Lecture 2 + Textbook Ch. 2 (Silberschatz Ch. 1-2, Stallings Ch. 2, 15, Stevens & Rago Ch. 2)

items.title: Single Processor Systems
items.text:
• One general-purpose CPU
  • Special-purpose processors: disk controller, keyboard controller, GPU
  • Run limited instruction sets; offload main CPU (e.g., disk controller handles scheduling)

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• Two or more processors in close communication
  • Share: system bus, clock, memory, peripheral devices

items.title: Three Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Increased Throughput More work in less time (not N× due to sync overhead) Economy of Scale Share peripherals, storage, power — cheaper than N single-CPU systems Fault Tolerance Failure of one CPU ≠ system halt; graceful degradation

items.title: Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP)
items.text:
Master CPU → Controls system, schedules, allocates work
Worker CPUs → Execute assigned tasks only
- Simple but master becomes bottleneck

items.title: Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) — Modern Standard
items.text:
All CPUs are PEERS — no master-slave
Each runs kernel + user code
Each has private registers + cache
All share physical memory via system bus
- Used by: Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS

SMP Architecture:
  CPU 0          CPU 1          CPU 2
  [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache]
     │             │             │
     └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                   ▼
            System Bus
                   │
                   ▼
           Shared Memory

items.title: 2.4 Multicore Design
items.text:
• Multiple computing cores on single chip
  • Each core = independent physical CPU to OS
  • Benefits: Faster on-chip communication, less power/heat than multi-chip
Dual-Core Chip:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │         PROCESSOR CHIP          │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐     │
  │  │  CORE 0  │  │  CORE 1  │     │
  │  │ [Regs]   │  │ [Regs]   │     │
  │  │ [L1]     │  │ [L1]     │     │
  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘     │
  │       │             │           │
  │       └──────┬──────┘           │
  │              ▼                  │
  │       [Shared L2/L3 Cache]      │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                 │

items.text: Architecture Description Blade Servers High-density: multiple processor/I/O boards in one chassis; each boots independently Clustered Systems Independent nodes + shared SAN; Asymmetric (hot-standby) / Symmetric (all active) / HPC (MPI/OpenMP) NUMA Non-Uniform Memory Access — latency varies by CPU-memory distance; scheduler must consider locality big.LITTLE Heterogeneous cores (performance + efficiency); scheduler migrates tasks based on workload

items.title: Dual-Mode Operation
items.text:
• User Mode (bit = 1): Applications run; restricted instructions
  • Kernel Mode (bit = 0): OS runs; privileged instructions allowed
USER MODE (bit=1)                 KERNEL MODE (bit=0)
+-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+
| User Process executing      |   |                             |
|                             |   |                             |
| Calls system call           |   |                             |
| (e.g. read())               |   |                             |
|         │                   |   |                             |
|         v                   |   |                             |
|   [ TRAP / SYSCALL ] ------>|-->| System call handled         |
|   (HW sets bit = 0)         |   | Execute privileged routine  |
|                             |   |         │                   |
|                             |<--|<--------|--- [ RETURN ]     |
| Resume user execution <-----+   |     (HW resets bit = 1)    |
+-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+

items.title: Transition Lifecycle
items.text:
1. User program executes in user mode (bit = 1)
  2. Program needs OS service → executes system call (trap instruction)
  3. Hardware: traps, saves CPU state, switches mode bit to 0 (kernel mode)
  4. Kernel: looks up syscall table, verifies parameters, executes privileged function
  5. Kernel: executes return-from-trap (privileged instruction)
  6. Hardware: restores state, sets mode bit to 1 (user mode)
  7. Control returns to user process

items.title: Privileged Instructions (Kernel Mode Only)
items.text:
• Direct I/O manipulation
  • Clearing interrupts
  • Setting timer counters
  • Modifying page tables
  • Context switching

items.title: 2.7 Timer & CPU Protection
items.text:
Purpose: Prevent user programs from hogging CPU (infinite loops)

Mechanism:
1. Hardware timer set to interrupt after interval (fixed or variable)
2. Variable timers: fixed-rate clock + internal counter
3. OS loads initial counter via PRIVILEGED INSTRUCTION before dispatch
4. Each clock tick: counter decrements
5. Counter reaches 0 → hardware timer interrupt
6. Interrupt → OS scheduler → preempt current process → assign CPU to another

items.title: 2.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. SMP = peer CPUs sharing memory; standard for modern OS (Silberschatz §2.1.2)
  2. Multicore = multiple cores on one die; each appears as CPU to OS (Silberschatz §2.2)
  3. Clusters = independent nodes + shared SAN; for HA and HPC (Silberschatz §2.3.2)
  4. NUMA/big.LITTLE = modern complexities OS scheduler must handle (Silberschatz §2.3.3-4)
  5. Dual-mode: mode bit in PSW; hardware enforces privileged instruction restriction
  6. System call = trap instruction → mode switch → kernel handler → return
  7. Timer = hardware mechanism enabling preemptive scheduling

items.title: 2.9 Quick Self-Test

Private registers + L1 cache What do cores share on-chip? L2/L3 cache What prevents user program from executing privileged instruction? Hardware checks mode bit; traps if user mode (bit=1) How does timer enable preemption? Counter decrements each tick; at 0 → interrupt → scheduler runs

items.title: Topic 2 (Detailed): Computer Architecture & OS Operations
items.text: Source: Lecture 2 + Textbook Ch. 2 (Silberschatz Ch. 1-2, Stallings Ch. 2, 15, Stevens & Rago Ch. 2)

items.title: Single Processor Systems
items.text:
• One general-purpose CPU
  • Special-purpose processors: disk controller, keyboard controller, GPU
  • Run limited instruction sets; offload main CPU (e.g., disk controller handles scheduling)

items.title: Special-Purpose Processors
items.text:
• Device-specific: disk, keyboard, graphics controller
  • Run limited instruction sets
  • Low-level components built into hardware, managed by OS
  • OS monitors their status
  • Example: Disk controller microprocessor
  • Receives request sequences from CPU
  • Implements own disk queue and scheduling algorithm
  • Relieves main CPU of disk scheduling overhead

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• Two or more processors in close communication
  • Share: system bus, clock, memory, peripheral devices

items.title: Three Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Increased Throughput More work in less time (not N× due to sync overhead) Economy of Scale Share peripherals, storage, power — cheaper than N single-CPU systems Fault Tolerance Failure of one CPU ≠ system halt; graceful degradation

items.title: Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP)
items.text:
Master CPU → Controls system, schedules, allocates work
Worker CPUs → Execute assigned tasks only
- Simple but master becomes bottleneck

items.title: Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP) — Modern Standard
items.text:
All CPUs are PEERS — no master-slave
Each runs kernel + user code
Each has private registers + cache
All share physical memory via system bus
- Used by: Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS

SMP Architecture:
  CPU 0          CPU 1          CPU 2
  [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache] [Regs] [Cache]
     │             │             │
     └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                   ▼
            System Bus
                   │
                   ▼
           Shared Memory

items.title: 2.4 Multicore Design
items.text:
• Multiple computing cores on single chip
  • Each core = independent physical CPU to OS
  • Benefits: Faster on-chip communication, less power/heat than multi-chip
Dual-Core Chip:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │         PROCESSOR CHIP          │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐     │
  │  │  CORE 0  │  │  CORE 1  │     │
  │  │ [Regs]   │  │ [Regs]   │     │
  │  │ [L1]     │  │ [L1]     │     │
  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘     │
  │       │             │           │
  │       └──────┬──────┘           │
  │              ▼                  │
  │       [Shared L2/L3 Cache]      │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                 │
           Main Memory

# Check your CPU topology
cat /proc/cpuinfo | more

items.text: Architecture Description Blade Servers High-density: multiple processor/I/O boards in one chassis; each boots independently Clustered Systems Independent nodes + shared SAN; Asymmetric (hot-standby) / Symmetric (all active) / HPC (MPI/OpenMP) NUMA Non-Uniform Memory Access — latency varies by CPU-memory distance; scheduler must consider locality big.LITTLE Heterogeneous cores (performance + efficiency); scheduler migrates tasks based on workload

items.title: Clustered Systems Details
items.text:
• Multiple systems working together, sharing storage via SAN
  • Asymmetric clustering: one machine in hot-standby mode
  • Symmetric clustering: multiple nodes running applications, monitoring each other
  • HPC clusters: apps must use parallelization (MPI/OpenMP)
  • DLM (Distributed Lock Manager): avoids conflicting operations when multiple hosts access shared storage on SAN

items.title: Multiprogramming (Batch System)
items.text:
• Single user cannot keep CPU and I/O busy at all times
  • Multiprogramming organizes jobs so CPU always has one to execute
  • Subset of total jobs kept in memory
  • One job selected and run via job scheduling
  • When it waits (I/O), OS switches to another job

items.title: Multitasking (Time-Sharing)
items.text:
• Logical extension: CPU switches jobs frequently so users can interact
  • Response time < 1 second
  • Each user has at least one program executing in memory → process
  • If several jobs ready → CPU scheduling
  • If processes don't fit in memory → swapping moves them in/out

items.title: Hardware vs Software Interrupts
items.text: Type Source Examples Hardware Interrupt Devices Disk I/O complete, network packet, timer Software Interrupt (Trap/Exception) Current instruction Division by zero, invalid memory access (SIGSEGV), system call

items.title: Dual-Mode Transition
items.text:
• Trap/Interrupt: Hardware switches from user → kernel mode (mode bit = 0)
  • Return: System switches back to user mode (mode bit = 1) before returning to user program

items.title: Multi-Mode Operation (Modern CPUs)
items.text:
• Increasingly support multi-mode operations
  • e.g., Virtual Machine Manager (VMM) mode for guest VMs

items.title: Timer Details
items.text:
• Fixed interval (e.g., 1/60 sec) or variable (1 msec to 1 sec)
  • Variable timer: fixed-rate clock + counter
  • OS sets counter via privileged instruction
  • Each clock tick decrements counter
  • Counter = 0 → hardware timer interrupt
  • Can terminate program running too long

items.title: Interrupt-Driven Operations
items.text:
• Hardware interrupt by devices
  • Software interrupt (exception/trap):
  • Software error (division by zero)
  • Request for OS service (system call)
  • Infinite loop, processes modifying each other or OS

  • Processes modifying each other or the OS

items.title: Problem 1: AMP vs SMP
items.text:
Describe the bottleneck in AMP and how SMP solves it.
Answer: AMP master CPU becomes bottleneck scheduling all work; SMP makes all CPUs peers with own run queues.

items.title: Problem 2: Multicore
items.text:
Explain why SMT (Hyper-Threading) improves utilization.
Answer: Two threads on one core fill memory stall cycles of each other; near 100% core utilization.

items.title: Problem 3: Dual-Mode
items.text: Draw the user/kernel mode transition diagram for a system call.

items.title: Problem 4: Timer
items.text:
Explain how the timer interrupt enables preemptive scheduling.
Answer: Counter decrements each tick; at 0 → interrupt → scheduler preempts current process.

items.title: Problem 5: NUMA
items.text:
What is NUMA and why does the scheduler need to be NUMA-aware?
Answer: Memory latency varies by CPU-node distance; scheduler must prefer local memory allocation.

items.title: 3.2 System Calls
items.text: Definition: Programmatic interface to kernel services; written in C/assembly; exposed via APIs.

items.title: Example: File Copy Sequence (Silberschatz Fig 2.2)
items.text:
1. Acquire input file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

2. Acquire output file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

3. Open input file:
   open()  → if not exist, abort & print error

4. Create destination file:
   create() / open(O_CREAT) → abort/truncate if exists

5. Copy Loop:
   read()  → from input file buffer
   write() → to destination file buffer
   repeat until read() returns 0 (EOF) or error

6. Clean up:
   close() input file
   close() destination file

7. Output status:
   write() → completion message

8. Termination:
   exit() → normal termination

items.title: Standard C Library → System Call (printf → write)
items.text:
USER MODE:
main.c:      printf("Greetings\n");
                  │
                  ▼ Calls library function
libc:        Formats string buffer
             Invokes write() syscall stub
                  │ TRAP to Kernel (syscall instruction)
                  ▼
KERNEL MODE:
sys_write(): Executes, sends data to terminal
             Returns bytes written
                  │ Return from Trap
                  ▼
USER MODE:
libc write() stub passes control back to main()

items.title: 3.3 Process Concept
path: Topic 3 (Detailed): OS Services, System Calls & Process Concept

items.title: Program vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Program Process Nature Passive (file on disk) Active (in execution) Context None PC, registers, memory space, stack Instances One file Multiple from same program

Silberschatz: "A program is a passive entity... A process is a program in execution."
path: Topic 3 (Detailed): OS Services, System Calls & Process Concept

items.title: Process Memory Layout (32-bit)
items.text:
High Address (0xFFFFFFFF)
├── Command-line args & Environment (argc, argv, envp)
├── STACK (grows ↓: frames, locals, params, return addresses)
│       ↑
│       │   (free space)
│       ↓
├── HEAP (grows ↑: malloc/free)
├── BSS (uninitialized globals/statics → zeroed)
├── DATA (initialized globals/statics)
└── TEXT (code, read-only)
Low Address (0x00000000)
path: Topic 3 (Detailed): OS Services, System Calls & Process Concept

items.title: C Mapping Example
items.text:
int x;              // → BSS (uninitialized)
int y = 15;         // → DATA (initialized)

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {  // args in high memory
    int *values;    // → STACK (pointer)
    int i;          // → STACK (local)
    values = malloc(5 * sizeof(int)); // → HEAP
    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) values[i] = i;  // → TEXT executes
    return 0;
}

items.title: 3.4 Process State Model (5-State)
items.text:
[ NEW ]
                        │
                     admitted
                        ▼
         +────────> [ READY ] <─────────+
         │           │                   │
         │  dispatch │                   │
         │           ▼                   │
         │    [ RUNNING ] ──────────────+
         │        │        interrupt
         │        │
         │        │ I/O wait
         │        ▼
         │    [ WAITING ]
         │        │
         +────────┘
          I/O complete

   [ RUNNING ] ─────────> [ TERMINATED ]
             exit
State Meaning New Being created Ready In memory, waiting for CPU Running Executing on CPU Waiting Blocked on I/O/event Terminated Finished, awaiting cleanup

items.title: 3.5 Process Control Block (PCB / task_struct)
items.text:
Kernel representation of each process

PCB Field Description Process State Ready, Running, Waiting... Process ID (PID) Unique identifier Program Counter Next instruction address CPU Registers Accumulator, index, stack pointer Scheduling Info Priority, queue pointers Memory Management Page tables, base/limit Accounting CPU time used, time limits I/O Status Allocated devices, open files

Linux task_struct: pid, state, mm (memory), files (fd table), parent, children

items.text: Queue Contents Job Queue All processes in system Ready Queue In memory, ready to execute Device/Waiting Queues Blocked on specific I/O/event

items.title: Scheduler Types
items.text: Scheduler Frequency Role Short-term (CPU) Milliseconds Pick next ready process → dispatch Long-term (Job) Seconds/minutes Admit from disk to memory (controls degree of multiprogramming) Medium-term (Swapper) As needed Swap out to disk (free memory) → swap in later

items.text:
Type Behavior CPU Bursts I/O-Bound More I/O than compute Many, short CPU-Bound More compute than I/O Few, long

Scheduler goal: Balance mix for good utilization + responsiveness

items.title: 3.7 Context Switching
items.text:
Mechanism: Save current process state to PCB, load next process state from PCB

P0 Running → Interrupt → Save PCB0 → Load PCB1 → P1 Running
             ↑                               │
             └── Interrupt → Save PCB1 → Load PCB0 ───┘
path: Topic 3 (Detailed): OS Services, System Calls & Process Concept

items.title: Overhead (Pure System Cost)
items.text:
• Save/restore: GPRs, PC, SP, FP registers
  • Flush/invalidate TLB
  • Switch address space (page table base register)
  • Factors: Hardware register sets, PCB size, OS complexity

Silberschatz: "Context-switch time is pure overhead, because the system does no useful work while switching."

items.title: 3.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. OS Services: User-facing (UI, exec, I/O, files, comm, errors) + System-facing (resource allocation, accounting, protection)
  2. System Calls: API to kernel; categories: process, file, device, info, comm, protection
  3. Process = active entity with memory layout (TEXT, DATA, BSS, HEAP, STACK)
  4. 5-State Model: New → Ready ↔ Running → Waiting → Terminated
  5. PCB = kernel's process representation (Linux: task_struct)
  6. Three Schedulers: Short-term (CPU), Long-term (admission), Medium-term (swapping)
  7. Context Switch = save/restore PCB + TLB flush + address space switch

items.text: Service Description User Interface CLI (shells), GUI (windows), Batch (scripts) Program Execution Load, schedule, allocate, handle termination I/O Operations Safe abstracted access to devices File System Create/delete/read/write, permissions, metadata Communications Shared memory, message passing, pipes, sockets Error Detection Hardware errors, I/O errors, program errors (overflow, segfault)

items.title: Services for System Efficiency
items.text: Service Description Resource Allocation CPU, memory, disk, I/O — fair & efficient Accounting Track usage per user/process (billing, capacity planning) Protection & Security Controlled access, authentication, isolation, defense

items.title: 3.2 System Calls
items.text: Definition: Programmatic interface to kernel services; written in C/assembly; exposed via APIs.

items.title: Example: File Copy Sequence (Silberschatz Fig 2.2)
items.text:
1. Acquire input file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

2. Acquire output file name:
   write() → display prompt
   read()  → accept keyboard input

3. Open input file:
   open()  → if not exist, abort & print error

4. Create destination file:
   create() / open(O_CREAT) → abort/truncate if exists

5. Copy Loop:
   read()  → from input file buffer
   write() → to destination file buffer
   repeat until read() returns 0 (EOF) or error

6. Clean up:
   close() input file
   close() destination file

7. Output status:
   write() → completion message

8. Termination:
   exit() → normal termination

items.title: System Call Categories (Windows vs Unix)
items.text: Category Windows API Unix/Linux Syscalls Process Control CreateProcess, ExitProcess, WaitForSingleObject fork, exec, wait, exit File Manipulation CreateFile, ReadFile, WriteFile, CloseHandle open, creat, read, write, close Device Manipulation SetConsoleMode, ReadConsole, WriteConsole ioctl, read, write Information Maintenance GetCurrentProcessId, SetTimer, Sleep getpid, alarm, sleep Communications CreatePipe, CreateFileMapping, MapViewOfFile pipe, shm_open, mmap Protection SetFileSecurity, InitializeSecurityDescriptor chmod, umask, chown

items.title: Standard C Library → System Call (printf → write)
items.text:
USER MODE:
main.c:      printf("Greetings\n");
                  │
                  ▼ Calls library function
libc:        Formats string buffer
             Invokes write() syscall stub
                  │ TRAP to Kernel (syscall instruction)
                  ▼
KERNEL MODE:
sys_write(): Executes, sends data to terminal
             Returns bytes written
                  │ Return from Trap
                  ▼
USER MODE:
libc write() stub passes control back to main()

items.title: Program vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Program Process Nature Passive (file on disk) Active (in execution) Context None PC, registers, memory space, stack Instances One file Multiple from same program

Silberschatz: "A program is a passive entity... A process is a program in execution."

items.title: Process Memory Layout (32-bit)
items.text:
High Address (0xFFFFFFFF)
├── Command-line args & Environment (argc, argv, envp)
├── STACK (grows ↓: frames, locals, params, return addresses)
│       ↑
│       │   (free space)
│       ↓
├── HEAP (grows ↑: malloc/free)
├── BSS (uninitialized globals/statics → zeroed)
├── DATA (initialized globals/statics)
└── TEXT (code, read-only)
Low Address (0x00000000)

items.title: C Mapping Example
items.text:
int x;              // → BSS (uninitialized)
int y = 15;         // → DATA (initialized)

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {  // args in high memory
    int *values;    // → STACK (pointer)
    int i;          // → STACK (local)
    values = malloc(5 * sizeof(int)); // → HEAP
    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) values[i] = i;  // → TEXT executes
    return 0;
}

items.title: 3.4 Process State Model (5-State)
items.text:
[ NEW ]
                        │
                     admitted
                        ▼
         +────────> [ READY ] <─────────+
         │           │                   │
         │  dispatch │                   │
         │           ▼                   │
         │    [ RUNNING ] ──────────────+
         │        │        interrupt
         │        │
         │        │ I/O wait
         │        ▼
         │    [ WAITING ]
         │        │
         +────────┘
          I/O complete

   [ RUNNING ] ─────────> [ TERMINATED ]
             exit
State Meaning New Being created Ready In memory, waiting for CPU Running Executing on CPU Waiting Blocked on I/O/event Terminated Finished, awaiting cleanup

items.title: 3.5 Process Control Block (PCB / task_struct)
items.text:
Kernel representation of each process

PCB Field Description Process State Ready, Running, Waiting... Process ID (PID) Unique identifier Program Counter Next instruction address CPU Registers Accumulator, index, stack pointer Scheduling Info Priority, queue pointers Memory Management Page tables, base/limit Accounting CPU time used, time limits I/O Status Allocated devices, open files

Linux task_struct: pid, state, mm (memory), files (fd table), parent, children

items.title: Three Queues
items.text: Queue Contents Job Queue All processes in system Ready Queue In memory, ready to execute Device/Waiting Queues Blocked on specific I/O/event

items.title: Scheduler Types
items.text: Scheduler Frequency Role Short-term (CPU) Milliseconds Pick next ready process → dispatch Long-term (Job) Seconds/minutes Admit from disk to memory (controls degree of multiprogramming) Medium-term (Swapper) As needed Swap out to disk (free memory) → swap in later

items.title: Process Types
items.text:
Type Behavior CPU Bursts I/O-Bound More I/O than compute Many, short CPU-Bound More compute than I/O Few, long

Scheduler goal: Balance mix for good utilization + responsiveness

items.title: 3.7 Context Switching
items.text:
Mechanism: Save current process state to PCB, load next process state from PCB

P0 Running → Interrupt → Save PCB0 → Load PCB1 → P1 Running
             ↑                               │
             └── Interrupt → Save PCB1 → Load PCB0 ───┘

items.title: Overhead (Pure System Cost)
items.text:
• Save/restore: GPRs, PC, SP, FP registers
  • Flush/invalidate TLB
  • Switch address space (page table base register)
  • Factors: Hardware register sets, PCB size, OS complexity

Silberschatz: "Context-switch time is pure overhead, because the system does no useful work while switching."

items.title: 3.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. OS Services: User-facing (UI, exec, I/O, files, comm, errors) + System-facing (resource allocation, accounting, protection)
  2. System Calls: API to kernel; categories: process, file, device, info, comm, protection
  3. Process = active entity with memory layout (TEXT, DATA, BSS, HEAP, STACK)
  4. 5-State Model: New → Ready ↔ Running → Waiting → Terminated
  5. PCB = kernel's process representation (Linux: task_struct)
  6. Three Schedulers: Short-term (CPU), Long-term (admission), Medium-term (swapping)
  7. Context Switch = save/restore PCB + TLB flush + address space switch

items.title: 3.9 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer What are the 3 scheduler types? Short-term (CPU), Long-term (Job), Medium-term (Swapper) What does long-term scheduler control? Degree of multiprogramming What's in the PCB? State, PID, PC, registers, scheduling info, memory mgmt, accounting, I/O status Difference: I/O-bound vs CPU-bound? I/O-bound: many short bursts; CPU-bound: few long bursts Context switch overhead includes? Save/restore registers, TLB flush, page table switch printf → write syscall path? User: printf → libc formats → write stub → TRAP → Kernel: sys_write → returns

items.title: 3.10 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns (from prep file)
items.text:
• Q9: PCB contents — PC, registers, process state, scheduling info
  • Q10: Ready → Running is dispatcher/scheduler transition
  • Q11: Context switch = pure overhead (no useful user work)
  • Q12: Microkernel vs Monolithic — microkernel moves FS, drivers to user space, uses message passing
  • Q13: Dual-mode — mode bit checked by hardware; privileged instructions only in kernel mode (bit=0)
  • Q14: Interrupt (async, hardware) vs Trap (sync, syscall/division by zero)
  • Q15: Large syscall params → memory block + register with address
  • Q16: Cascading termination — parent termination kills all children
  • Q17: Accounting service tracks CPU burst, memory, disk for billing
  • Q18: Symmetric cluster + SAN → local semaphore invisible across nodes → need DLM
  • Q19: Interactive editor = I/O-bound (many short CPU bursts)
  • Q20: Dispatcher does context switch + mode switch + jump to user code

items.title: 4.1 Process Creation: The Unix Philosophy
path: Topic 4 (Detailed): Process Creation, Termination & System Calls

items.title: Why fork() + exec() Instead of One spawn()?
items.text:
Historical context: Unix was designed for simplicity and composability.

Windows CreateProcess(): One heavy call does everything
    - Creates process
    - Loads executable
    - Sets up environment
    - Starts execution
    → 50+ parameters, complex, inflexible

Unix fork() + exec(): Two simple calls
    fork()  → Creates child (exact copy)
    exec()  → Replaces with new program
    → 2-3 parameters each, composable, flexible

The genius: Between fork() and exec(), the child can: - Redirect stdin/stdout/stderr (pipes, files) - Change working directory - Drop privileges (setuid/setgid) - Set environment variables - Close unwanted file descriptors - All without special parameters to the creation call

items.title: 4.2 Deep Dive: fork() Mechanics
path: Topic 4 (Detailed): Process Creation, Termination & System Calls

items.title: What Actually Happens (Step by Step)
items.text:
PARENT PROCESS                          KERNEL                          CHILD PROCESS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pid_t pid = fork();
         │
         ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 1. Allocate new task_struct (PCB) for child                         │
    │ 2. Copy parent's page tables (mark pages COW)                       │
    │ 3. Copy file descriptor table (reference counts++)                  │
    │ 4. Copy signal handlers, credentials, timers, etc.                  │
    │ 5. Assign new PID                                                   │
    │ 6. Set child's return value = 0                                     │
    │ 7. Set parent's return value = child's PID                          │
    │ 8. Schedule both processes                                          │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
    Returns PID to parent          Returns 0 to child
path: Topic 4 (Detailed): Process Creation, Termination & System Calls

items.title: Copy-on-Write (COW) - The Performance Secret
items.text:
Without COW: fork() copies ALL memory pages → slow, memory-hungry With COW: - Parent and child share physical pages (read-only) - Page table entries marked read-only + COW flag - On first write by either: 1. Page fault triggered 2. Kernel allocates new physical page 3. Copies content 4. Updates page table (writable, private) 5. Resumes instruction

BEFORE WRITE:                    AFTER PARENT WRITES:
┌──────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────┐
│ Parent VA 0x1000 │             │ Parent VA 0x1000 │
│       │          │             │       │          │
│       ▼          │             │       ▼          │
│  ┌────────┐      │             │  ┌────────┐      │
│  │ Page A │◄─────┼────┐        │  │Page A' │      │ (new copy)
│  │ (RO)   │      │    │        │  │ (RW)   │      │
│  └────────┘      │    │        │  └────────┘      │
│       ▲          │    │        │       ▲          │
│       │          │    │        │       │          │
│ Child VA 0x1000  │    │        │ Child VA 0x1000  │ (still original)
│       │          │    │        │       │          │
└───────│──────────┘    │        └───────│──────────┘
        │               │               │
        └───────────────┘               └───────────────
        Shared physical page              Separate pages

Result: fork() is ~1000x faster than full copy; exec() discards COW pages anyway.

items.title: Program 1: Basic fork() + exec() + wait()
items.text:
/*
 * File: fork_exec_wait.c
 * Purpose: Demonstrate the classic fork-exec-wait pattern
 * Compile: gcc -o fork_exec_wait fork_exec_wait.c
 * Run: ./fork_exec_wait
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    printf("=== START: Parent PID = %d ===\n", getpid());

    // FORK: Create child process
    // Returns: 0 in child, child's PID in parent, -1 on error
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        // ERROR HANDLING: fork() failed
        perror("fork failed");  // Prints: "fork failed: Cannot allocate memory"
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (pid == 0) {
        // ========== CHILD PROCESS ==========
        // pid == 0 means we are the child
        printf("[CHILD] PID=%d, PPID=%d\n", getpid(), getppid());

        // EXEC: Replace this process image with a new program
        // execlp() searches PATH for the executable
        // Arguments: (file, arg0, arg1, ..., NULL)
        // arg0 is conventionally the program name
        printf("[CHILD] Calling execlp(\"ls\", \"ls\", \"-l\", NULL)...\n");

        // execlp() only returns if it FAILS
        execlp("ls", "ls", "-l", NULL);

        // If we reach here, execlp() failed
        perror("[CHILD] execlp failed");
        _exit(EXIT_FAILURE);  // Use _exit() to avoid flushing parent's buffers
    } else {
        // ========== PARENT PROCESS ==========
        // pid > 0 means we are the parent, pid = child's PID
        printf("[PARENT] PID=%d, created child PID=%d\n", getpid(), pid);

        // WAIT: Block until child terminates
        // wait(NULL) means we don't care about exit status
        int status;
        pid_t waited_pid = wait(&status);

        if (waited_pid == -1) {
            perror("wait failed");
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        printf("[PARENT] wait() returned: child PID=%d\n", waited_pid);

        // Extract exit status
        if (WIFEXITED(status)) {
            int exit_code = WEXITSTATUS(status);
            printf("[PARENT] Child exited normally with code=%d\n", exit_code);
        } else if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) {
            int sig = WTERMSIG(status);
            printf("[PARENT] Child killed by signal=%d (%s)\n", sig, strsignal(sig));
        }
    }

    printf("=== END: Parent PID = %d ===\n", getpid());
    return 0;
}

Expected Output: 

=== START: Parent PID = 12345 ===
[PARENT] PID=12345, created child PID=12346
[CHILD] PID=12346, PPID=12345
[CHILD] Calling execlp("ls", "ls", "-l", NULL)...
total 8
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 16800 Nov 3 16:40 fork_exec_wait
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user  5432 Nov 3 16:40 fork_exec_wait.c
[PARENT] wait() returned: child PID=12346
[PARENT] Child exited normally with code=0
=== END: Parent PID = 12345 ===

items.title: Program 2: fork() Variable Isolation Demo
items.text:
/*
 * File: fork_variables.c
 * Purpose: Prove that parent and child have INDEPENDENT address spaces
 * Compile: gcc -o fork_variables fork_variables.c
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    int shared_var = 100;  // In parent's memory
    int *heap_var = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *heap_var = 200;

    printf("=== BEFORE fork() ===\n");
    printf("Parent: shared_var=%d (addr=%p), heap_var=%d (addr=%p)\n", 
           shared_var, &shared_var, *heap_var, heap_var);

    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Modify both variables
        shared_var = 999;
        *heap_var = 888;
        printf("[CHILD] After modification: shared_var=%d (addr=%p), heap_var=%d (addr=%p)\n",
               shared_var, &shared_var, *heap_var, heap_var);
        _exit(0);
    } else {
        // PARENT: Wait, then check variables
        wait(NULL);
        printf("=== AFTER fork() (in parent) ===\n");
        printf("Parent: shared_var=%d (addr=%p), heap_var=%d (addr=%p)\n",
               shared_var, &shared_var, *heap_var, heap_var);
        printf("Notice: Parent's values UNCHANGED! Child got its own copy.\n");

        free(heap_var);
    }
    return 0;
}

Output: 

=== BEFORE fork() ===
Parent: shared_var=100 (addr=0x7ffc1234), heap_var=200 (addr=0x55a12345)
[CHILD] After modification: shared_var=999 (addr=0x7ffc1234), heap_var=888 (addr=0x55a12345)
=== AFTER fork() (in parent) ===
Parent: shared_var=100 (addr=0x7ffc1234), heap_var=200 (addr=0x55a12345)
Notice: Parent's values UNCHANGED! Child got its own copy.

Key observation: Same virtual addresses, different physical pages (COW).

items.title: Program 3: vfork() vs fork() - Shared Memory Danger
items.text:
/*
 * File: vfork_danger.c
 * Purpose: Show how vfork() shares memory with parent (DANGEROUS!)
 * Compile: gcc -o vfork_danger vfork_danger.c
 * 
 * WARNING: This program demonstrates UNSAFE behavior!
 * Never use vfork() unless you immediately exec() or _exit()
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    int counter = 0;

    printf("=== Using vfork() ===\n");
    printf("Initial counter = %d\n", counter);

    pid_t pid = vfork();  // CHILD RUNS FIRST, PARENT SUSPENDED

    if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Runs FIRST, shares ALL memory with parent
        printf("[CHILD] Incrementing counter 5 times...\n");
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            counter++;
            printf("[CHILD] counter = %d\n", counter);
        }
        printf("[CHILD] Calling _exit()...\n");
        _exit(0);  // MUST use _exit(), NOT exit()!
    } else {
        // PARENT: Resumes AFTER child calls _exit() or exec()
        wait(NULL);
        printf("[PARENT] After child, counter = %d\n", counter);
        printf("[PARENT] Parent's counter was MODIFIED by child!\n");
    }

    return 0;
}

Output: 

=== Using vfork() ===
Initial counter = 0
[CHILD] Incrementing counter 5 times...
[CHILD] counter = 1
[CHILD] counter = 2
[CHILD] counter = 3
[CHILD] counter = 4
[CHILD] counter = 5
[CHILD] Calling _exit()...
[PARENT] After child, counter = 5
[PARENT] Parent's counter was MODIFIED by child!

Contrast with fork(): 

// Change vfork() to fork() and run again:
// Parent's counter stays 0 (independent copies)

items.title: Program 4: Zombie & Orphan Demonstration
items.text:
/*
 * File: zombie_orphan.c
 * Purpose: Create and observe zombie and orphan processes
 * Compile: gcc -o zombie_orphan zombie_orphan.c
 * 
 * Run in two terminals:
 * Terminal 1: ./zombie_orphan zombie
 * Terminal 2: watch -n 1 'ps aux | grep zombie_orphan'
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

void create_zombie() {
    printf("=== CREATING ZOMBIE ===\n");
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Exit immediately
        printf("[CHILD] PID=%d exiting now...\n", getpid());
        exit(42);  // Exit code 42
    } else {
        // PARENT: Sleep WITHOUT calling wait()
        printf("[PARENT] Sleeping 30s WITHOUT wait()...\n");
        printf("[PARENT] Check 'ps aux' - child will show as <defunct>\n");
        sleep(30);

        // Now reap the zombie
        int status;
        wait(&status);
        printf("[PARENT] Reaped zombie. Exit code: %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status));
    }
}

void create_orphan() {
    printf("\n=== CREATING ORPHAN ===\n");
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Sleep longer than parent
        printf("[CHILD] PID=%d, PPID=%d - sleeping 30s\n", getpid(), getppid());
        sleep(30);
        printf("[CHILD] Woke up! New PPID=%d (adopted by init/systemd)\n", getppid());
        exit(0);
    } else {
        // PARENT: Exit immediately
        printf("[PARENT] PID=%d exiting immediately\n", getpid());
        printf("[PARENT] Child becomes orphan, adopted by PID 1\n");
        exit(0);
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc < 2) {
        printf("Usage: %s [zombie|orphan]\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    if (strcmp(argv[1], "zombie") == 0) {
        create_zombie();
    } else if (strcmp(argv[1], "orphan") == 0) {
        create_orphan();
    }
    return 0;
}

Observe with: 

# Terminal 1:
./zombie_orphan zombie

# Terminal 2 (watch process table):
watch -n 1 'ps aux | grep -E "(zombie_orphan|defunct)"'

Expected ps output: 

# Zombie state (before parent waits):
user  12346  0.0  0.0      0     0 pts/0  Z+   16:45   0:00 [zombie_orphan] <defunct>

# Orphan state (after parent exits):
user  12346  0.0  0.0   1234  456 pts/0  S    16:45   0:00 ./zombie_orphan orphan
# Note PPID = 1 (systemd)

items.title: Program 5: exec() Family Comparison
items.text:
/*
 * File: exec_family.c
 * Purpose: Demonstrate all exec() variants
 * Compile: gcc -o exec_family exec_family.c
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc < 2) {
        printf("Usage: %s <1-6>\n", argv[0]);
        printf("  1: execl  2: execv  3: execle\n");
        printf("  4: execve 5: execlp 6: execvp\n");
        return 1;
    }

    int choice = atoi(argv[1]);
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid == 0) {
        printf("[CHILD] Trying exec variant %d...\n", choice);

        switch (choice) {
            case 1:  // execl - list, no PATH search
                execl("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", NULL);
                break;
            case 2:  // execv - vector, no PATH search
                {
                    char *args[] = {"ls", "-l", NULL};
                    execv("/bin/ls", args);
                }
                break;
            case 3:  // execle - list, custom env
                {
                    char *env[] = {"PATH=/bin:/usr/bin", "TERM=xterm", NULL};
                    execle("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", NULL, env);
                }
                break;
            case 4:  // execve - vector, custom env (THE syscall)
                {
                    char *args[] = {"ls", "-l", NULL};
                    char *env[] = {"PATH=/bin:/usr/bin", NULL};
                    execve("/bin/ls", args, env);
                }
                break;
            case 5:  // execlp - list, PATH search
                execlp("ls", "ls", "-l", NULL);
                break;
            case 6:  // execvp - vector, PATH search
                {
                    char *args[] = {"ls", "-l", NULL};
                    execvp("ls", args);
                }
                break;
        }

        // Only reached on failure
        perror("exec failed");
        _exit(1);
    } else {
        wait(NULL);
        printf("[PARENT] Child finished\n");
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: 4.4 Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them
items.text: Pitfall Wrong Code Correct Code Why Forgetting wait() fork(); // no wait wait(NULL); Creates zombie processes Using exit() in vfork child vfork(); if(pid==0) exit(0); vfork(); if(pid==0) _exit(0); exit() flushes parent's stdio buffers twice Passing stack address to thread int x; pthread_create(..., &x); int *p = malloc(sizeof(int)); pthread_create(..., p); Stack frame destroyed when function returns Not checking fork() return fork(); // no check pid_t pid = fork(); if(pid<0) handle_error(); Silent failures, zombie children Using return in child after exec execl(...); return 0; execl(...); _exit(1); return never reached on success; on failure, use _exit() wait() without status check wait(NULL); int s; wait(&s); if(WIFEXITED(s))... Misses signal termination, core dumps

items.title: Topic 4: Process Creation, Termination & System Calls
items.text: Source: Lecture 5 + Textbook Ch. 3 (Silberschatz §3.4-3.5, Stevens & Rago Ch. 8)

items.title: The Unix Way
items.text:
pid = fork();  // Clone current process!
if (pid == 0) {
    // CHILD: Different program entirely
    exec("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL);  // Replaces memory with new program
} else {
    // PARENT: Continues original program
    wait(NULL);  // Wait for child to finish
}

Stevens & Rago: "The fork() function is the only way a new process is created by an existing process."

items.title: Why This Design?
items.text:
• fork() copies everything (with Copy-on-Write optimization)
  • exec() loads new program
  • Separation allows: setup pipes, change directories, drop privileges before loading new program

items.title: fork() Semantics
items.text: Context Return Child 0 Parent Child's PID (>0) Error -1

items.title: Copy-on-Write (COW)
items.text:
• Parent and child share physical pages read-only initially
  • When either writes → page is duplicated (page fault → kernel copies page)
  • Makes fork() fast; exec() discards COW pages anyway

items.title: 4.2 Complete fork() + exec() + wait() Program
items.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Fork Failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    else if (pid == 0) {
        // CHILD: Execute new program
        execlp("/bin/ls", "ls", NULL);
    }
    else {
        // PARENT: Wait for child
        wait(NULL);
        printf("Child Complete\n");
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: 4.3 exec() Family
items.text:
Function Arguments Environment PATH Search execl(path, arg0, ..., NULL) List Inherited No execv(path, argv[]) Vector Inherited No execle(path, arg0, ..., NULL, envp[]) List Custom No execve(path, argv[], envp[]) Vector Custom TRUE SYSCALL execlp(file, arg0, ..., NULL) List Inherited Yes execvp(file, argv[]) Vector Inherited Yes fexecve(fd, argv[], envp[]) Vector Custom From fd

Mnemonic: l=list, v=vector, p=PATH search, e=environment, f=file descriptor

items.title: Normal Termination (5 ways)
items.text:
1. return from main()
  2. exit() — flushes buffers, runs atexit handlers
  3. _exit() / _Exit() — direct kernel call, no cleanup
  4. Last thread returns from start routine
  5. pthread_exit() from last thread

items.title: Abnormal Termination (3 ways)
items.text:
1. abort() → SIGABRT
  2. Signals: SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, SIGFPE
  3. Last thread responds to cancellation

items.title: 4.4 Zombie vs Orphan Processes
items.text:
Zombie Orphan Cause Child exited, parent hasn't wait() Parent exited before child State Dead but PID+status in process table Alive, no parent Resolution Parent calls wait() → reaped Re-parented to init/systemd (PID 1) In ps <defunct> Normal process

Stevens & Rago: "A process that has terminated, but whose parent has not yet waited for it, is called a zombie."

items.title: Lab Patterns (from your prep file)
items.text:
Zombie (zombie.c): 

// Child: exit(0) immediately
// Parent: sleep(50) WITHOUT wait()
// Child stays as <defunct> for 50 seconds

Orphan (orphan.c): 

// Parent: exit(0) immediately
// Child: sleep(30)
// Child adopted by init/systemd (PID 1)

items.title: 4.5 wait() & waitpid()
items.text:
#include <sys/wait.h>

pid_t wait(int *statloc);           // Blocks until ANY child terminates
pid_t waitpid(pid_t pid, int *statloc, int options);
pid value Meaning > 0 Wait for specific child PID -1 Wait for any child (like wait()) 0 Wait for any child in same process group < -1 Wait for any child in process group \|pid\|

Options: WNOHANG = non-blocking (returns 0 if no child terminated)

items.title: Extracting Exit Status
items.text:
wait(&status);
int child_code = WEXITSTATUS(status);  // Gets 0-255 from child's exit()

items.title: 4.6 Race Conditions Post-fork()
items.text:
// After fork(), parent and child run CONCURRENTLY
// NEVER assume which runs first!

// FLAWED POLLING (never do this):
while (getppid() != 1) {  // Wait for reparenting to init
    sleep(1);  // Wastes CPU, induces latency
}

items.title: 4.7 I/O Request Life Cycle (I/O-Bound Process)
items.text:
1. Running: Process executes until I/O syscall (read/write)
2. Blocked: OS moves process to Waiting/Blocked queue
3. Preemption: CPU reassigned to another ready process
4. Device Servicing: Controller transfers data asynchronously
5. Interrupt: Device signals completion via hardware interrupt
6. Ready: OS moves process from Waiting → Ready queue
7. Resume: Scheduler dispatches process back to CPU

items.title: 4.8 Key Takeaways (Memorize)
items.text:
1. fork() = creates child (COW), returns 0 to child, PID to parent, -1 on error
  2. exec() = replaces process image with new program; never returns on success
  3. wait()/waitpid() = reap zombies, get exit status via WEXITSTATUS
  4. Zombie = child dead, parent hasn't waited; Orphan = parent dead, child reparented to init
  5. COW = pages shared read-only until write → then duplicated
  6. Never assume parent/child execution order post-fork()
  7. Normal exit: return/exit()/_exit(); Abnormal: signals/abort()

items.title: 4.9 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer fork() returns what in child? 0 fork() returns what in parent? Child's PID (>0) What does successful exec() do? Never returns; overwrites process image Zombie cause? Child exited, parent didn't wait() Orphan cause? Parent exited before child Orphan resolution? Re-parented to init/systemd (PID 1) WEXITSTATUS(status) extracts? 8-bit exit code (0-255) from child COW = ? Copy-on-Write: share pages read-only until write _exit() vs exit()? _exit() = no cleanup, direct kernel call

items.title: 4.10 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns (from prep file)
items.text:
• Q1: fork() with int y=0 — parent y=-1, child y=+1 (independent copies)
  • Q2: vfork() — child runs FIRST, increments y 0→5, parent decrements 5→0 (shared memory)
  • Q3: wait(&status) + WEXITSTATUS extracts exit code (0-255)
  • Q4: Multi-level fork hierarchy — bottom-up: Grandchild → Child → Parent
  • Q5: Successful execl() — code after exec never executes
  • Q6: Parent exits first → child becomes orphan → adopted by init (PID 1)
  • Q7: Child exits, parent sleeps without wait → child = zombie (<defunct>)
  • Q8: No synchronization → output interleaves non-deterministically (OS scheduler)

items.title: When Does Scheduling Occur?
items.text:
Trigger Scheduler Called? Preemptive? Process created Yes No (new process) Process exits Yes No I/O request (block) Yes No (voluntary) I/O completion (unblock) Yes Yes Timer interrupt (time slice) Yes Yes Higher priority process arrives Yes Yes

Non-preemptive decisions: Process switches only when it voluntarily gives up CPU (blocks or terminates). Preemptive decisions: OS can forcibly take CPU away.

items.title: 5.2 Scheduling Metrics (Must Memorize Formulas)
items.text:
Timeline for Process P:
Arrival ──────────────────────────────► Completion
   │                                      │
   ▼                                      ▼
Start (first CPU)                     End (last CPU)
   │                                      │
   └────── Response Time ────────────────┘

   └──────────────── Turnaround Time ───────────────┘

   └── Wait 1 ──┘  Running  └── Wait 2 ──┘  Running
   └────────────── Waiting Time ───────────────────┘
Metric Formula What It Measures Turnaround Time (TAT) Completion - Arrival Total time in system Waiting Time (WT) TAT - Burst Time Time spent ready but not running Response Time (RT) First Run - Arrival Time to first response (interactive) CPU Utilization Busy Time / Total Time Keep CPU busy Throughput Processes Completed / Time Maximize jobs done

Relationship: WT = TAT - BT (for non-preemptive, or sum of wait periods for preemptive)

items.title: Example with Arrival Times
items.text:
Process Arrival Burst P1 0 8 P2 1 4 P3 2 9 P4 3 5

Step-by-Step Trace:

t=0: P1 arrives (rem=8). Only P1 ready. RUN P1.
t=1: P2 arrives (rem=4). 4 < 7 (P1's rem). PREEMPT P1, RUN P2.
t=2: P3 arrives (rem=9). 9 > 3 (P2's rem). P2 continues.
t=3: P4 arrives (rem=5). 5 > 2 (P2's rem). P2 continues.
t=5: P2 completes. Ready: P1(rem=7), P3(9), P4(5). RUN P4 (shortest=5).
t=10: P4 completes. Ready: P1(7), P3(9). RUN P1.
t=17: P1 completes. RUN P3.
t=26: P3 completes.

Gantt: 

Time: 0  1  5  10  17  26

      ▼  ▼  ▼   ▼   ▼   ▼
┌────┬──┬────┬────┬────┐
│ P1 │P2│ P4 │ P1 │ P3 │
│ 0-1│1-5│5-10│10-17│17-26
└────┴──┴────┴────┴────┘

Calculations: | Process | Arrival | Burst | Completion | TAT = C-A | WT = TAT-BT | |---------|---------|-------|------------|-----------|-------------| | P1 | 0 | 8 | 17 | 17 | 9 | | P2 | 1 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 0 | | P3 | 2 | 9 | 26 | 24 | 15 | | P4 | 3 | 5 | 10 | 7 | 2 | | Avg | | | | 13.0 | 6.5 |

items.title: Priority Inversion Problem
items.text:
High-priority H needs mutex held by Low-priority L
    H blocks
Medium-priority M runs (preempts L)
    L can't release mutex
    H blocked by M indirectly!
Fix: Priority Inheritance (L temporarily inherits H's priority).

items.title: 5.8 Complete Calculation Program
items.text:
/*
 * File: scheduling_calc.c
 * Purpose: Calculate FCFS, SJF, SRTF, RR, Priority metrics
 * Compile: gcc -o scheduling_calc scheduling_calc.c -lm
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#define MAX_PROCESSES 100

typedef struct {
    int pid;
    int arrival;
    int burst;
    int priority;
    int remaining;
    int completion;
    int tat;
    int wt;
    int rt;
    int started;
} Process;

void print_gantt(Process p[], int n, int quantum) {
    printf("\nGantt Chart (time quantum = %d):\n", quantum);
    // Simplified - real implementation would track execution segments
}

void calculate_metrics(Process p[], int n) {
    float avg_tat = 0, avg_wt = 0, avg_rt = 0;
    printf("\n%-5s %-10s %-10s %-12s %-10s %-10s %-10s\n",
           "PID", "Arrival", "Burst", "Completion", "TAT", "WT", "RT");
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        p[i].tat = p[i].completion - p[i].arrival;
        p[i].wt = p[i].tat - p[i].burst;
        avg_tat += p[i].tat;
        avg_wt += p[i].wt;
        avg_rt += p[i].rt;
        printf("%-5d %-10d %-10d %-12d %-10d %-10d %-10d\n",
               p[i].pid, p[i].arrival, p[i].burst,
               p[i].completion, p[i].tat, p[i].wt, p[i].rt);
    }
    printf("Average: TAT=%.2f, WT=%.2f, RT=%.2f\n",
           avg_tat/n, avg_wt/n, avg_rt/n);
}

/* FCFS Implementation */
void fcfs(Process p[], int n) {
    // Sort by arrival, then by original order
    for (int i = 0; i < n-1; i++) {
        for (int j = i+1; j < n; j++) {
            if (p[i].arrival > p[j].arrival ||
                (p[i].arrival == p[j].arrival && p[i].pid > p[j].pid)) {
                Process tmp = p[i]; p[i] = p[j]; p[j] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }

    int time = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (time < p[i].arrival) time = p[i].arrival;
        p[i].rt = time - p[i].arrival;
        time += p[i].burst;
        p[i].completion = time;
    }
    printf("\n=== FCFS ===\n");
    calculate_metrics(p, n);
}

/* SJF Non-Preemptive */
void sjf_np(Process p[], int n) {
    int completed = 0, time = 0;
    int done[MAX_PROCESSES] = {0};

    while (completed < n) {
        int shortest = -1;
        int min_burst = 999999;

        // Find shortest job among arrived processes
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (!done[i] && p[i].arrival <= time && p[i].burst < min_burst) {
                min_burst = p[i].burst;
                shortest = i;
            }
        }

        if (shortest == -1) {
            time++; // No job ready, advance time
            continue;
        }

        if (time < p[shortest].arrival) time = p[shortest].arrival;
        p[shortest].rt = time - p[shortest].arrival;
        time += p[shortest].burst;
        p[shortest].completion = time;
        done[shortest] = 1;
        completed++;
    }
    printf("\n=== SJF (Non-Preemptive) ===\n");
    calculate_metrics(p, n);
}

/* SRTF Preemptive */
void srtf(Process p[], int n) {
    // Reset remaining times
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        p[i].remaining = p[i].burst;
        p[i].started = 0;
        p[i].completion = 0;
    }

    int time = 0, completed = 0;

    while (completed < n) {
        int shortest = -1;
        int min_rem = 999999;

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (p[i].remaining > 0 && p[i].arrival <= time && p[i].remaining < min_rem) {
                min_rem = p[i].remaining;
                shortest = i;
            }
        }

        if (shortest == -1) {
            time++;
            continue;
        }

        if (!p[shortest].started) {
            p[shortest].rt = time - p[shortest].arrival;
            p[shortest].started = 1;
        }

        p[shortest].remaining--;
        time++;

        if (p[shortest].remaining == 0) {
            p[shortest].completion = time;
            completed++;
        }
    }
    printf("\n=== SRTF (Preemptive SJF) ===\n");
    calculate_metrics(p, n);
}

/* Round Robin */
void rr(Process p[], int n, int quantum) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        p[i].remaining = p[i].burst;
        p[i].started = 0;
        p[i].completion = 0;
    }

    int time = 0, completed = 0;
    int queue[MAX_PROCESSES];
    int front = 0, rear = 0;
    int in_queue[MAX_PROCESSES] = {0};

    // Initial queue by arrival
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (p[i].arrival == 0) {
            queue[rear++] = i;
            in_queue[i] = 1;
        }
    }

    while (completed < n) {
        // Add newly arrived
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (p[i].arrival == time && !in_queue[i] && p[i].remaining > 0) {
                queue[rear++] = i;
                in_queue[i] = 1;
            }
        }

        if (front == rear) {
            time++;
            continue;
        }

        int idx = queue[front++];
        if (!p[idx].started) {
            p[idx].rt = time - p[idx].arrival;
            p[idx].started = 1;
        }

        int exec = (p[idx].remaining < quantum) ? p[idx].remaining : quantum;
        p[idx].remaining -= exec;
        time += exec;

        // Add arrivals during execution
        for (int t = time - exec + 1; t <= time; t++) {
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                if (p[i].arrival == t && !in_queue[i] && p[i].remaining > 0) {
                    queue[rear++] = i;
                    in_queue[i] = 1;
                }
            }
        }

        if (p[idx].remaining > 0) {
            queue[rear++] = idx; // Re-queue
        } else {
            p[idx].completion = time;
            completed++;
        }
    }
    printf("\n=== Round Robin (q=%d) ===\n", quantum);
    calculate_metrics(p, n);
}

int main() {
    // Example: P1(0,24), P2(0,3), P3(0,3)
    Process processes[] = {
        {1, 0, 24, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0},
        {2, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0},
        {3, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0},
    };
    int n = 3;

    // Make copies for each algorithm
    Process p_fcfs[MAX_PROCESSES], p_sjf[MAX_PROCESSES];
    Process p_srtf[MAX_PROCESSES], p_rr[MAX_PROCESSES];

    memcpy(p_fcfs, processes, n * sizeof(Process));
    memcpy(p_sjf, processes, n * sizeof(Process));
    memcpy(p_srtf, processes, n * sizeof(Process));
    memcpy(p_rr, processes, n * sizeof(Process));

    fcfs(p_fcfs, n);
    sjf_np(p_sjf, n);
    srtf(p_srtf, n);
    rr(p_rr, n, 4);

    return 0;
}

Run it: 

gcc -o scheduling_calc scheduling_calc.c -lm
./scheduling_calc

items.title: Topic 5: CPU Scheduling — FCFS & SJF
items.text: Source: Lecture 7 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5, Stallings Ch. 9, Stevens & Rago Ch. 9)

items.title: Why Scheduling?
items.text:
• Single CPU core → only one process executes at a time
  • Others wait in ready queue
  • Goal: Keep CPU busy at all times (maximize utilization)
  • When process waits for I/O → scheduler switches to another ready process

items.title: CPU-I/O Burst Cycle
items.text:
CPU burst → I/O burst → CPU burst → I/O burst → ...
- CPU burst distribution drives scheduling algorithm design - I/O-bound: many short CPU bursts - CPU-bound: few long CPU bursts

items.title: 5.2 Scheduler & Dispatcher
items.text: Component Role Short-term scheduler Picks next process from ready queue Dispatcher Context switch, mode change, jump to user code Dispatch latency Time to stop one process, start another

items.title: Four Decision Points
items.text: # Transition Non-Preemptive Preemptive 1 Running → Waiting (I/O) ✅ ✅ 2 Running → Ready (interrupt) ❌ ✅ 3 Waiting → Ready (I/O done) ❌ ✅ 4 Running → Terminated ✅ ✅ Type Description Non-Preemptive Process keeps CPU until it voluntarily releases (I/O or terminate) Preemptive OS can forcibly preempt on timer interrupt or higher-priority arrival

items.title: 5.4 Scheduling Criteria (Metrics)
items.text: Metric Formula Goal Turnaround Time (TAT) Completion - Arrival Minimize Waiting Time (WT) TAT - Burst = Completion - Arrival - Burst Minimize Response Time (RT) First Start - Arrival Minimize CPU Utilization % time CPU busy Maximize Throughput Processes completed / time Maximize

items.title: 5.5 First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
items.text:
• Algorithm: FIFO ready queue, non-preemptive
  • Simple but suffers Convoy Effect

items.title: Example 1: P1(24), P2(3), P3(3) at t=0
Example 2: P2(3), P3(3), P1(24) at t=0
Convoy Effect
items.text: Short I/O-bound processes stuck behind long CPU-bound process → poor CPU & device utilization.

items.title: 5.6 Shortest-Job-First (SJF) — Non-Preemptive
items.text:
• Algorithm: Pick process with smallest next CPU burst
  • Tie-breaker: FCFS
  • Provably optimal for minimum average waiting time (stationary processes)

items.title: Example: All arrive at t=0
items.text:
Process Burst P1 6 P2 8 P3 7 P4 3

Order: P4(3) → P1(6) → P3(7) → P2(8) 

Gantt: | P4 | P1 | P3 | P2 |
       0    3    9   16   24

Wait: P4=0, P1=3, P3=9, P2=16 → Avg = 7.0
vs FCFS (P1,P2,P3,P4): Avg = 10.25

items.title: 5.7 Shortest-Remaining-Time-First (SRTF) — Preemptive SJF
items.text: • Preempt if new arrival has shorter remaining burst than current

items.title: Example with Arrival Times
items.text:
Process Arrival Burst P1 0 8 P2 1 4 P3 2 9 P4 3 5

Timeline: 

t=0: P1 starts (rem=8)
t=1: P2 arrives (4 < 7) → preempt P1, run P2
t=2: P3 arrives (9 > 3) → P2 continues
t=3: P4 arrives (5 > 2) → P2 continues
t=5: P2 done. Ready: P1(7), P3(9), P4(5) → run P4
t=10: P4 done. Ready: P1(7), P3(9) → run P1
t=17: P1 done. Run P3
t=26: P3 done.

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P4 | P1 | P3 |
       0    1    5   10   17   26

Waiting Times: | Process | Completion | Arrival | Burst | WT = CT - AT - BT | |---------|------------|---------|-------|-------------------| | P1 | 17 | 0 | 8 | 9 | | P2 | 5 | 1 | 4 | 0 | | P3 | 26 | 2 | 9 | 15 | | P4 | 10 | 3 | 5 | 2 | | Avg | | | | 6.5 |

items.title: 5.8 Key Formulas (Memorize)
items.text: Metric Formula Turnaround Time Completion - Arrival Waiting Time Turnaround - Burst = Completion - Arrival - Burst Response Time First Start - Arrival Avg Waiting Σ Wait_i / n RR Max Wait Bound (n - 1) × q

items.title: 5.9 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer FCFS convoy effect? Short processes wait behind long CPU-bound process SJF optimality? Minimum average waiting time for non-preemptive SRTF vs SJF? SRTF = preemptive SJF; can preempt on new arrival FCFS preemptive? No SRTF preemptive? Yes SRTF avg wait vs SJF? SRTF ≤ SJF (always better or equal)

items.title: 5.10 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns (from prep file)
items.text:
• Q22: FCFS convoy effect — short processes wait behind long job
  • Q23: SJF optimal — minimum average waiting time
  • Q24: SJF starvation → fix with Aging
  • Q25: SRTF provides absolute minimal average waiting time
  • Q26: SRTF numerical — P1(0,8), P2(1,4), P3(2,2), P4(3,1) → CT of P1 = 15
  • Q27: FCFS turnaround calc — AT 0,1,2 with BT 4,3,1 → Avg TAT = 5.33

items.title: 5.11 Practice: Trace These By Hand
items.text:
1. FCFS: P1(0,10), P2(1,5), P3(2,8) → Gantt + Avg WT/TAT
  2. SJF: P1(0,7), P2(0,4), P3(0,1), P4(0,4) → Order + Avg WT
  3. SRTF: P1(0,8), P2(1,4), P3(2,9), P4(3,5) → Full trace (from slides)

items.title: Topic 6: CPU Scheduling — Priority & Round Robin
items.text: Source: Lecture 8 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5, Stallings Ch. 9)

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Each process has an integer priority
  • CPU → highest priority process
  • Conventions:
  • Silberschatz: Smaller integer = Higher priority (1 = highest)
  • Some systems: Larger integer = Higher priority
  • Always verify convention in problem

items.title: Modes
items.text: Mode Behavior Non-Preemptive Once CPU given, runs to completion (or I/O) Preemptive New arrival with higher priority preempts current

items.title: Relationship with SJF
items.text: • SJF = special case of Priority where priority = 1 / predicted burst time

items.title: Major Problem: Starvation
items.text:
• Low-priority process waits indefinitely if high-priority stream continues
  • Real case: MIT's IBM 7094 (1973) — low-priority job from 1967 still waiting!

items.title: Solution: Aging
items.text:
• Gradually increase priority of waiting processes (e.g., +1 every 15 min)
  • Eventually gets high enough priority to execute

items.title: Example 1: Non-Preemptive (Smaller = Higher Priority)
items.text:
Process Burst Priority P1 10 3 P2 1 1 (Highest) P3 2 4 P4 1 5 (Lowest) P5 5 2

Order: P2 → P5 → P1 → P3 → P4 

Gantt: | P2 | P5 | P1 | P3 | P4 |
       0    1    6   16   18   19

Wait: P1=6, P2=0, P3=16, P4=18, P5=1 → Avg = 8.2

items.title: Example 2: Preemptive (Larger = Higher Priority)
items.text:
Process Arrival Burst Priority P1 0 4 2 P2 1 3 3 P3 2 1 4 P4 3 5 5 (Highest) P5 4 2 5 (Highest)

Timeline: 

t=0: P1 starts (pri 2)
t=1: P2 arrives (pri 3 > 2) → preempt P1, run P2
t=2: P3 arrives (pri 4 > 3) → preempt P2, run P3
t=3: P3 done. P4 arrives (pri 5) → run P4
t=4: P5 arrives (pri 5 = P4) → FCFS keeps P4
t=8: P4 done. P5 (pri 5) runs 8-10
t=10: P5 done. Ready: P2(pri 3, rem 2), P1(pri 2, rem 3) → P2 runs 10-12
t=12: P2 done. P1 runs 12-15
t=15: P1 done.

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 | P5 | P2 | P1 |
       0    1    2    3    8   10   12   15

Waiting Times: | Process | CT | AT | BT | WT = CT - AT - BT | |---------|-----|-----|-----|-------------------| | P1 | 15 | 0 | 4 | 11 | | P2 | 12 | 1 | 3 | 8 | | P3 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | | P4 | 8 | 3 | 5 | 0 | | P5 | 10 | 4 | 2 | 4 | | Avg | | | | 4.6 |

items.title: Principles
items.text:
• Preemptive, based on FCFS
  • Time Quantum (q): 10-100ms typical
  • Ready queue = circular FIFO
  • Process runs ≤ q; if not done → preempted → appended to tail

items.title: Example: q=4, P1(24), P2(3), P3(3) at t=0
items.text:
t=0:  P1 runs 4ms (rem=20) → tail
t=4:  P2 runs 3ms (done) → terminates at 7
t=7:  P3 runs 3ms (done) → terminates at 10
t=10: Only P1 remains → runs in 4ms quanta until done at 30

Gantt: | P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 | P1 | P1 | P1 | P1 |
       0    4    7   10   14   18   22   26   30

Waiting Times: - P1: Runs [0-4], waits [4-10], runs to finish → Wait = 6 - P2: Waits [0-4] → Wait = 4 - P3: Waits [0-7] → Wait = 7 - Avg WT = 5.66

items.title: Time Quantum Trade-offs
items.text: Quantum Size Behavior q → ∞ Degenerates to FCFS q → 0 Approaches processor sharing (each gets 1/n speed) but context-switch overhead dominates

items.title: Maximum Waiting Bound
items.text:
If n processes in ready queue, time quantum = q:
No process waits longer than (n - 1) × q time units

items.title: Rule of Thumb (Silberschatz)
items.text: ~80% of CPU bursts should complete within one quantum

items.title: 6.5 Quick Comparison Table
items.text: Algorithm Preemptive? Starvation? Best For FCFS No No Simple batch SJF No Yes (long jobs) Minimum wait SRTF Yes Yes (long jobs) Responsive batch Priority Both Yes (fix: aging) Importance-based RR Yes No Time-sharing MLFQ Yes No (with aging) General purpose

items.title: 6.6 Quick Self-Test
items.text: Question Answer Priority convention (Silberschatz)? Smaller integer = higher priority SJF is special case of? Priority scheduling (priority = 1/burst) Priority starvation fix? Aging (gradually boost waiting process priority) RR quantum → ∞? Becomes FCFS RR quantum → 0? Processor sharing but context-switch overhead kills performance RR max wait bound? (n - 1) × q RR quantum guideline? 80% of bursts complete within one quantum

items.title: 6.7 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns (from prep file)
items.text:
• Q28: RR quantum → ∞ → degenerates to FCFS
  • Q29: 80% rule for quantum selection
  • Q30: Priority inversion — high blocked on low, medium runs → fix: Priority Inheritance
