items.title: Topic 7: CPU Scheduling — Multilevel Queue & Multilevel Feedback Queue
items.text: Source: Lecture 10 + Textbook Ch. 4 (Silberschatz Ch. 5)

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
• Processes can be classified into distinct groups with different response-time requirements
  • Single ready queue is inadequate

items.title: Common Partitioning
items.text: Queue Type Processes Scheduling Foreground Interactive (low response time) Round-Robin Background Batch jobs (throughput priority) FCFS

items.title: Permanent Assignment
items.text:
• Processes permanently assigned to one queue at creation
  • Based on: memory size, process priority, process type

items.title: Inter-Queue Scheduling Policies
items.text: Policy Behavior Fixed-Priority Preemptive Higher queues must empty first; lower queues starve if higher busy Time-Sliced Each queue gets CPU fraction (e.g., 80% foreground, 20% background)

items.title: Core Innovation
items.text:
• Unlike MLQ, processes migrate between queues dynamically
  • Adapts to runtime CPU-burst characteristics
  • Implements Aging to prevent starvation

items.title: Defining Parameters (5)
items.text:
1. Number of queues
  2. Scheduling algorithm per queue
  3. Promotion (upgrade) method
  4. Demotion (downgrade) method
  5. Initial queue for new processes

items.title: Execution & Demotion Rules
items.text:
1. Q0 (RR, q=8): New process enters; if uses full 8ms → demoted to Q1
  2. Q1 (RR, q=16): Runs only when Q0 empty; if uses full 16ms → demoted to Q2
  3. Q2 (FCFS): Runs only when Q0 & Q1 empty
  4. Preemption: Q0 arrival preempts Q1/Q2; Q1 arrival preempts Q2

items.title: Promotion (Aging) Policy
items.text:
• If process waits too long in Q2 without CPU → promoted to Q1 or Q0
  • Guarantees long-running jobs eventually make progress

items.title: 7.3 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. MLQ: Fixed queues, no migration → starvation risk in lower queues
  2. MLFQ: Dynamic migration → learns process behavior (I/O-bound stay high, CPU-bound sink low)
  3. Aging: Prevents starvation by promoting long-waiting processes
  4. Modern OS: Linux CFS, Windows, macOS use MLFQ variants

items.title: 7.4 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q31: MLQ rigidity — processes permanently assigned, cannot migrate
  • Q32: MLFQ demotion — CPU-bound processes use full quantum → demoted; I/O-bound release early → stay high

items.title: Execution & Demotion Rules
items.text:
1. Q0 (RR, q=8): New process enters; if uses full 8ms → demoted to Q1
  2. Q1 (RR, q=16): Runs only when Q0 empty; if uses full 16ms → demoted to Q2
  3. Q2 (FCFS): Runs only when Q0 & Q1 empty
  4. Preemption: Q0 arrival preempts Q1/Q2; Q1 arrival preempts Q2
path: Topic 7 (Detailed): CPU Scheduling — Multilevel Queue & Multilevel Feedback Queue

items.title: Promotion (Aging) Policy
items.text:
• If process waits too long in Q2 without CPU → promoted to Q1 or Q0
  • Guarantees long-running jobs eventually make progress
path: Topic 7 (Detailed): CPU Scheduling — Multilevel Queue & Multilevel Feedback Queue

items.title: 7.3 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. MLQ: Fixed queues, no migration → starvation risk in lower queues
  2. MLFQ: Dynamic migration → learns process behavior (I/O-bound stay high, CPU-bound sink low)
  3. Aging: Prevents starvation by promoting long-waiting processes
  4. Modern OS: Linux CFS, Windows, macOS use MLFQ variants
path: Topic 7 (Detailed): CPU Scheduling — Multilevel Queue & Multilevel Feedback Queue

items.title: 7.4 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q31: MLQ rigidity — processes permanently assigned, cannot migrate
  • Q32: MLFQ demotion — CPU-bound processes use full quantum → demoted; I/O-bound release early → stay high

items.title: Topic 8: Shell Programming & Cron Scheduling
items.text: Source: Lecture 11 + Textbook Ch. 10 (Stevens & Rago Ch. 9-10)

items.title: Definition & Role
items.text:
[ User / Terminal ] ↔ [ Shell Interpreter ] ↔ [ OS Kernel ] ↔ [ Hardware ]
- Command-line interpreter (CLI) — reads commands, parses, resolves executables, requests kernel to spawn processes - Also a programming language (variables, conditionals, loops, functions)

items.title: Command Syntax & Parsing
items.text:
command [options] [arguments]
- Tokenizes into: command name, flags/options, target arguments - Path resolution: - Absolute/relative path (./script, /bin/ls) → direct access - Name only (ls) → searches $PATH directories left-to-right

items.title: Common Shells
items.text:
Shell Origin Notes sh Stephen Bourne, AT&T Bell Labs Original Bourne shell csh/tcsh Bill Joy, UC Berkeley C-like syntax ksh David Korn Combines Bourne + C shell features bash GNU Project Default on modern Linux 
echo $SHELL  # Shows active login shell

items.title: Scope & Inheritance
items.text: Property Shell Variables Environment Variables Scope Current shell only Current shell + all children Inheritance ❌ Not inherited ✅ Auto-inherited by children Naming Any case Convention: UPPERCASE Use case Local/ephemeral state Global configuration

items.title: Standard Environment Variables
items.text: Variable Purpose SHELL Active interpreter path (/bin/bash) TERM Terminal type (xterm-256color) USER Current username PWD Current working directory OLDPWD Previous directory (enables cd -) PATH Colon-separated executable search paths

items.title: Bash-Specific Variables
items.text:
• BASHOPTS — Active options (comma-separated)
  • BASH_VERSION — Version string
  • BASH_VERSINFO — Array [major, minor, patch]

items.title: 8.3 Variable Operations
items.text:
# Define & access (shell variable)
MY_VAR="Hello world"
echo $MY_VAR

# Export to environment (inherited by children)
export MY_VAR="Hello world"
# or
export MY_VAR

# Unset
unset MY_VAR

# Persistent: add to ~/.profile or ~/.bashrc
export PATH="$HOME/my_tools/bin:$PATH"

items.title: Subshell Inheritance Demo
items.text:
MY_VAR="Hello"
bash              # Spawn child subshell
echo $MY_VAR      # Empty! Child has no access to parent's local variable.
exit              # Return to parent

export MY_VAR="Hello"
bash
echo $MY_VAR      # Prints: Hello world (successfully inherited!)
exit

items.title: Conditional: if-elif-else
items.text:
if [ -f welcome.txt ]; then
    echo "File exists"
else
    echo "File does not exist"
fi

Common File Tests: | Test | Meaning | |------|---------| | -f | Regular file exists | | -d | Directory exists | | -r | Readable | | -w | Writable | | -x | Executable |

items.title: Loops: for
items.text:
# Single loop
for i in {1..5}; do
    echo "i = $i"
done

# Nested loop
for i in {1..5}; do
    for j in {1..3}; do
        echo "i = $i and j = $j"
    done
done

items.title: Loop Control
items.text:
Statement Effect continue Skip rest of current iteration → next iteration break Exit loop entirely → statement after loop 
# continue example (skips i=3)
for i in {1..5}; do
    if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then continue; fi
    for j in {1..3}; do
        echo "i = $i and j = $j"
    done
done

# break example (exits at i=3)
for i in {1..5}; do
    if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then break; fi
    for j in {1..3}; do
        echo "i = $i and j = $j"
    done
done

items.title: Overview
items.text:
• Daemon: crond / cron.service — background job scheduler
  • Auto-starts at boot via systemd
  • Executes tasks at scheduled times
sudo systemctl status cron.service  # Check status

items.title: Crontab Management
items.text: Command Action crontab -l List current user's jobs crontab -e Edit crontab (opens in $EDITOR) crontab -r Remove all jobs for current user

items.title: Crontab Syntax (5 Fields)
items.text:
* * * * *  command_to_execute
│ │ │ └─── Day of Week (0-6) (0=Sun)
│ │ └───── Month (1-12)
│ └─────── Day of Month (1-31)
└───────── Hour (0-23)
          Minute (0-59)

items.title: Practical Examples
items.text: Expression Meaning 5 0 * 8 * 00:05 every day in August 5 4 * * 6 04:05 every Saturday 0 22 * * 1-5 22:00 Mon-Fri (weekdays) */1 * * * * Every minute

items.title: Example with Output Redirection
items.text:
# In crontab -e:
*/1 * * * * /bin/bash $HOME/OS/hello.exe &> $HOME/OS/cron_output.log
- &> redirects both stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2) to log file

items.title: Verification
items.text:
tail -f /var/log/syslog
# Shows:
# Jan 24 08:40:01 host CRON[2935]: (user) CMD (/bin/bash $HOME/OS/hello.exe &> $HOME/OS/cron_output.log)

items.title: 8.6 Standard Library Helpers: popen() / pclose()
items.text:
#include <stdio.h>
FILE *popen(const char *cmdstring, const char *type);  // type: "r" or "w"
int pclose(FILE *fp);

Automates: pipe creation, fork, fd redirection, shell exec, cleanup

// Read output of command
FILE *fp = popen("ls -la", "r");
while (fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), fp)) printf("%s", buf);
pclose(fp);  // wait()s for child, returns exit status

// Write input to command
FILE *fp = popen("sort", "w");
fprintf(fp, "delta\nalpha\nepsilon\n");
pclose(fp);

items.title: 8.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• Shell = CLI interpreter between user and kernel
  • Variables: Shell (local) vs Environment (exported, inherited)
  • Control flow: if, for, continue, break — standard scripting
  • Cron = time-based job scheduler daemon
  • Crontab: 5-field syntax + command; manage with -l, -e, -r
  • Logging: Check /var/log/syslog for execution verification
  • popen/pclose = easy "run command, get output" wrapper

items.title: 8.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q33: Crontab 30 2 * * 1 → 02:30 AM every Monday
  • Q34: Bash shell execution flow — fork() → exec*() in child → wait() in parent
  • Q35: Mobile OS lifecycle — Android kills background processes by importance hierarchy

items.title: 9.1 Why IPC?
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Process Types
items.text: Type Description Independent Cannot affect/be affected by others; shares no data Cooperating Can affect/be affected; shares data, memory, messages
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Reasons for Cooperation
items.text:
1. Information Sharing — Concurrent access to shared resources (files, DBs)
  2. Computation Speedup — Parallel subtasks across CPU cores
  3. Modularity — Divide OS/apps into cooperating processes (client-server, microservices)
  4. Convenience — User running concurrent tasks
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.2 Two Fundamental Models
items.text: Aspect Shared Memory Message Passing Mechanism OS maps shared region into both address spaces send()/receive() via kernel Speed Fastest (memory speed, no kernel copies) Slower (user→kernel→user copies) Sync Manual (semaphores, mutexes) Built into send/receive Best For Large data, same machine Distributed systems, small data
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Architectural Comparison
items.text:
SHARED MEMORY                    MESSAGE PASSING
Process A    Process B            Process A    Process B
    │           │                    │           │
    ▼           ▼                    ▼           ▼
┌───────────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────────┐
│    SHARED MEMORY      │      │       OS KERNEL       │
│    [ Data Buffer ]    │      │  [M1] [M2] [M3] Queue │
└───────────────────────┘      └───────────────────────┘
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.3 Shared Memory Model
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• OS establishes shared region mapped into both address spaces
  • Subsequent reads/writes at memory speed in user mode — no OS intervention
  • Fastest IPC
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Challenges
items.text:
• Synchronization — If writer writes while reader reads → corruption
  • Must use: POSIX Semaphores, Mutex Locks, File/Record Locking
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Linux Memory Layout with Shared Memory
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.4 Message Passing Model
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Core Primitives
items.text:
• send(message) — blocks or returns immediately
  • receive(message) — blocks or returns immediately
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Communication Link Design Questions
items.text:
1. How are links established?
  2. Can a link connect >2 processes?
  3. How many links between a pair?
  4. What is message capacity?
  5. Fixed or variable message size?
  6. Unidirectional or bidirectional?
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.5 Direct Communication
items.text:
send(P, message);        // Send directly to process P
receive(Q, &message);    // Receive directly from process Q
Property Behavior Naming Explicit (PID) Link Auto-established between pair Multiplicity One link per pair Direction Usually bidirectional

Disadvantage: Hardcoded PIDs → fragile; changing PID requires updating all references
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.6 Indirect Communication (Mailboxes / Ports)
items.text:
send(A, message);        // Send to mailbox A
receive(A, &message);    // Receive from mailbox A
Property Behavior Naming Via mailbox/port ID Link Exists only if processes share mailbox Multiplicity Many processes can share mailbox; pair can share multiple mailboxes Direction Unidirectional or bidirectional
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Multi-Receiver Ambiguity
items.text:
P1 → Mailbox A ← P2
               ← P3
If P1 sends, both P2 and P3 receive() → who gets it?

Solutions: 1. Restrict mailbox to ≤2 processes 2. Mutex on receive() (only one receiver at a time) 3. OS arbitrates, notifies sender of chosen recipient
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.7 Synchronization Modes
items.text: Mode Send Behavior Receive Behavior Blocking (Synchronous) Blocks until message received Blocks until message available Non-blocking (Async) Returns immediately Returns message or null immediately
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Rendezvous
items.text:
• Both send and receive are blocking
  • Sender and receiver synchronize tightly at exchange moment
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.8 Buffering Capacities
items.text: Capacity Behavior Zero (No Buffer) Sender blocks until receiver ready (strict rendezvous) Bounded (n messages) Sender blocks only when queue full Unbounded Sender never blocks; risk of memory exhaustion
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.9 Producer-Consumer Problem
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Bounded Buffer (Circular Array)
items.text:
#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
item buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0;   // Next free slot
int out = 0;  // First full slot

// Empty: in == out
// Full:  (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE == out
// Usable capacity: BUFFER_SIZE - 1
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Naive Code (Busy Waiting = Bad)
items.text:
// Producer
while (true) {
    produce(item);
    while (((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out); // SPIN
    buffer[in] = item;
    in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
}

// Consumer
while (true) {
    while (in == out); // SPIN
    item = buffer[out];
    out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    consume(item);
}
Problem: Busy waiting burns CPU — use blocking semaphores instead!
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: 9.10 System V IPC (Legacy but Exam-Relevant)
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: Pipes (Anonymous) — pipe()
items.text:
int fd[2];
pipe(fd);  // fd[0]=read, fd[1]=write
- Half-duplex (unidirectional) - Ancestry required — only parent/child (must pipe() before fork())
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: FIFOs (Named Pipes) — mkfifo()
items.text:
mkfifo("/tmp/myfifo", 0666);
- Exists in filesystem (type p) - Unrelated processes can communicate - Open with open(), use read()/write()/close()
path: Topic 9 (Detailed): Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing

items.title: System V Message Queues
items.text:
struct msgbuf { long mtype; char mtext[...]; };
msgget(key, flags);     // Create/get queue
msgsnd(msqid, &msg, ...); // Send
msgrcv(msqid, &msg, ..., type); // Receive with TYPE FILTERING
- Key feature: msgrcv() can selectively fetch by mtype (priority)

items.title: System V Semaphores
items.text:
semget(key, nsems, flags);
semctl(semid, semnum, cmd, ...);
semop(semid, sembuf_array, nops); // ATOMIC multiple operations

items.title: Unix Domain Sockets (AF_UNIX)
items.text:
• Bidirectional, full socket API, no network overhead
  • Supports file descriptor passing (SCM_RIGHTS)
  • Used by: systemd, Docker, X11/Wayland, PostgreSQL

items.title: 9.11 POSIX Shared Memory (Modern)
items.text:
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <fcntl.h>

// Create/open shared memory object
int fd = shm_open("/myshm", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0666);
ftruncate(fd, SIZE);  // Set size

// Map into address space
void *ptr = mmap(NULL, SIZE, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);

// Use ptr as shared memory
*(int*)ptr = 42;

// Cleanup
munmap(ptr, SIZE);
shm_unlink("/myshm");

items.title: 9.12 POSIX Message Queues (Modern)
items.text:
#include <mqueue.h>

mqd_t mq = mq_open("/myqueue", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0666, &attr);
mq_send(mq, "msg", 4, 10);  // Priority 10
mq_receive(mq, buf, size, &prio);
mq_close(mq);
mq_unlink("/myqueue");

items.title: Topic 9: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) — Shared Memory & Message Passing
items.text: Source: Lecture 1 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 5 (Silberschatz Ch. 3, Stallings Ch. 5, 17, Stevens & Rago Ch. 14-15, 17)

items.title: Process Types
items.text: Type Description Independent Cannot affect/be affected by others; shares no data Cooperating Can affect/be affected; shares data, memory, messages

items.title: Reasons for Cooperation
items.text:
1. Information Sharing — Concurrent access to shared resources (files, DBs)
  2. Computation Speedup — Parallel subtasks across CPU cores
  3. Modularity — Divide OS/apps into cooperating processes (client-server, microservices)
  4. Convenience — User running concurrent tasks

items.title: 9.2 Two Fundamental Models
items.text: Aspect Shared Memory Message Passing Mechanism OS maps shared region into both address spaces send()/receive() via kernel Speed Fastest (memory speed, no kernel copies) Slower (user→kernel→user copies) Sync Manual (semaphores, mutexes) Built into send/receive Best For Large data, same machine Distributed systems, small data

items.title: Architectural Comparison
items.text:
SHARED MEMORY                    MESSAGE PASSING
Process A    Process B            Process A    Process B
    │           │                    │           │
    ▼           ▼                    ▼           ▼
┌───────────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────────┐
│    SHARED MEMORY      │      │       OS KERNEL       │
│    [ Data Buffer ]    │      │  [M1] [M2] [M3] Queue │
└───────────────────────┘      └───────────────────────┘

items.title: Characteristics
items.text:
• OS establishes shared region mapped into both address spaces
  • Subsequent reads/writes at memory speed in user mode — no OS intervention
  • Fastest IPC

items.title: Challenges
items.text:
• Synchronization — If writer writes while reader reads → corruption
  • Must use: POSIX Semaphores, Mutex Locks, File/Record Locking

items.title: Linux Memory Layout with Shared Memory
Core Primitives
items.text:
• send(message) — blocks or returns immediately
  • receive(message) — blocks or returns immediately

items.title: Communication Link Design Questions
items.text:
1. How are links established?
  2. Can a link connect >2 processes?
  3. How many links between a pair?
  4. What is message capacity?
  5. Fixed or variable message size?
  6. Unidirectional or bidirectional?

items.title: 9.5 Direct Communication
items.text:
send(P, message);        // Send directly to process P
receive(Q, &message);    // Receive directly from process Q
Property Behavior Naming Explicit (PID) Link Auto-established between pair Multiplicity One link per pair Direction Usually bidirectional

Disadvantage: Hardcoded PIDs → fragile; changing PID requires updating all references

items.title: 9.6 Indirect Communication (Mailboxes / Ports)
items.text:
send(A, message);        // Send to mailbox A
receive(A, &message);    // Receive from mailbox A
Property Behavior Naming Via mailbox/port ID Link Exists only if processes share mailbox Multiplicity Many processes can share mailbox; pair can share multiple mailboxes Direction Unidirectional or bidirectional

items.title: Multi-Receiver Ambiguity
items.text:
P1 → Mailbox A ← P2
              ← P3
If P1 sends, both P2 and P3 receive() → who gets it?

Solutions: 1. Restrict mailbox to ≤2 processes 2. Mutex on receive() (only one receiver at a time) 3. OS arbitrates, notifies sender of chosen recipient

items.title: 9.7 Synchronization Modes
items.text: Mode Send Behavior Receive Behavior Blocking (Synchronous) Blocks until message received Blocks until message available Non-blocking (Async) Returns immediately Returns message or null immediately

items.title: Rendezvous
items.text:
• Both send and receive are blocking
  • Sender and receiver synchronize tightly at exchange moment

items.title: 9.8 Buffering Capacities
items.text: Capacity Behavior Zero (No Buffer) Sender blocks until receiver ready (strict rendezvous) Bounded (n messages) Sender blocks only when queue full Unbounded Sender never blocks; risk of memory exhaustion

items.title: Bounded Buffer (Circular Array)
items.text:
#define BUFFER_SIZE 10
item buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0;   // Next free slot
int out = 0;  // First full slot

// Empty: in == out
// Full:  (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE == out
// Usable capacity: BUFFER_SIZE - 1

items.title: Naive Code (Busy Waiting = Bad)
items.text:
// Producer
while (true) {
    produce(item);
    while (((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out); // SPIN
    buffer[in] = item;
    in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
}

// Consumer
while (true) {
    while (in == out); // SPIN
    item = buffer[out];
    out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    consume(item);
}
Problem: Busy waiting burns CPU — use blocking semaphores instead!

items.title: Pipes (Anonymous) — pipe()
items.text:
int fd[2];
pipe(fd);  // fd[0]=read, fd[1]=write
- Half-duplex (unidirectional) - Ancestry required — only parent/child (must pipe() before fork())

items.title: FIFOs (Named Pipes) — mkfifo()
items.text:
mkfifo("/tmp/myfifo", 0666);
- Exists in filesystem (type p) - Unrelated processes can communicate - Open with open(), use read()/write()/close()

items.title: System V Message Queues
items.text:
struct msgbuf { long mtype; char mtext[...]; };
msgget(key, flags);     // Create/get queue
msgsnd(msqid, &msg, ...); // Send
msgrcv(msqid, &msg, ..., type); // Receive with TYPE FILTERING
- Key feature: msgrcv() can selectively fetch by mtype (priority)

items.title: System V Semaphores
items.text:
semget(key, nsems, flags);
semctl(semid, semnum, cmd, ...);
semop(semid, sembuf_array, nops); // ATOMIC multiple operations

items.title: Unix Domain Sockets (AF_UNIX)
items.text:
• Bidirectional, full socket API, no network overhead
  • Supports file descriptor passing (SCM_RIGHTS)
  • Used by: systemd, Docker, X11/Wayland, PostgreSQL

items.title: 9.11 Modern IPC (What You Actually Use)
items.text: Instead of Raw... Use... shmget + mutex Redis, memcached, SQLite WAL, mmap'ed files msgget/msgsnd RabbitMQ, Kafka, ZeroMQ, gRPC, D-Bus Pipes Shell pipelines cmd1 \| cmd2 Sockets systemd, Docker, databases

items.title: 9.12 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• IPC = controlled isolation breaking for cooperation [Silberschatz §3.1]
  • Shared memory = speed + manual sync (whiteboard model) [Silberschatz §3.3]
  • Message passing = safety + built-in sync + distribution (postal model) [Silberschatz §3.4]
  • Producer-consumer = fundamental pattern [Silberschatz §3.5]
  • Busy waiting = bad in user space — use blocking primitives [Silberschatz §3.5.2]
  • Bounded buffers give backpressure for free
  • Mailboxes decouple sender/receiver → modularity [Silberschatz §3.4.4]

items.title: Topic 10 (Detailed): Threads & Multicore Programming
items.text: Source: Lectures 2 & 4 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 6 (Silberschatz Ch. 4, Stallings Ch. 4, Stevens & Rago Ch. 11-12)

items.title: Thread vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Process Thread Memory Isolated address space Shared (code, data, heap, files) Private PID, address space, FD table TID, PC, registers, stack, errno Creation cost High (~30× thread) Low Context switch Slow (~5× thread) Fast Protection Strong (fault isolates) None (bug crashes all)

Silberschatz: "A thread is a basic unit of CPU utilization; it comprises a thread ID, a program counter, a register set, and a stack."

items.title: Thread Structure
items.text: Thread = (TID, Program Counter, Register Set, Private Stack)

items.title: Process Architecture
items.text:
SINGLE-THREADED                    MULTITHREADED
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ Code | Data | Files │           │ Code | Data | Files │  ← SHARED
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│ Registers | Stack   │           │ Regs | Regs | Regs  │
│             │       │           │ Stack|Stack|Stack  │  ← PER-THREAD
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

items.title: 10.2 Benefits of Multithreading
items.text: Benefit Description Responsiveness UI stays responsive while background thread computes Resource Sharing Threads share memory/files automatically — no IPC needed Economy Thread create ≈ 30× faster than process; context switch ≈ 5× faster Scalability Threads run on multiple cores simultaneously

items.title: Real-World Examples
items.text:
• Web Browser: Network thread, render thread, audio thread, UI thread
  • Word Processor: Input thread, spell-check thread, autosave thread

items.title: 10.3 Multithreading Models
items.text:
Model User:Kernel Parallelism Blocking Issue Used By Many-to-One (M:1) Many:1 ❌ No One blocks → all block Old Solaris, Green threads One-to-One (1:1) 1:1 ✅ Yes No blocking propagation Linux, Windows, macOS Many-to-Many (M:N) Many:Many ✅ Yes Flexible multiplexing Old Solaris Two-Level (Hybrid) Hybrid ✅ Yes Critical threads bound 1:1 IRIX, HP-UX, Solaris 8- 
1:1 Model (Modern Standard):
User:  T1  T2  T3  T4
        │  │  │  │
Kernel: KT1 KT2 KT3 KT4

Silberschatz: "The one-to-one model is the most common model used in modern operating systems."

items.title: Thread Creation
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>

int pthread_create(
    pthread_t *thread,           // OUT: thread ID
    const pthread_attr_t *attr,  // Attributes (NULL = defaults)
    void *(*start_routine)(void *), // Function pointer
    void *arg                    // Single argument (void*)
);

// Thread function signature:
void *my_thread_func(void *arg) {
    // do work
    return NULL;  // or pthread_exit(retval)
}

Stevens & Rago: "The pthread_create() function creates a new thread of control that executes concurrently with the calling thread."

items.title: Critical: Stack-Escape Bug
items.text:
// ❌ WRONG - passes address of LOCAL variable
void start_thread(int value) {
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value); // DANGER!
    // if start_thread() returns before worker runs...
    // value is gone! Stack frame destroyed!
}

// ✅ CORRECT - allocate on heap
void start_thread(int value) {
    int *arg = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *arg = value;
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, arg);
    // worker must free(arg) when done
}

// ✅ CORRECT - pass from main() stack (main never returns)
int main() {
    int value = 42;  // lives until program ends
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);
}

Rule: Argument pointer must remain valid until thread finishes using it.

items.title: Thread Join — Synchronization & Cleanup
items.text:
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
// Blocks until 'thread' terminates
// retval receives return value

Why join? 1. Wait for result — main needs worker's output 2. Prevent zombie threads — unjoined threads leak resources (TCB, stack) 3. Orderly shutdown — ensure workers done before exit

// Fork-Join Pattern [Silberschatz Fig. 4.3]
pthread_t threads[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, worker, &args[i]);

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_join(threads[i], &results[i]);  // Collect results

items.title: pthread_exit() vs exit() vs return in main()
items.text: Call Effect pthread_exit(val) Current thread only dies; process lives if other threads exist return val in thread func Same as pthread_exit(val) exit(val) or return in main() Entire process dies — all threads killed instantly pthread_exit() in main() Main thread dies, other threads keep running

items.title: Scheduling Scopes
Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock)
items.text:
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);   // Blocks if busy
// CRITICAL SECTION
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); // Must be called by owner

items.title: Condition Variables (Wait for Predicate)
items.text:
pthread_cond_t cond = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

// Waiter
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
while (!condition) pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
// Condition is true, mutex held
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

// Signaler
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
condition = true;
pthread_cond_signal(&cond);  // or broadcast
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

items.title: 10.6 Thread Cancellation
10.7 Thread Pools
items.text:
Problem: Creating/destroying threads per request = overhead + unbounded resource use

Architecture: 

// Startup: create fixed pool
for (i = 0; i < POOL_SIZE; i++)
    pthread_create(&pool[i], NULL, worker_loop, &queue);

// Worker loop
void *worker_loop(void *arg) {
    while (true) {
        Task *t = queue_pop(&queue);  // Blocks if empty
        execute(t);
        // Thread returns to pool, doesn't die
    }
}

// Submit work
queue_push(&queue, new_task);  // Wakes one worker

Used everywhere: nginx, Apache, Java ExecutorService, C++ std::thread_pool

Silberschatz: "A thread pool provides a more efficient way to manage threads... it reduces the overhead of creating and destroying threads."

items.title: Program 1: Parallel Sum with Fork-Join
items.text:
/*
 * File: parallel_sum.c
 * Parallel array summation using fork-join
 * Compile: gcc -o parallel_sum parallel_sum.c -lpthread
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>

typedef struct {
    int *array;
    int start;
    int end;
    long long sum;
} Task;

void *sum_worker(void *arg) {
    Task *t = (Task*)arg;
    long long local_sum = 0;
    for (int i = t->start; i < t->end; i++) {
        local_sum += t->array[i];
    }
    t->sum = local_sum;
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    const int SIZE = 10000000;
    const int THREADS = 4;

    int *array = malloc(SIZE * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) array[i] = 1;  // Sum = SIZE

    pthread_t threads[THREADS];
    Task tasks[THREADS];
    int chunk = SIZE / THREADS;

    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        tasks[i].array = array;
        tasks[i].start = i * chunk;
        tasks[i].end = (i == THREADS - 1) ? SIZE : (i + 1) * chunk;
        tasks[i].sum = 0;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, sum_worker, &tasks[i]);
    }

    long long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
        total += tasks[i].sum;
        printf("Thread %d: sum = %lld\n", i, tasks[i].sum);
    }

    printf("Total: %lld (expected: %d)\n", total, SIZE);
    free(array);
    return 0;
}

items.title: Program 2: Mutex Counter (Race Condition Demo)
items.text:
/*
 * File: mutex_counter.c
 * Demonstrates race condition and mutex fix
 * Compile: gcc -o mutex_counter mutex_counter.c -lpthread
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#define THREADS 4
#define ITERATIONS 1000000

int counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    int iterations = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
        // CRITICAL SECTION
        int temp = counter;
        temp++;
        counter = temp;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, increment, &ITERATIONS);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("Expected: %d, Actual: %d\n", THREADS * ITERATIONS, counter);
    pthread_mutex_destroy(&lock);
    return 0;
}

Without mutex: Race condition → lost updates → counter < expected With mutex: Correct synchronization → counter = expected

items.title: Program 3: Condition Variable (Producer-Consumer)
items.text:
/*
 * File: condvar_producer_consumer.c
 * Producer-consumer with condition variables
 * Compile: gcc -o condvar_pc condvar_producer_consumer.c -lpthread
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define BUFFER_SIZE 5

int buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0, out = 0, count = 0;

pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t not_full = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t not_empty = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;

void *producer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        while (count == BUFFER_SIZE) {
            printf("[Producer %d] Buffer full, waiting...\n", id);
            pthread_cond_wait(&not_full, &mutex);
        }

        buffer[in] = i;
        in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        count++;
        printf("[Producer %d] Produced %d (count=%d)\n", id, i, count);

        pthread_cond_signal(&not_empty);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

        usleep(100000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        while (count == 0) {
            printf("[Consumer %d] Buffer empty, waiting...\n", id);
            pthread_cond_wait(&not_empty, &mutex);
        }

        int item = buffer[out];
        out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        count--;
        printf("[Consumer %d] Consumed %d (count=%d)\n", id, item, count);

        pthread_cond_signal(&not_full);
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

        usleep(150000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t prod[2], cons[2];
    int prod_ids[2] = {1, 2};
    int cons_ids[2] = {1, 2};

    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        pthread_create(&prod[i], NULL, producer, &i);
        pthread_create(&cons[i], NULL, consumer, &i);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        pthread_join(prod[i], NULL);
        pthread_join(cons[i], NULL);
    }
    return 0;
}

items.title: Program 4: Thread Pool
items.text:
/*
 * File: thread_pool.c
 * Simple thread pool implementation
 * Compile: gcc -o thread_pool thread_pool.c -lpthread
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define POOL_SIZE 4
#define QUEUE_SIZE 100

typedef struct {
    void (*func)(void*);
    void *arg;
} Task;

Task queue[QUEUE_SIZE];
int q_head = 0, q_tail = 0, q_count = 0;

pthread_mutex_t q_mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t q_not_empty = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t q_not_full = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;

int shutdown = 0;

void queue_push(Task t) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&q_mutex);
    while (q_count == QUEUE_SIZE && !shutdown) {
        pthread_cond_wait(&q_not_full, &q_mutex);
    }
    if (shutdown) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&q_mutex); return; }

    queue[q_tail] = t;
    q_tail = (q_tail + 1) % QUEUE_SIZE;
    q_count++;
    pthread_cond_signal(&q_not_empty);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&q_mutex);
}

Task queue_pop() {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&q_mutex);
    while (q_count == 0 && !shutdown) {
        pthread_cond_wait(&q_not_empty, &q_mutex);
    }
    if (shutdown && q_count == 0) {
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&q_mutex);
        Task empty = {NULL, NULL};
        return empty;
    }

    Task t = queue[q_head];
    q_head = (q_head + 1) % QUEUE_SIZE;
    q_count--;
    pthread_cond_signal(&q_not_full);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&q_mutex);
    return t;
}

void *worker(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    while (1) {
        Task t = queue_pop();
        if (t.func == NULL && shutdown) break;
        if (t.func) {
            printf("[Worker %d] Executing task\n", id);
            t.func(t.arg);
        }
    }
    printf("[Worker %d] Exiting\n", id);
    return NULL;
}

void example_task(void *arg) {
    int n = *(int*)arg;
    printf("  Task %d executing\n", n);
    usleep(100000);
}

int main() {
    pthread_t pool[POOL_SIZE];
    int ids[POOL_SIZE];

    for (int i = 0; i < POOL_SIZE; i++) {
        ids[i] = i;
        pthread_create(&pool[i], NULL, worker, &ids[i]);
    }

    // Submit work
    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        int *arg = malloc(sizeof(int));
        *arg = i;
        Task t = {example_task, arg};
        queue_push(t);
    }

    sleep(2);
    shutdown = 1;
    pthread_cond_broadcast(&q_not_empty);
    pthread_cond_broadcast(&q_not_full);

    for (int i = 0; i < POOL_SIZE; i++) {
        pthread_join(pool[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("All done\n");
    return 0;
}

items.title: 10.8 Variable Sharing in Threads
items.text:
int global = 0;           // SHARED (data segment)
static int static_var = 0; // SHARED (data segment)

void *thread_func(void *arg) {
    int local = 1;           // PRIVATE (stack)
    static int static_local = 1; // SHARED (data segment)

    // global, static_var, static_local shared across threads
    // local is private to this thread
}
Variable Type Location Shared? Global Data segment ✅ Yes Static global Data segment ✅ Yes Static local Data segment ✅ Yes Local (stack) Stack ❌ No (per-thread) malloc() heap Heap ✅ Yes Thread-local storage TLS ❌ No (per-thread)

items.title: 10.9 Complete Exam-Focused Summary
items.text: Concept Key Points Thread Lightweight execution unit sharing process resources 1:1 model Modern standard (Linux, Windows, macOS) Pthreads POSIX standard; pthread_create, join, exit, mutex, cond Stack-escape bug Never pass local stack address to new thread Join prevents zombies Always join non-detached threads Shared vs Private Globals/heap shared; stack/registers/PC private SCS (System scope) Linux default; threads compete globally Thread pools Reuse threads, bound resources, lower latency Deferred cancellation Safe; async cancellation = dangerous

items.title: 10.10 Common Pitfalls

items.title: Topic 10: Threads & Multicore Programming
items.text: Source: Lecture 2 & 4 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 6 (Silberschatz Ch. 4, Stallings Ch. 4, Stevens & Rago Ch. 11-12)

items.title: Thread vs Process
items.text:
Aspect Process Thread Memory Isolated address space Shared (code, data, heap, files) Private PID, address space, FD table TID, PC, registers, stack, errno Creation cost High (~30× thread) Low Context switch Slow (~5× thread) Fast Protection Strong (fault isolates) None (bug crashes all)

Silberschatz: "A thread is a basic unit of CPU utilization; it comprises a thread ID, a program counter, a register set, and a stack."

items.title: Thread Structure
items.text: Thread = (TID, Program Counter, Register Set, Private Stack)

items.title: Process Architecture
items.text:
SINGLE-THREADED                    MULTITHREADED
┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐
│ Code | Data | Files │           │ Code | Data | Files │  ← SHARED
├─────────────────────┤           ├─────────────────────┤
│ Registers | Stack   │           │ Regs | Regs | Regs  │
│             │       │           │ Stack|Stack|Stack  │  ← PER-THREAD
└─────────────────────┘           └─────────────────────┘

items.title: 10.2 Benefits of Multithreading
items.text: Benefit Description Responsiveness UI stays responsive while background thread computes Resource Sharing Threads share memory/files automatically — no IPC needed Economy Thread create ≈ 30× faster than process; context switch ≈ 5× faster Scalability Threads run on multiple cores simultaneously

items.title: Real-World Examples
items.text:
• Web Browser: Network thread, render thread, audio thread, UI thread
  • Word Processor: Input thread, spell-check thread, autosave thread

items.title: 10.3 Multithreading Models
items.text:
Model User:Kernel Parallelism Blocking Issue Used By Many-to-One (M:1) Many:1 ❌ No One blocks → all block Old Solaris, Green threads One-to-One (1:1) 1:1 ✅ Yes No blocking propagation Linux, Windows, macOS Many-to-Many (M:N) Many:Many ✅ Yes Flexible multiplexing Old Solaris Two-Level (Hybrid) Hybrid ✅ Yes Critical threads bound 1:1 IRIX, HP-UX, Solaris 8- 
1:1 Model (Modern Standard):
User:  T1  T2  T3  T4
        │  │  │  │
Kernel: KT1 KT2 KT3 KT4

Silberschatz: "The one-to-one model is the most common model used in modern operating systems."

items.title: Thread Creation
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>

int pthread_create(
    pthread_t *thread,           // OUT: thread ID
    const pthread_attr_t *attr,  // Attributes (NULL = defaults)
    void *(*start_routine)(void *), // Function pointer
    void *arg                    // Single argument (void*)
);

// Thread function signature:
void *my_thread_func(void *arg) {
    // do work
    return NULL;  // or pthread_exit(retval)
}

Stevens & Rago: "The pthread_create() function creates a new thread of control that executes concurrently with the calling thread."

items.title: Critical: Stack-Escape Bug
items.text:
// ❌ WRONG - passes address of LOCAL variable
void start_thread(int value) {
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value); // DANGER!
    // if start_thread() returns before worker runs...
    // value is gone! Stack frame destroyed!
}

// ✅ CORRECT - allocate on heap
void start_thread(int value) {
    int *arg = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *arg = value;
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, arg);
    // worker must free(arg) when done
}

// ✅ CORRECT - pass from main() stack (main never returns)
int main() {
    int value = 42;  // lives until program ends
    pthread_create(&tid, NULL, worker, &value);
    pthread_join(tid, NULL);
}

Rule: Argument pointer must remain valid until thread finishes using it.

items.title: Thread Join — Synchronization & Cleanup
items.text:
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
// Blocks until 'thread' terminates
// retval receives return value

Why join? 1. Wait for result — main needs worker's output 2. Prevent zombie threads — unjoined threads leak resources (TCB, stack) 3. Orderly shutdown — ensure workers done before exit

// Fork-Join Pattern [Silberschatz Fig. 4.3]
pthread_t threads[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, worker, &args[i]);

for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    pthread_join(threads[i], &results[i]);  // Collect results

items.title: pthread_exit() vs exit() vs return in main()
items.text: Call Effect pthread_exit(val) Current thread only dies; process lives if other threads exist return val in thread func Same as pthread_exit(val) exit(val) or return in main() Entire process dies — all threads killed instantly pthread_exit() in main() Main thread dies, other threads keep running

items.title: Scheduling Scopes
Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock)
items.text:
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);   // Blocks if busy
// CRITICAL SECTION
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); // Must be called by owner

items.title: Condition Variables (Wait for Predicate)
items.text:
pthread_cond_t cond = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

// Waiter
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
while (!condition) pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
// Condition is true, mutex held
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

// Signaler
pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
condition = true;
pthread_cond_signal(&cond);  // or broadcast
pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);

items.title: 10.6 Thread Cancellation
10.7 Thread Pools
items.text:
Problem: Creating/destroying threads per request = overhead + unbounded resource use

Architecture: 

// Startup: create fixed pool
for (i = 0; i < POOL_SIZE; i++)
    pthread_create(&pool[i], NULL, worker_loop, &queue);

// Worker loop
void *worker_loop(void *arg) {
    while (true) {
        Task *t = queue_pop(&queue);  // Blocks if empty
        execute(t);
        // Thread returns to pool, doesn't die
    }
}

// Submit work
queue_push(&queue, new_task);  // Wakes one worker

Used everywhere: nginx, Apache, Java ExecutorService, C++ std::thread_pool

Silberschatz: "A thread pool provides a more efficient way to manage threads... it reduces the overhead of creating and destroying threads."

items.title: 10.8 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• Thread = lightweight execution unit sharing process resources [Silberschatz §4.1]
  • 1:1 model = modern standard (Linux, Windows, macOS) [Silberschatz §4.3.2]
  • Pthreads = POSIX standard; pthread_create, join, exit, mutex, cond [Stevens & Rago Ch. 11]
  • Stack-escape bug = never pass local stack address to new thread [Stevens & Rago §11.3]
  • Join prevents zombies = always join non-detached threads [Stevens & Rago §11.4]
  • Shared vs Private = globals/heap shared; stack/registers/PC private [Silberschatz §4.2]
  • SCS (System scope) = Linux default; threads compete globally [Silberschatz §4.4.2]
  • Thread pools = reuse threads, bound resources, lower latency [Silberschatz §4.5]
  • Deferred cancellation = safe; async cancellation = dangerous [Stevens & Rago §11.8]

items.title: 10.9 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q36: Thread vs process — threads share heap, globals, files; private: PC, registers, stack
  • Q37: M:1 vulnerability — one blocking syscall blocks entire process
  • Q38: 1:1 advantage — true multicore parallelism, blocking doesn't halt others
  • Q39: M:N — multiplexes user threads onto fewer kernel threads
  • Q40: Amdahl's Law — S=0.20, N=4 → speedup=2.5x; max=5x
  • Q41: demo_threads.c — local=1 always; static/global accumulate across threads
  • Q42: pthread_join() — blocks parent until worker done, prevents race on shared results
  • Q43: Pipe descriptors — parent closes fd[0], child closes fd[1]
  • Q44: Ordinary pipe — unidirectional, requires shared ancestry
  • Q45: FIFO vs pipe — FIFO has filesystem path, unrelated processes
  • Q46: Shared memory fastest — zero kernel copy after setup
  • Q47: Message passing — kernel syscall per message, slower but distributed
  • Q48: Socket = IP + Port
  • Q49: Race condition definition
  • Q50: Critical section 3 requirements — Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting
  • Q51: Peterson's variables — turn + flag[2]
  • Q52: test_and_set — returns original, sets to true
  • Q53: compare_and_swap — if equal, sets new; returns original
  • Q54: Mutex vs semaphore — mutex has ownership; semaphore no ownership
  • Q55: Spinlock effective on multiprocessor for short CS — avoids context switch overhead
  • Q56: sem_init(&mutex, 0, 1) — 2nd arg 0 = thread-shared; 3rd = binary semaphore
  • Q57: demo_semaphore_2.c vs 3.c — without sync: interleaved; with: mutual exclusion
  • Q58: Producer-consumer semaphores — mutex=1, empty=N, full=0
  • Q59: Wrong order wait(mutex); wait(empty) → DEADLOCK when buffer full
  • Q60: Readers-writers — reader preference starves writers
  • Q61: Dining philosophers — asymmetric pickup (odd left→right, even right→left)
  • Q62: Hold and Wait — process holds resource while requesting more
  • Q63: Eliminate Hold and Wait — request all at once, or release before requesting
  • Q64: Deadlock prevention — global linear lock ordering
  • Q65: RAG multi-instance — cycle = necessary but not sufficient
  • Q66: Banker's Need = Max - Allocation
  • Q67: Safe state — exists sequence where all can finish
  • Q68: Unsafe ≠ deadlocked; all deadlocked are unsafe
  • Q69: Wait-for graph — collapse RAG, cycle = deadlock
  • Q70: Uncatchable signals — SIGKILL, SIGSTOP

items.title: Core vs Thread
items.text:
Term Meaning Physical Core Actual silicon with execution units (ALU, FPU) Hardware Thread / Logical CPU Architectural state (registers, PC, stack pointer) SMT Simultaneous Multi-Threading (generic) Hyper-Threading Intel's SMT (2 threads/core) 
4 Cores × 2 Threads = 8 Logical CPUs

│ CORE 0              CORE 1                      │
│  Thread 0  Thread 1    Thread 0  Thread 1      │
│   (CPU 0)  (CPU 1)      (CPU 2)  (CPU 3)       │
│       │       │           │       │             │
│       └───────┼───────────┼───────┘             │
│               ▼           ▼                     │

items.title: Why SMT?
items.text:
Single Thread on Core:
┌─────────┬──────────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
│ Compute │  MEMORY      │ Compute │  MEMORY      │  Time
│  (C)    │  STALL (M)   │  (C)    │  STALL (M)   │  →
└─────────┴──────────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘
  50%      50% idle       50%      50% idle

CPU runs at ~3-4 GHz, DRAM latency ~100-300 cycles → core sits idle on cache miss.

items.title: SMT: Two Threads Fill Stalls
items.text:
Thread 0:  [ C0 ] [ M0 ] [ C0 ] [ M0 ] [ C0 ]
Thread 1:  [ M1 ] [ C1 ] [ M1 ] [ C1 ] [ M1 ]
           ┬      ┬      ┬      ┬      ┬
Core:      C0     C1     C0     C1     C0   → Near 100% utilization!

Hardware provides duplicate register file, PC, stack pointer per thread. Shared: ALU, FPU, L1/L2 cache, TLB.

items.title: 11.3 Ready Queue Organization
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Common Ready Queue (Doesn't Scale)
items.text:
All CPUs → [GLOBAL LOCK] → Single Queue → CPU 0
                         │
                         ├──→ CPU 1
                         │
                         └──→ CPU 2
  • One global lock protects queue
  • All cores serialize on lock
  • Contention → cache line ping-pong → throughput collapses
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Per-Core Run Queues (Modern Standard — Linux CFS)
items.text:
Core 0: [Queue 0] → CPU 0
Core 1: [Queue 1] → CPU 1
Core 2: [Queue 2] → CPU 2

Linux CFS: each CPU has `struct rq` (run queue)

Key: No lock on fast path — each core owns its queue. Lock only needed for migration (load balancing).

items.title: Kernel Parallelism
items.text:
• Multiple cores run kernel code simultaneously
  • Solution: Partition kernel state (per-CPU variables, RCU, per-CPU allocators)
  • Synchronize only for cross-core operations (migration, IPI)

items.title: Hardware View
items.text:
Per Hardware Thread:
- Program Counter (PC)
- General Purpose Registers (RAX, RBX, ...)
- Stack Pointer (RSP)
- Flags Register (RFLAGS)
- Control Registers (CR0, CR3, ...)
- Debug Registers
- FPU/SSE/AVX State (sometimes shared)

Shared:
- L1 Instruction Cache
- L1 Data Cache
- L2 Cache
- Execution Units (ALU, FPU, SIMD)
- TLB (often shared, sometimes duplicated)
- Branch Predictor

items.title: Scheduling on SMT
items.text:
Linux CFS: Treats each thread as independent CPU
- Sibling threads share core resources
- Scheduler prefers spreading tasks across cores first
- Only packs onto same core when necessary

Kernel aware of topology:
/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/topology/thread_siblings_list

path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Push Migration (Periodic)
items.text:
Kernel daemon (every few ms):
1. Scan all run queues
2. Find overloaded (len > avg + threshold) and underloaded
3. PUSH tasks from overloaded → underloaded
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Pull Migration (Work Stealing)
items.text:
Idle Core:
1. Detect own queue empty
2. Randomly pick victim core
3. STEAL half its tasks
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Linux CFS Uses BOTH
items.text:
Push: Periodic, for large imbalances
Pull: Reactive, for idle cores

NUMA-aware:
- Prefer same-node migration
- Cross-node only for severe imbalance

items.title: 11.6 Processor Affinity
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Why It Matters
items.text:
Thread runs on Core 0:
  L1/L2 cache fills with thread's data (WARM)

Thread migrates to Core 1:
  Core 0 cache lines invalidated
  Core 1 suffers COLD misses (100+ cycles each)
  Performance tanks until cache re-warms
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: Affinity Types
items.text: Type Guarantee Soft Affinity Scheduler prefers same core but will migrate for load balancing (Linux default) Hard Affinity OS pins thread to specific CPU subset via syscall

items.title: Linux Hard Affinity API
items.text:
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sched.h>
#include <stdio.h>

void pin_to_cpu(int cpu) {
    cpu_set_t mask;
    CPU_ZERO(&mask);
    CPU_SET(cpu, &mask);

    // pid = 0 means current thread
    if (sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(mask), &mask) == -1) {
        perror("sched_setaffinity");
    }
}

void pin_to_cpus(int *cpus, int n) {
    cpu_set_t mask;
    CPU_ZERO(&mask);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) CPU_SET(cpus[i], &mask);
    sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(mask), &mask);
}

void print_affinity() {
    cpu_set_t mask;
    CPU_ZERO(&mask);
    sched_getaffinity(0, sizeof(mask), &mask);

    printf("Affinity: ");
    for (int i = 0; i < CPU_SETSIZE; i++) {
        if (CPU_ISSET(i, &mask)) printf("%d ", i);
    }
    printf("\n");
}

items.title: 11.7 Cache Coherency (MESI Protocol)
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: The Problem
items.text:
Core 0 reads X=5  → Core 0 cache: X=5 (Shared)
Core 1 reads X=5  → Core 1 cache: X=5 (Shared)
Core 0 writes X=7 → Must invalidate Core 1's copy!
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: MESI States
items.text: State Meaning Can Read? Can Write? Modified Only this cache has it, dirty Yes Yes (silent) Exclusive Only this cache has it, clean Yes Yes (silent → M) Shared Multiple caches have it, clean Yes No (must invalidate) Invalid Not in this cache No No
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: State Transitions
items.text:
Core 0 reads X:
  Miss → Bus Read → Memory → Core 0: E

Core 1 reads X:
  Miss → Bus Read → Core 0: S, Core 1: S

Core 0 writes X:
  Hit in E → Silent → M

Core 1 reads X (after Core 0 wrote):
  Miss → Bus Read → Core 0: S (writeback), Core 1: S

Core 1 writes X:
  Hit in S → Bus Upgrade → Core 0: I, Core 1: M
path: Topic 11 (Detailed): Multicore Kernel Concepts & SMP Scheduling

items.title: False Sharing
items.text:
Thread 0 writes a[0]  → Cache line with a[0..15] goes to M on Core 0
Thread 1 writes a[16] → Same cache line! → Core 1 gets it, Core 0 invalidated
                                                        ↓
                                                Ping-pong!

Fix: Pad data to cache line size (64 bytes):

struct alignas(64) Counter {
    long value;
    char padding[64 - sizeof(long)];
};

items.title: 11.1 SMP vs AMP
items.text:
Architecture Description AMP (Asymmetric) Master handles OS scheduling, syscalls, I/O; Workers run user apps only. Simple but master = bottleneck SMP (Symmetric) All cores peers — any core runs user processes, kernel code, handles interrupts. Modern standard (Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS)

Silberschatz: "In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), each processor is self-scheduling; all processes in the ready queue can be scheduled on any processor."

items.title: Common Ready Queue (Doesn't Scale)
items.text:
All cores → [GLOBAL LOCK] → Single Queue → Core 0
                         │
                         ├──→ Core 1
                         │
                         └──→ Core 2
- One global lock protects queue - All cores serialize on lock - Contention → cache line ping-pong → throughput collapses

Silberschatz Fig. 5.11: "Common ready queue vs. per-processor run queues"

items.title: Per-Core Run Queues (Modern Standard — Linux CFS)
items.text:
Core 0: [Queue 0] → Core 0
Core 1: [Queue 1] → Core 1
Core 2: [Queue 2] → Core 2
- No lock on fast path — each core owns its queue - Lock only needed for migration (load balancing) - Linux CFS: each CPU has struct rq (run queue)

Silberschatz: "To avoid the lock contention of a single ready queue, most modern SMP kernels use per-processor run queues."

items.title: Kernel Parallelism
items.text:
• Multiple cores run kernel code simultaneously
  • Solution: Partition kernel state (per-CPU variables, RCU, per-CPU allocators)
  • Synchronize only for cross-core operations (migration, IPI)

items.title: The Memory Stall Problem
items.text:
Single Thread on Core:
┌─────────┬──────────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
│ Compute │  MEMORY      │ Compute │  MEMORY      │  Time
│  (C)    │  STALL (M)   │  (C)    │  STALL (M)   │  →
└─────────┴──────────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘
  50%      50% idle       50%      50% idle
- CPU ~3-4 GHz, DRAM ~100-300 cycles latency - Cache miss = core sits idle for 100-400 cycles

Silberschatz Fig. 5.12: "Memory stall timeline on a single hardware thread"

items.title: SMT Solution: Two Hardware Threads per Core
items.text:
Thread 0:  [ C0 ] [ M0 ] [ C0 ] [ M0 ] [ C0 ]
Thread 1:  [ M1 ] [ C1 ] [ M1 ] [ C1 ] [ M1 ]
           ┬      ┬      ┬      ┬      ┬
Core:      C0     C1     C0     C1     C0   → Near 100% utilization!

Hardware provides: Duplicate register file, PC, stack pointer per hardware thread Shared: Execution units (ALU, FPU), L1/L2 cache, TLB

Silberschatz Fig. 5.13: "Multithreaded core cycle interleaving"

items.title: Terminology
items.text:
Term Meaning Physical Core Actual silicon core with execution units Hardware Thread / Logical CPU Architectural state (registers, PC) — appears as CPU to OS SMT Simultaneous Multi-Threading (generic) Hyper-Threading Intel's SMT (2 threads/core) CMT Chip Multi-Threading = Multi-core + SMT 
4 cores × 2 threads = 8 Logical CPUs → OS sees 8 CPUs

Silberschatz Fig. 5.14: "Chip multithreading architecture"

items.title: 11.4 Multicore Load Balancing
items.text: With per-core queues, imbalance happens: Core 0 has 10 tasks, Core 1 has 0.

items.title: Push Migration
items.text:
Kernel daemon (periodic):
  1. Scan all run queues
  2. Find overloaded (len > avg + threshold) and idle
  3. PUSH tasks from overloaded → underloaded
- Proactive, centralized - Overhead: periodic scanning

items.title: Pull Migration (Work Stealing)
items.text:
Idle Core 1:
  1. Detect own queue empty
  2. Randomly pick victim core
  3. STEAL half its tasks
- Reactive, decentralized - Linux CFS uses BOTH — push for large imbalances, pull for idle cores

items.title: NUMA Awareness
items.text:
Node 0 (CPUs 0-3, Local RAM)     Node 1 (CPUs 4-7, Local RAM)
     │                                    │
     └── Prefer migrating within node ────┘
           (local RAM access = fast)
           Cross-node = slow (interconnect)
- Linux scheduler tracks NUMA topology - Prefers same-node migration; cross-node only if severe imbalance

Silberschatz: "Load balancing is essential for effective use of SMP systems."

items.title: Why It Matters
items.text:
Thread runs on Core 0:
  L1/L2 cache fills with thread's data (WARM)

Thread migrates to Core 1:
  Core 0 cache lines invalidated
  Core 1 suffers COLD misses (100+ cycles each)
  Performance tanks until cache re-warms

items.title: Affinity Types
items.text: Type Guarantee Soft Affinity Scheduler prefers same core but will migrate for load balancing (Linux default) Hard Affinity OS pins thread to specific CPU subset via syscall

items.title: Linux Hard Affinity API
items.text:
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sched.h>

cpu_set_t mask;
CPU_ZERO(&mask);
CPU_SET(2, &mask);   // Pin to CPU 2 only
CPU_SET(3, &mask);   // Or CPU 3

sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(mask), &mask);  // pid=0 = current process

Use cases: - Real-time tasks (deterministic latency) - HPC (MPI processes pinned to cores) - License-bound software (per-core licensing) - Cache-sensitive workloads (databases, games)

Check affinity: 

taskset -cp <pid>        # View
taskset -cp 2,3 <pid>    # Set

items.title: 11.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• SMP = all cores peers; any core runs kernel, schedules, handles interrupts [Silberschatz §2.1.2]
  • Per-core run queues = eliminate global lock contention (Linux CFS) [Silberschatz §5.6.2]
  • SMT/Hyper-Threading = fills memory stall cycles with another thread's work [Silberschatz §5.4]
  • Load balancing = push (periodic) + pull (work stealing), NUMA-aware [Silberschatz §5.6.4]
  • Affinity = soft (preference) vs hard (pinning via sched_setaffinity) [Silberschatz §5.6.5]
  • Cache warmth = migration costs 1000s of cycles in cold misses [Silberschatz §5.6.5]

items.title: What is a Race Condition?
items.text:
// counter++ is NOT atomic! It compiles to:
load  counter → register
inc   register
store register → counter

// Two threads doing counter++ simultaneously:
Thread A: load 5     (register=5)
Thread B: load 5     (register=5)  ← PREEMPTION!
Thread A: inc  → 6
Thread A: store 6  (counter=6)
Thread B: inc  → 6
Thread B: store 6  (counter=6)  ← LOST UPDATE! Should be 7.

items.title: Peterson's Algorithm (2 Processes Only)
items.text:
boolean flag[2] = {false, false};
int turn;

void process_i() {
    int j = 1 - i;  // Other process

    flag[i] = true;      // "I want in"
    turn = j;            // "You go first"

    while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // Spin wait

    // CRITICAL SECTION

    flag[i] = false;     // "I'm done"
}

Why it fails on modern CPUs: - Compiler/CPU reorder instructions: turn = j may execute BEFORE flag[i] = true - Store buffers: writes not immediately visible to other cores - Fix requires memory barriers → architecture-specific, not portable

boolean lock = false;

void acquire_lock() {
    while (test_and_set(&lock)) ;  // Spin until we get it

items.title: 12.4 Bounded-Waiting Spinlock (Circular Queue)
items.text:
boolean waiting[N] = {false};
boolean lock = false;

void acquire_lock(int i) {
    waiting[i] = true;
    boolean key = true;
    while (waiting[i] && key) {
        key = test_and_set(&lock);
    }
    waiting[i] = false;

    // CRITICAL SECTION
}

void release_lock(int i) {
    int j = (i + 1) % N;
    while (j != i && !waiting[j]) j = (j + 1) % N;

    if (j == i) lock = false;       // Nobody waiting
    else waiting[j] = false;        // Wake next waiter
}

Guarantees bounded waiting: Each waiter served in turn (max N-1 others before you).

items.title: Mutex (Blocking, Not Spinning)
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

// Shared counter
int counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *increment(void *arg) {
    int iterations = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
        // CRITICAL SECTION
        int temp = counter;
        temp++;
        counter = temp;
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    const int THREADS = 4;
    const int ITERATIONS = 1000000;

    pthread_t threads[THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, increment, &ITERATIONS);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    printf("Expected: %d, Actual: %d\n", THREADS * ITERATIONS, counter);
    pthread_mutex_destroy(&lock);
    return 0;
}

items.title: Condition Variables (Wait for Predicate)
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>

pthread_mutex_t mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t cond = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
int buffer = 0;
int has_data = 0;

void *producer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        // Wait for buffer to be empty
        while (has_data) {
            pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
        }

        buffer = i;
        has_data = 1;
        printf("Produced: %d\n", i);

        pthread_cond_signal(&cond);  // Wake consumer
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);

        // Wait for buffer to have data
        while (!has_data) {
            pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);
        }

        int val = buffer;
        has_data = 0;
        printf("Consumed: %d\n", val);

        pthread_cond_signal(&cond);  // Wake producer
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t prod, cons;
    pthread_create(&prod, NULL, producer, NULL);
    pthread_create(&cons, NULL, consumer, NULL);
    pthread_join(prod, NULL);
    pthread_join(cons, NULL);
    return 0;
}

items.title: Problem 1: Producer-Consumer (Bounded Buffer)
items.text:
/*
 * File: producer_consumer.c
 * Complete solution with 3 semaphores
 * Buffer size = 10
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define BUFFER_SIZE 10

int buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
int in = 0, out = 0;

// Semaphores
sem_t empty;   // Counts empty slots (initially BUFFER_SIZE)
sem_t full;    // Counts filled slots (initially 0)
sem_t mutex;   // Binary semaphore for buffer access (initially 1)

void *producer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) {
        int item = id * 100 + i;  // Unique item

        sem_wait(&empty);    // 1. Wait for EMPTY SLOT
        sem_wait(&mutex);    // 2. Get EXCLUSIVE ACCESS

        buffer[in] = item;
        printf("[Producer %d] Produced item %d at index %d\n", id, item, in);
        in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;

        sem_post(&mutex);    // 3. Release buffer
        sem_post(&full);     // 4. Signal: ITEM AVAILABLE

        usleep(100000);  // Simulate work
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) {
        sem_wait(&full);     // 1. Wait for ITEM
        sem_wait(&mutex);    // 2. Get EXCLUSIVE ACCESS

        int item = buffer[out];
        printf("[Consumer %d] Consumed item %d from index %d\n", id, item, out);
        out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;

        sem_post(&mutex);    // 3. Release buffer
        sem_post(&empty);    // 4. Signal: SLOT FREE

        usleep(150000);  // Simulate work
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    // Initialize semaphores
    sem_init(&empty, 0, BUFFER_SIZE);  // 10 empty slots
    sem_init(&full, 0, 0);             // 0 filled slots
    sem_init(&mutex, 0, 1);            // 1 = unlocked

    pthread_t prod[2], cons[2];
    int prod_ids[2] = {1, 2};
    int cons_ids[2] = {1, 2};

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        pthread_create(&prod[i], NULL, producer, &prod_ids[i]);
        pthread_create(&cons[i], NULL, consumer, &cons_ids[i]);
    }

    // Wait for completion
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        pthread_join(prod[i], NULL);
        pthread_join(cons[i], NULL);
    }

    // Cleanup
    sem_destroy(&empty);
    sem_destroy(&full);
    sem_destroy(&mutex);

    return 0;
}

CRITICAL ORDER (Producer): 

sem_wait(&empty);   // Wait for slot FIRST
sem_wait(&mutex);   // Then get mutex

WRONG ORDER (causes deadlock when buffer full): 

sem_wait(&mutex);   // Hold mutex
sem_wait(&empty);   // Wait for slot while holding mutex → DEADLOCK!

items.title: Problem 2: Readers-Writers (Reader Preference)
items.text:
/*
 * File: readers_writers.c
 * Multiple readers allowed, writers exclusive
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>
#include <unistd.h>

sem_t rw_mutex;  // Writer exclusion + first/last reader gate
sem_t mutex;     // Protects read_count
int read_count = 0;
int shared_data = 0;

void *reader(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        // Entry section
        sem_wait(&mutex);
        read_count++;
        if (read_count == 1) {
            sem_wait(&rw_mutex);  // First reader locks out writers
        }
        sem_post(&mutex);

        // READING
        printf("[Reader %d] Reading data = %d\n", id, shared_data);
        usleep(100000);

        // Exit section
        sem_wait(&mutex);
        read_count--;
        if (read_count == 0) {
            sem_post(&rw_mutex);  // Last reader unlocks writers
        }
        sem_post(&mutex);

        usleep(200000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

void *writer(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        sem_wait(&rw_mutex);  // Exclusive access

        // WRITING
        shared_data++;
        printf("[Writer %d] Wrote data = %d\n", id, shared_data);
        usleep(300000);

        sem_post(&rw_mutex);
        usleep(500000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    sem_init(&rw_mutex, 0, 1);
    sem_init(&mutex, 0, 1);

    pthread_t readers[3], writers[2];
    int r_ids[3] = {1, 2, 3};
    int w_ids[2] = {1, 2};

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) pthread_create(&readers[i], NULL, reader, &r_ids[i]);
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) pthread_create(&writers[i], NULL, writer, &w_ids[i]);

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) pthread_join(readers[i], NULL);
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) pthread_join(writers[i], NULL);

    sem_destroy(&rw_mutex);
    sem_destroy(&mutex);
    return 0;
}

Starvation Note: This implementation starves writers if readers keep coming. Fix: Writer preference or fair queuing (Linux qrwlock).

items.title: Problem 3: Dining Philosophers — 3 Deadlock-Free Solutions
items.text:
/*
 * File: dining_philosophers.c
 * All 3 solutions implemented
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <semaphore.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define N 5

// ============================================================
// SOLUTION 1: Capacity Limiting (Semaphore = N-1 = 4)
// ============================================================
sem_t chopstick1[N];
sem_t seats;  // Max 4 at table

void *philosopher1(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % N;

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        sem_wait(&seats);              // Reserve seat (max 4)
        sem_wait(&chopstick1[left]);   // Pick left
        sem_wait(&chopstick1[right]);  // Pick right

        printf("[Phil %d] Eating (Solution 1)\n", id);
        usleep(200000);

        sem_post(&chopstick1[left]);
        sem_post(&chopstick1[right]);
        sem_post(&seats);              // Free seat

        printf("[Phil %d] Thinking\n", id);
        usleep(100000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

// ============================================================
// SOLUTION 2: Asymmetric (Odd/Even Pick Order)
// ============================================================
sem_t chopstick2[N];

void *philosopher2(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % N;

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        if (id % 2 == 0) {  // Even: right first
            sem_wait(&chopstick2[right]);
            sem_wait(&chopstick2[left]);
        } else {  // Odd: left first
            sem_wait(&chopstick2[left]);
            sem_wait(&chopstick2[right]);
        }

        printf("[Phil %d] Eating (Solution 2)\n", id);
        usleep(200000);

        sem_post(&chopstick2[left]);
        sem_post(&chopstick2[right]);

        usleep(100000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

// ============================================================
// SOLUTION 3: Atomic Acquisition (Monitor/Mutex)
// ============================================================
sem_t chopstick3[N];
pthread_mutex_t table_mutex = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

void *philosopher3(void *arg) {
    int id = *(int*)arg;
    int left = id;
    int right = (id + 1) % N;

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&table_mutex);
        // Check if BOTH available atomically
        int left_val, right_val;
        sem_getvalue(&chopstick3[left], &left_val);
        sem_getvalue(&chopstick3[right], &right_val);

        if (left_val > 0 && right_val > 0) {
            sem_wait(&chopstick3[left]);
            sem_wait(&chopstick3[right]);
        } else {
            pthread_mutex_unlock(&table_mutex);
            usleep(10000);  // Back off
            continue;
        }
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&table_mutex);

        printf("[Phil %d] Eating (Solution 3)\n", id);
        usleep(200000);

        sem_post(&chopstick3[left]);
        sem_post(&chopstick3[right]);
        usleep(100000);
    }
    return NULL;
}

// ============================================================
// Test harness
// ============================================================
void run_solution(int sol_num, void *(*phil_func)(void*)) {
    sem_t chopsticks[N];
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sem_init(&chopsticks[i], 0, 1);

    if (sol_num == 1) sem_init(&seats, 0, 4);
    if (sol_num == 3) pthread_mutex_init(&table_mutex, NULL);

    pthread_t threads[N];
    int ids[N] = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4};

    printf("\n=== Solution %d ===\n", sol_num);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, phil_func, &ids[i]);
    }

    sleep(3);  // Let them run

    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pthread_cancel(threads[i]);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);

    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sem_destroy(&chopsticks[i]);
    if (sol_num == 1) sem_destroy(&seats);
    if (sol_num == 3) pthread_mutex_destroy(&table_mutex);
}

int main() {
    run_solution(1, philosopher1);
    run_solution(2, philosopher2);
    run_solution(3, philosopher3);
    return 0;
}

items.title: The Problem
items.text:
HIGH (H) needs mutex held by LOW (L)
    H blocks
MEDIUM (M) becomes ready → preempts L
    L can't run → can't release mutex → H blocked by M indirectly!
path: Topic 12 (Detailed): Process Synchronization — Complete Programs with Comments

items.title: Priority Inheritance Protocol
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

pthread_mutex_t mutex;
pthread_mutexattr_t attr;

void *high_priority(void *arg) {
    printf("[HIGH] Trying to lock mutex...\n");
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
    printf("[HIGH] Got mutex, doing work...\n");
    sleep(2);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    printf("[HIGH] Released mutex\n");
    return NULL;
}

void *low_priority(void *arg) {
    printf("[LOW] Locking mutex first...\n");
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);
    printf("[LOW] Got mutex, doing long work...\n");
    sleep(5);  // Long critical section
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);
    printf("[LOW] Released mutex\n");
    return NULL;
}

void *medium_priority(void *arg) {
    sleep(1);  // Let low get mutex first
    printf("[MEDIUM] Running CPU-intensive work (no mutex)...\n");
    sleep(3);
    printf("[MEDIUM] Done\n");
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    // Enable priority inheritance
    pthread_mutexattr_init(&attr);
    pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(&attr, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT);
    pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, &attr);

    pthread_t high, low, medium;

    // Create with priorities (requires root for real-time)
    pthread_create(&low, NULL, low_priority, NULL);
    sleep(1);  // Ensure low gets mutex
    pthread_create(&medium, NULL, medium_priority, NULL);
    pthread_create(&high, NULL, high_priority, NULL);

    pthread_join(high, NULL);
    pthread_join(low, NULL);
    pthread_join(medium, NULL);

    pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex);
    pthread_mutexattr_destroy(&attr);
    return 0;
}

Without inheritance: Medium blocks Low → High waits forever indirectly. With inheritance: Low inherits High's priority → Medium can't preempt → Low finishes → High proceeds.
