items.title: Topic 12: Process Synchronization — Software Approaches & Principles
items.text: Source: Lecture 7 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 5, 6, Stallings Ch. 5, 6, Stevens & Rago Ch. 10, 11)

items.title: Race Condition
items.text:
// counter++ compiles to 3 instructions:
register = counter;    // LOAD
register = register + 1;  // INC
counter = register;    // STORE

// Interleaving (counter starts at 5):
Thread A: LOAD 5          counter=5
Thread A: INC 6
Thread B: LOAD 5          ← PREEMPTION! counter still 5
Thread B: INC 4
Thread B: STORE 4         counter=4
Thread A: STORE 6         counter=6  ← LOST UPDATE! Should be 5.

Race Condition: Outcome depends on timing of execution — non-deterministic, hard to reproduce.

Silberschatz: "A race condition occurs when multiple processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently, and the outcome of the execution depends on the particular order in which the access takes place." [§6.1.1]

items.title: Kernel Example: PID Allocation
items.text:
P0: fork() → read next_pid (2615)
P1: fork() → read next_pid (2615)  ← both get same PID!
Both write back 2616 → duplicate PIDs assigned

items.title: Requirements (ALL must hold)
items.text: Requirement Meaning Mutual Exclusion Only one thread in CS at a time Progress If CS free, some waiting thread enters (no deadlock) Bounded Waiting No starvation — limit on how many times others can cut in line

items.title: Process Structure
items.text:
do {
    /* ENTRY SECTION */  // Request permission
    /* CRITICAL SECTION */  // Mutate shared data
    /* EXIT SECTION */   // Notify done
    /* REMAINDER SECTION */
} while (true);

items.title: Peterson's Algorithm (2 Processes)
items.text:
boolean flag[2] = {false, false};
int turn;

Process i:
flag[i] = true;
turn = j;
while (flag[j] && turn == j);  // spin
// CRITICAL SECTION
flag[i] = false;

Assumption: load/store atomic and execute in program order.

Reality on modern CPUs: 

Compiler/CPU may reorder:
  turn = j;        →  moves BEFORE flag[i] = true
  flag[i] = true;

Or writes sit in store buffer (not visible to other cores yet)
Result: Both threads enter CS → mutual exclusion violated.

Fix: Memory barriers (mfence, dmb, sync) — but now architecture-specific.

Silberschatz: "Peterson's algorithm is a classic software-based solution to the critical-section problem for two processes." [§6.3.1]

items.title: 12.4 Hardware Atomic Instructions
items.text: Modern CPUs provide indivisible read-modify-write instructions.

items.title: test_and_set (TSL) — x86 XCHG, ARM LDREX/STREX
items.text:
boolean test_and_set(boolean *target) {
    boolean rv = *target;  // atomic read
    *target = TRUE;        // atomic write
    return rv;             // return old value
}

items.title: compare_and_swap (CAS) — x86 CMPXCHG, ARM CAS
items.text:
int compare_and_swap(int *addr, int expected, int new_val) {
    int old = *addr;
    if (*addr == expected) *addr = new_val;
    return old;  // all atomic
}

Key: Single bus cycle — no interleaving possible.

Silberschatz: "Modern computer architectures provide special atomic hardware instructions." [§6.4]

items.title: TSL Spinlock
items.text:
boolean lock = false;

while (test_and_set(&lock)) ;  // spin until we get false (lock was free)
// CRITICAL SECTION
lock = false;  // release

items.title: CAS Spinlock
items.text:
int lock = 0;

while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0) ;  // spin until 0→1 succeeds
// CRITICAL SECTION
lock = 0;

items.title: Evaluation
items.text:
Property TSL Spinlock CAS Spinlock Mutual Exclusion ✅ ✅ Progress ✅ ✅ Bounded Waiting ❌ (starvation possible) ❌

Problem: No queue — whoever wins the race gets the lock. A thread can starve forever.

items.title: 12.6 Bounded-Waiting Spinlock
items.text:
boolean waiting[N] = {false};
boolean lock = false;

// Process i:
waiting[i] = true;
key = true;
while (waiting[i] && key) {
    key = test_and_set(&lock);  // try to get lock
}
waiting[i] = false;

// CRITICAL SECTION

// Hand off to next waiter (circular queue)
j = (i + 1) % N;
while (j != i && !waiting[j]) j = (j + 1) % n;

if (j == i) lock = false;       // nobody waiting
else waiting[j] = false;        // wake next waiter

Guarantees bounded waiting: Each waiter served in turn (max N-1 others before you).

Silberschatz: "This algorithm satisfies all three critical-section requirements." [§6.6]

items.title: Spinlock vs Mutex
items.text: Spinlock Mutex (Blocking) Wait behavior Busy loop (burns CPU) block() → yield CPU, scheduler runs other thread Context switch None Yes (costly) Best for Very short CS, multicore Longer CS, uniprocessor, general use

items.title: Mutex Implementation (Conceptual)
items.text:
typedef struct {
    boolean available;
    queue<thread> waiters;
} mutex;

acquire(mutex *m) {
    if (test_and_set(&m->available) == false) return;  // fast path
    // contended: enqueue self, block()
    enqueue(&m->waiters, current_thread);
    block();  // scheduler switches away
}

release(mutex *m) {
    if (m->waiters.empty()) {
        m->available = true;
    } else {
        thread *next = dequeue(&m->waiters);
        wakeup(next);  // handoff directly (no lock release gap)
    }
}

items.title: Mutex
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>

// Static init
pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;

// Dynamic init
pthread_mutex_t lock;
pthread_mutex_init(&lock, NULL);

// Use
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);   // blocks if busy
// CRITICAL SECTION
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock); // must be called by owner

// Cleanup
pthread_mutex_destroy(&lock);

items.title: Semaphores (Dijkstra's Generalization)
items.text:
• Semaphore S: Integer + wait queue
  • P() / wait(): "Proberen" (test) — acquire resource
  • V() / signal(): "Verhogen" (increment) — release resource
#include <semaphore.h>

// Init: pshared=0 (threads), !=0 (processes, in shared memory)
sem_t sem;
sem_init(&sem, 0, 10);  // 10 available slots

// Wait (P)
sem_wait(&sem);         // blocks if value == 0

// Signal (V)
sem_post(&sem);         // increments, wakes one waiter

// Cleanup
sem_destroy(&sem);

items.title: Semaphore Value Meaning
items.text: Value Meaning S > 0 S resources available S = 0 No resources, no waiters S < 0 \|S\| threads blocked waiting

items.title: Types
items.text: Type Range Use Case Binary 0 or 1 Mutual exclusion (mutex equivalent) Counting ≥ 0 Resource pools (DB connections, buffer slots)

items.title: 12.9 Classical Problem: Producer-Consumer with Semaphores
items.text:
sem_t empty = N;   // counting: N free slots
sem_t full = 0;    // counting: 0 filled slots
sem_t mutex = 1;   // binary: protect buffer

// PRODUCER
produce(item);
sem_wait(&empty);      // 1. Wait for FREE SLOT (blocks if full)
sem_wait(&mutex);      // 2. Get EXCLUSIVE ACCESS
add_to_buffer(item);
sem_post(&mutex);      // 3. Release buffer
sem_post(&full);       // 4. Signal: one more item available

// CONSUMER
sem_wait(&full);       // 1. Wait for ITEM (blocks if empty)
sem_wait(&mutex);      // 2. Get EXCLUSIVE ACCESS
item = remove_from_buffer();
sem_post(&mutex);      // 3. Release buffer
sem_post(&empty);      // 4. Signal: one more slot free
consume(item);

Critical Order: Wait on counting semaphore FIRST, then mutex. - Reverse → deadlock (hold mutex while waiting for slot)

items.title: Rules
items.text: Operation Allowed Concurrently? Multiple Readers ✅ Yes Multiple Writers ❌ No Reader + Writer ❌ No

items.title: Solution: Reader Preference
items.text:
sem_t rw_mutex = 1;  // Writer exclusion + first/last reader gate
sem_t mutex = 1;     // Protects read_count
int read_count = 0;  // Active readers

// Writer (Simple)
wait(rw_mutex);
// ... write ...
signal(rw_mutex);

// Reader (Tricky)
wait(mutex);
read_count++;
if (read_count == 1) wait(rw_mutex);  // First reader locks out writers
signal(mutex);

// ... READ ...

wait(mutex);
read_count--;
if (read_count == 0) signal(rw_mutex);  // Last reader unlocks writers
signal(mutex);

items.title: Starvation Variants
items.text: Variation Who Starves Reader Preference Writers — if readers keep coming, read_count never hits 0 Writer Preference Readers — new readers wait behind queued writers

items.title: Linux Solutions
items.text: Mechanism How It Works rwlock_t Simple RW spinlock, reader-biased qrwlock Fair FIFO queue — no starvation RCU (Read-Copy-Update) Readers NEVER block — zero overhead reads!

items.title: RCU Magic
items.text:
Writer:
  1. Allocate new copy of data
  2. Modify copy
  3. Atomic pointer swap (new → live)
  4. Wait for "grace period" (all pre-existing readers done)
  5. Free old copy

Reader:
  1. Read pointer (no lock!)
  2. Access data
  3. Done
Used in: Linux VFS, networking, RCU-protected linked lists

items.title: Problem
items.text:
• 5 philosophers, 5 chopsticks (shared between neighbors)
  • Need 2 chopsticks to eat
  • Cycle: Think → Pick left → Pick right → Eat → Put both → Think

items.title: Naive Solution (Deadlocks!)
items.text:
wait(chopstick[i]);           // Left
wait(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);     // Right
// eat
signal(chopstick[i]);
signal(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
Deadlock: All 5 pick up left simultaneously → all wait for right forever.

items.title: 1. Capacity Limiting (Semaphore = 4)
items.text:
sem_t seats = 4;  // Max 4 at table

wait(seats);          // Reserve seat
wait(chopstick[i]);
wait(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
// eat
signal(chopstick[i]);
signal(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
signal(seats);        // Free seat
Why it works: With 4 philosophers and 5 chopsticks, at least one can always get both.

items.title: 2. Asymmetric (Odd/Even)
items.text:
if (i % 2 == 0) {          // Even: right first
    wait(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
    wait(chopstick[i]);
} else {                    // Odd: left first
    wait(chopstick[i]);
    wait(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
}
// eat (same for both)
signal(chopstick[i]);
signal(chopstick[(i+1)%5]);
Why it works: Breaks circular wait — adjacent philosophers grab in opposite order.

items.title: 3. Atomic Acquisition (Monitor)
items.text:
// Inside a mutex (only one philosopher checks at a time):
wait(table_mutex);
if (chopstick[i] && chopstick[(i+1)%5]) {
    take_both();
}
signal(table_mutex);
Why it works: Check-and-acquire is atomic — no partial state possible.

items.title: The Problem
items.text:
P1 (High) needs mutex held by P3 (Low)
    P1 blocks
P2 (Medium) becomes ready → preempts P3
    P3 can't run → can't release mutex → P1 blocked by P2 indirectly!

items.title: Priority Inheritance Protocol
items.text:
When P1 (High) blocks on mutex held by P3 (Low):
    P3 temporarily inherits P1's priority
    P2 (Medium) can no longer preempt P3
    P3 finishes CS, releases mutex
    P3 drops to Low priority
    P1 acquires mutex, runs

Implemented in: Linux pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT), Windows, VxWorks (fixed Mars Pathfinder)

Silberschatz: "The priority inheritance protocol is a technique for preventing priority inversion." [§6.10]

items.title: 12.13 Modern Synchronization Stack
items.text:
APPLICATION CODE
    │
    ▼
pthread_mutex_lock() / sem_wait() / pthread_cond_wait()
    │
    ▼
LIBRARY (glibc/pthreads)
    │  - Fast path: atomic CAS in userspace (futex)
    │  - Slow path: syscall (futex_wait / futex_wake)
    ▼
KERNEL
    │  - Wait queues
    │  - Scheduler integration
    │  - Priority inheritance
    ▼
HARDWARE
    │  - test_and_set / compare_and_swap
    │  - Cache coherency (MESI protocol)
    │  - Memory barriers

Modern optimization: futex (Fast Userspace Mutex) — uncontended lock/unlock entirely in userspace via atomic CAS. Syscall only on contention.

items.title: 12.14 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• Race conditions = non-atomic read-modify-write + preemption [Silberschatz §6.1]
  • Critical section needs: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting [Silberschatz §6.2]
  • Software algorithms (Peterson) fail on modern CPUs due to reordering/store buffers [Silberschatz §6.3]
  • Hardware atomics (TSL, CAS) provide indivisible RMW — foundation of all locks [Silberschatz §6.4]
  • Spinlocks = busy-wait on atomic; good for short CS, bad for long/uniprocessor [Silberschatz §6.5]
  • Mutexes/Semaphores = blocking (yield CPU) + wait queues — general purpose [Silberschatz §6.7-8]
  • Semaphores generalize mutexes: counting = resource pools [Silberschatz §6.8]
  • Producer-consumer: 3 semaphores (mutex + empty + full) [Silberschatz §6.9.1]
  • Readers-Writers: read_count tracks readers; first/last reader gates writers [Silberschatz §6.9.2]
  • RCU: Readers never block — extreme read scalability [Silberschatz §6.9.2]
  • Priority inversion: medium blocks low blocks high → fix with priority inheritance [Silberschatz §6.10]
  • Real code: Use pthread_mutex, sem_t, pthread_cond — not raw atomics

items.title: Topic 13: Deadlocks — Characterization, Prevention, Avoidance
items.text: Source: Lecture 11 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 9 (Silberschatz Ch. 7, Stallings Ch. 6, Stevens & Rago Ch. 10)

items.title: 13.1 Deadlock Definition
items.text:
Deadlock: Two or more waiting processes unable to change state because the resources they requested are held by other waiting processes. [Silberschatz §7.1]

P1 holds A, needs B
P2 holds B, needs A
Neither can proceed. Neither will release. Forever.

items.title: System Model
items.text:
• Resource types: R₁, R₂, ..., Rₘ
  • Each type Rᵢ has Wᵢ instances (e.g., 3 printers = 3 instances)
  • Resource types: Physical (CPU, memory, I/O) + Logical (semaphores, mutexes, DB records)

items.title: Resource Utilization Lifecycle
items.text: Request → Use → Release

items.title: 13.2 Four Coffman Conditions
items.text:
# Condition Meaning Preventable? 1 Mutual Exclusion Resource non-shareable (printer, mutex) ❌ Hard (hardware reality) 2 Hold and Wait Hold some, request more ✅ Yes 3 No Preemption Can't forcibly take resources ✅ Sometimes 4 Circular Wait P₀→P₁→...→Pₙ→P₀ ✅ Yes (standard method)

Deadlock iff all 4 true simultaneously.

Silberschatz: "A deadlock situation can arise if and only if the following four conditions hold simultaneously..." [§7.3]

items.title: 13.3 Deadlock vs Starvation
items.text: Aspect Starvation Deadlock Definition Process waits indefinitely due to higher-priority tasks Circular dependency of waiting threads Resolution Can end if load subsides Cannot end without external intervention Relationship All deadlocked processes are starved Not all starved processes are deadlocked

items.title: Notation
items.text: Element Symbol Meaning Process Circle (○) P₁, P₂, ... Resource Rectangle with dots R₁, R₂, ... (dots = instances) Request Edge Pᵢ → Rⱼ Process Pᵢ requests Rⱼ Assignment Edge Rⱼ → Pᵢ Instance of Rⱼ allocated to Pᵢ

items.title: Cycle Theorems
items.text:
Graph Has Single-Instance Resources Multi-Instance Resources No cycle ✅ No deadlock ✅ No deadlock Cycle ❌ Deadlock guaranteed ⚠️ Possible deadlock

Silberschatz: "If the resource-allocation graph contains no cycles, then the system is not deadlocked. If the graph contains a cycle, then the system may be deadlocked." [§7.4.2]

items.title: 13.5 Four Handling Strategies
items.text: Strategy Approach Used In Practice? Prevention Negate one Coffman condition Partial (circular wait) Avoidance Banker's Algorithm — stay in safe states Rare (needs max claims) Detection Periodic check + recovery Databases, distributed systems Ostrich Ignore it Linux, Windows, most OSes

items.title: 13.6 Deadlock Prevention (Negate One Condition)
items.text: Condition Prevention Method Drawback Mutual Exclusion Make all resources shareable Impossible for printers, mutexes Hold and Wait Request ALL at once, OR release all before new request Low utilization, starvation No Preemption If request fails, force-release ALL held Only works for saveable state (memory, CPU) Circular Wait Global resource ordering — request only in increasing order Standard practical method

items.title: Resource Ordering (The Practical One)
items.text:
Assign numbers: Disk=1, Printer=2, Tape=3, Network=4

Process can request: Disk → Printer ✅
Process CANNOT request: Printer → Disk ❌ (would create cycle)

Proof: Cycle requires F(R₀) < F(R₁) < ... < F(R₀) — mathematical impossibility.

Silberschatz: "We can prevent deadlock by ensuring that at least one of the four necessary conditions cannot hold." [§7.6]

items.title: Wait-For Graph (Single-Instance Resources)
items.text:
Collapse RAG by removing resource nodes: 

RAG: P1 → R1 → P2 → R2 → P1
WFG: P1 → P2 → P1  (cycle = deadlock)

Algorithm: DFS cycle detection, O(n²) — run periodically.

items.title: Key Insight
items.text: Avoidance ≠ Prevention. - Prevention = never allow conditions - Avoidance = dynamically check before each grant

items.title: Safe State
items.text:
There exists a safe sequence <P₁, P₃, P₄, P₀, P₂> where each process can get its max needs, finish, and release resources for the next.

Safe State          Unsafe State          Deadlock
    │                    │                    │
    ├─ All can finish   ├─ Some might finish  └─ None can finish
    │                    │                    │
    ▼                    ▼                    ▼
No deadlock         Deadlock possible      Deadlock actual

Avoidance Rule: Only grant request if resulting state is Safe.

items.title: Data Structures (n processes, m resource types)
items.text: Structure Size Meaning Available[m] Vector Free instances of each resource Max[n][m] Matrix Max demand of each process Allocation[n][m] Matrix Currently held by each process Need[n][m] Matrix Max - Allocation (remaining need)

items.title: Safety Algorithm (Is Current State Safe?)
items.text:
Work = Available[:]
Finish = [False] * n

while True:
    # Find process that can finish with current Work
    found = False
    for i in range(n):
        if not Finish[i] and Need[i] <= Work:  # element-wise
            Work = Work + Allocation[i]         # they finish, release
            Finish[i] = True
            found = True
            break
    if not found:
        break

return all(Finish)  # True = SAFE

items.title: Resource Request Algorithm (Can Pᵢ Get Request?)
items.text:
Requestᵢ arrives:

1. Requestᵢ ≤ Needᵢ?     → No: error (exceeds claim)
2. Requestᵢ ≤ Available? → No: wait (not enough free)
3. PRETEND to allocate:
   Available -= Requestᵢ
   Allocationᵢ += Requestᵢ
   Needᵢ -= Requestᵢ
4. Run Safety Algorithm:
   If SAFE → Commit (grant)
   If UNSAFE → Rollback, Pᵢ waits

items.title: System Setup
items.text:
• 5 Processes: P₀, P₁, P₂, P₃, P₄
  • 3 Resources: A(10), B(5), C(7)

items.title: Initial State (T₀)
items.text:
Process Allocation (A B C) Max (A B C) Need = Max−Alloc P₀ 0 1 0 7 5 3 7 4 3 P₁ 2 0 0 3 2 2 1 2 2 P₂ 3 0 2 9 0 2 6 0 0 P₃ 2 1 1 2 2 2 0 1 1 P₄ 0 0 2 4 3 3 4 3 1

Available = Total − ΣAllocation = (10,5,7) − (7,2,5) = (3, 3, 2)

items.title: Safety Check at T₀
items.text:
Work = (3,3,2), Finish = [F,F,F,F,F]

Step 1: P₁ need (1,2,2) ≤ (3,3,2)? YES
        Work = (3,3,2) + (2,0,0) = (5,3,2)
        Finish[1] = T

Step 2: P₃ need (0,1,1) ≤ (5,3,2)? YES
        Work = (5,3,2) + (2,1,1) = (7,4,3)
        Finish[3] = T

Step 3: P₄ need (4,3,1) ≤ (7,4,3)? YES
        Work = (7,4,3) + (0,0,2) = (7,4,5)
        Finish[4] = T

Step 4: P₂ need (6,0,0) ≤ (7,4,5)? YES
        Work = (7,4,5) + (3,0,2) = (10,4,7)
        Finish[2] = T

Step 5: P₀ need (7,4,3) ≤ (10,4,7)? YES
        Work = (10,4,7) + (0,1,0) = (10,5,7)
        Finish[0] = T

ALL TRUE → SAFE STATE ✅
Safe Sequence: ⟨P₁, P₃, P₄, P₂, P₀⟩

items.title: Scenario B: P₄ Requests (3, 3, 0)
items.text:
Available = (2,3,0)  (after Scenario A)
Request₄ = (3,3,0)

Request ≤ Available? (3,3,0) ≤ (2,3,0) ❌ (needs 3 A, only 2 free)

DENY → P₄ waits

items.title: Scenario C: P₀ Requests (0, 2, 0)
items.text:
Available = (2,3,0)
Request₀ = (0,2,0)

1. (0,2,0) ≤ (7,4,3) ✅
2. (0,2,0) ≤ (2,3,0) ✅

PRETEND:
Available' = (2,1,0)
Allocation₀' = (0,3,0)
Need₀' = (7,2,3)

Safety with Work=(2,1,0):
  P₀: (7,2,3) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌
  P₁: (0,2,0) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (B: 2>1)
  P₂: (6,0,0) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (A: 6>2)
  P₃: (0,1,1) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (C: 1>0)
  P₄: (4,3,1) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌

NO PROCESS CAN FINISH → UNSAFE ❌

ROLLBACK → DENY → P₀ waits

Key Insight: Even though resources exist, granting this request traps the system where no process can ever complete — unsafe state.

items.title: 13.11 Summary Table
items.text: Strategy Approach Pros Cons Prevention Negate one Coffman condition Guaranteed no deadlock Low utilization, restrictive Avoidance (Banker's) Dynamic safe-state checks Max utilization, no deadlock Needs max claims; O(n²m) per request Detection Periodic WFG cycle check Flexible, no advance info needed Recovery complex; deadlock occurs first Ostrich Ignore Simple, no overhead Deadlocks happen (rare)

items.title: 13.12 When to Use What
items.text: Situation Best Approach General OS Ostrich (ignore) — deadlocks rare, recovery via reboot Database Detection + victim rollback (timeout or WFG) Real-time/Embedded Prevention (resource ordering) or Avoidance Safety-critical Avoidance (Banker's) or static analysis Mutex locks in code Prevention: always acquire in fixed global order

items.title: 13.13 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• 4 Coffman conditions = deadlock iff ALL true [Silberschatz §7.3]
  • RAG cycle theorems = single vs multi-instance difference [Silberschatz §7.4.2]
  • Banker's Safety Algorithm = greedy; find any finishable process, add allocation to Work, repeat [Silberschatz §7.9.2]
  • Request Algorithm = 4 checks → pretend → safety → commit/rollback [Silberschatz §7.9.3]
  • Prevention = global lock ordering (practical) [Silberschatz §7.6.4]
  • Safe vs Unsafe vs Deadlock = Venn diagram relationships [Silberschatz §7.8.2]
  • For your code: Just use global lock ordering — prevents circular wait = prevents deadlock

items.title: 13.14 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:

items.title: 13.1 Deadlock Definition
items.text:
Deadlock: A set of processes is deadlocked if each process in the set is waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause.

P1 holds A, needs B
P2 holds B, needs A
Neither can proceed. Neither will release. Forever.

items.title: Safety Algorithm (Is Current State Safe?)
items.text:
Work = Available[:]           # (3,3,2)
Finish = [False] * n          # [F,F,F,F,F]

while True:
    found = False
    for i in range(n):
        if not Finish[i] and Need[i] <= Work:  # Element-wise comparison
            Work = Work + Allocation[i]        # They finish, release
            Finish[i] = True
            found = True
            break
    if not found:
        break

return all(Finish)  # True = SAFE

items.title: Step-by-Step Trace
items.text:
Step 1: Work=(3,3,2), Finish=[F,F,F,F,F]
        P₁: Need=(1,2,2) ≤ (3,3,2)? YES
        Work = (3,3,2) + (2,0,0) = (5,3,2)
        Finish[1]=T

Step 2: Work=(5,3,2), Finish=[F,T,F,F,F]
        P₃: Need=(0,1,1) ≤ (5,3,2)? YES
        Work = (5,3,2) + (2,1,1) = (7,4,3)
        Finish[3]=T

Step 3: Work=(7,4,3), Finish=[F,T,F,T,F]
        P₄: Need=(4,3,1) ≤ (7,4,3)? YES
        Work = (7,4,3) + (0,0,2) = (7,4,5)
        Finish[4]=T

Step 4: Work=(7,4,5), Finish=[F,T,F,T,T]
        P₂: Need=(6,0,0) ≤ (7,4,5)? YES
        Work = (7,4,5) + (3,0,2) = (10,4,7)
        Finish[2]=T

Step 5: Work=(10,4,7), Finish=[F,T,T,T,T]
        P₀: Need=(7,4,3) ≤ (10,4,7)? YES
        Work = (10,4,7) + (0,1,0) = (10,5,7)
        Finish[0]=T

ALL TRUE → SAFE STATE ✅
Safe Sequence: ⟨P₁, P₃, P₄, P₂, P₀⟩

items.title: Resource Request Algorithm
items.text:
Requestᵢ arrives for Request vector:

1. Requestᵢ ≤ Needᵢ?     → No: Error (exceeds claim)
2. Requestᵢ ≤ Available? → No: Wait (insufficient free)
3. PRETEND to allocate:
   Available  -= Requestᵢ
   Allocationᵢ += Requestᵢ
   Needᵢ      -= Requestᵢ
4. Run Safety Algorithm:
   If SAFE   → Commit (grant request)
   If UNSAFE → Rollback, Pᵢ waits

items.text:
Available = (2,3,0)
Request₀ = (0,2,0)

1. (0,2,0) ≤ (7,4,3) ✅
2. (0,2,0) ≤ (2,3,0) ✅

PRETEND:
Available'   = (2,1,0)
Allocation₀' = (0,3,0)
Need₀'       = (7,2,3)

Run Safety with Work=(2,1,0):
  P₀: (7,2,3) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌
  P₁: (0,2,0) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (B: 2>1)
  P₂: (6,0,0) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (A: 6>2)
  P₃: (0,1,1) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌ (C: 1>0)
  P₄: (4,3,1) ≤ (2,1,0) ❌

NO PROCESS CAN FINISH → UNSAFE ❌

ROLLBACK → DENY → P₀ waits

Key Insight: Even though resources exist, granting this request traps the system where no process can ever complete — unsafe state.

items.title: 13.4 Banker's Algorithm Implementation
items.text:
/*
 * File: bankers_algorithm.c
 * Complete Banker's Algorithm implementation
 * Compile: gcc -o bankers bankers_algorithm.c
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

#define MAX_PROCESSES 10
#define MAX_RESOURCES 5

typedef struct {
    int max[MAX_RESOURCES];
    int allocation[MAX_RESOURCES];
    int need[MAX_RESOURCES];
} Process;

int n_processes, n_resources;
int available[MAX_RESOURCES];
Process processes[MAX_PROCESSES];

void print_state(const char *title) {
    printf("\n=== %s ===\n", title);
    printf("Available: ");
    for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) printf("%d ", available[j]);
    printf("\n\n");

    printf("%-8s %-20s %-20s %-20s\n", "Process", "Max", "Allocation", "Need");
    for (int i = 0; i < n_processes; i++) {
        printf("P%-7d ", i);
        for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) printf("%d ", processes[i].max[j]);
        printf("     ");
        for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) printf("%d ", processes[i].allocation[j]);
        printf("     ");
        for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) printf("%d ", processes[i].need[j]);
        printf("\n");
    }
}

bool vector_leq(int a[], int b[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (a[i] > b[i]) return false;
    return true;
}

void vector_add(int a[], int b[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] += b[i];
}

void vector_sub(int a[], int b[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] -= b[i];
}

bool safety_check(int work[], bool finish[]) {
    // Find a process that can finish
    for (int i = 0; i < n_processes; i++) {
        if (!finish[i] && vector_leq(processes[i].need, work, n_resources)) {
            // Process i can finish
            vector_add(work, processes[i].allocation, n_resources);
            finish[i] = true;
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}

bool is_safe_state() {
    int work[MAX_RESOURCES];
    bool finish[MAX_PROCESSES] = {false};

    memcpy(work, available, n_resources * sizeof(int));

    // Try to find safe sequence
    for (int count = 0; count < n_processes; count++) {
        if (!safety_check(work, finish)) {
            return false;  // No process can finish, unsafe
        }
    }
    return true;
}

bool request_resources(int pid, int request[]) {
    printf("\n=== Request from P%d ===\n", pid);
    for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) printf("%d ", request[j]);
    printf("\n");

    // Check 1: Request ≤ Need
    if (!vector_leq(request, processes[pid].need, n_resources)) {
        printf("DENIED: Request exceeds Need\n");
        return false;
    }

    // Check 2: Request ≤ Available
    if (!vector_leq(request, available, n_resources)) {
        printf("DENIED: Request exceeds Available (must wait)\n");
        return false;
    }

    // PRETEND to allocate
    int saved_available[MAX_RESOURCES];
    int saved_allocation[MAX_RESOURCES];
    int saved_need[MAX_RESOURCES];

    memcpy(saved_available, available, n_resources * sizeof(int));
    memcpy(saved_allocation, processes[pid].allocation, n_resources * sizeof(int));
    memcpy(saved_need, processes[pid].need, n_resources * sizeof(int));

    vector_sub(available, request, n_resources);
    vector_add(processes[pid].allocation, request, n_resources);
    vector_sub(processes[pid].need, request, n_resources);

    // Check safety
    if (is_safe_state()) {
        printf("GRANTED: Safe state\n");
        return true;
    } else {
        printf("DENIED: Would lead to unsafe state\n");
        // Rollback
        memcpy(available, saved_available, n_resources * sizeof(int));
        memcpy(processes[pid].allocation, saved_allocation, n_resources * sizeof(int));
        memcpy(processes[pid].need, saved_need, n_resources * sizeof(int));
        return false;
    }
}

void compute_need() {
    for (int i = 0; i < n_processes; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) {
            processes[i].need[j] = processes[i].max[j] - processes[i].allocation[j];
        }
    }
}

int main() {
    // System from slides: 5 processes, 3 resources
    n_processes = 5;
    n_resources = 3;

    // Total resources: A=10, B=5, C=7
    int total[] = {10, 5, 7};

    // Initial state from slides
    Process init[] = {
        {{7,5,3}, {0,1,0}, {0}},
        {{3,2,2}, {2,0,0}, {0}},
        {{9,0,2}, {3,0,2}, {0}},
        {{2,2,2}, {2,1,1}, {0}},
        {{4,3,3}, {0,0,2}, {0}},
    };

    for (int i = 0; i < n_processes; i++) {
        processes[i] = init[i];
        for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) {
            processes[i].need[j] = processes[i].max[j] - processes[i].allocation[j];
        }
    }

    // Available = Total - Sum(Allocation)
    for (int j = 0; j < n_resources; j++) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n_processes; i++) sum += processes[i].allocation[j];
        available[j] = total[j] - sum;
    }

    print_state("INITIAL STATE");

    // Test initial safety
    printf("Initial state is %s\n", is_safe_state() ? "SAFE" : "UNSAFE");

    // Scenario A: P1 requests (1,0,2)
    int req1[] = {1, 0, 2};
    request_resources(1, req1);
    print_state("AFTER P1 REQUEST (1,0,2)");

    // Scenario B: P4 requests (3,3,0)
    int req2[] = {3, 3, 0};
    request_resources(4, req2);
    print_state("AFTER P4 REQUEST (3,3,0) - should be denied");

    // Scenario C: P0 requests (0,2,0)
    int req3[] = {0, 2, 0};
    request_resources(0, req3);
    print_state("AFTER P0 REQUEST (0,2,0) - should be denied");

    return 0;
}

Compile & Run: 

gcc -o bankers bankers_algorithm.c
./bankers

items.title: Negating Each Coffman Condition
items.text: Condition Prevention Method Drawback Mutual Exclusion Make all resources shareable Impossible for printers, mutexes Hold and Wait Request ALL at once, OR release all before new request Low utilization, starvation No Preemption If request fails, force-release ALL held Only works for saveable state Circular Wait Global resource ordering Standard practical method

items.title: Resource Ordering (The Practical One)
items.text:
/*
 * File: deadlock_prevention.c
 * Global linear lock ordering prevents circular wait
 */

#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>

// Resources assigned numbers:
#define LOCK_DISK     1
#define LOCK_PRINTER  2
#define LOCK_TAPE     3
#define LOCK_NETWORK  4

pthread_mutex_t locks[5];  // Index by resource number

// RULE: Always acquire locks in INCREASING order
void safe_operation_1() {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_DISK]);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_PRINTER]);
    // ... work ...
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&locks[LOCK_PRINTER]);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&locks[LOCK_DISK]);
}

void safe_operation_2() {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_PRINTER]);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_TAPE]);
    // ... work ...
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&locks[LOCK_TAPE]);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&locks[LOCK_PRINTER]);
}

// VIOLATION: Would create cycle
void unsafe_operation() {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_PRINTER]);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&locks[LOCK_DISK]);  // WRONG ORDER!
    // ...
}

int main() {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) pthread_mutex_init(&locks[i], NULL);

    // Test safe operations
    pthread_t t1, t2;
    pthread_create(&t1, NULL, (void*)safe_operation_1, NULL);
    pthread_create(&t2, NULL, (void*)safe_operation_2, NULL);
    pthread_join(t1, NULL);
    pthread_join(t2, NULL);

    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) pthread_mutex_destroy(&locks[i]);
    return 0;
}

Proof: Cycle requires F(R₀) < F(R₁) < ... < F(R₀) — mathematical impossibility.

items.title: Topic 14: Signals & Signal Handling
items.text: Source: Lecture 13 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 11

items.title: Definition
items.text: A signal is a software interrupt mechanism used in UNIX-like systems to notify a process/thread that a specific asynchronous or synchronous event has occurred.

items.title: Universal Signal Lifecycle
items.text:
1. Generation — Hardware exception, kernel event, timer, or user action triggers signal
  2. Delivery — Kernel marks signal as pending, delivers to target process/thread
  3. Handling — Process executes designated action (default or user-defined handler)

items.title: Synchronous Signals
items.text: Generated by internal operation of running program. - Delivered to the identical thread whose instruction triggered the event - Examples: - SIGSEGV — Illegal memory access - SIGFPE — Integer division by zero - SIGILL — Illegal machine instruction

items.title: Asynchronous Signals
items.text: Generated by external event. - Delivered to process or any thread capable of receiving it - Examples: - SIGINT — User presses <Ctrl>+<C> - SIGALRM — Timer expiration - SIGCHLD — Child process termination - Explicit kill() from another process

items.title: Two Types
items.text: Type Description Default Handler Kernel-provided; actions: Terminate, Core Dump, Ignore, Stop, Continue User-Defined Handler Custom C function registered via signal() or sigaction()

items.title: Non-Catchable Signals (Critical!)
items.text: Signal Number Description SIGKILL 9 Forceful termination — uncatchable, unignorable SIGSTOP 17/19/23 Forceful suspension — uncatchable, unignorable

items.title: The Delivery Problem
items.text:
• Single-threaded: unambiguous delivery to process
  • Multithreaded: which thread receives the signal?

items.title: Four Delivery Strategies
items.text:
1. Thread-specific — Mandatory for synchronous exceptions (SIGSEGV, SIGFPE)
  2. All threads — Process termination signals (SIGINT)
  3. Non-blocked threads — Deliver to first thread not blocking the signal
  4. Dedicated signal thread — Use sigwait() to handle all signals

items.title: Signal APIs
items.text:
// Process-targeted
#include <signal.h>
int kill(pid_t pid, int signal);
// Kernel decides which non-blocking thread receives it

// Thread-targeted (POSIX Pthreads)
#include <pthread.h>
int pthread_kill(pthread_t tid, int signal);
// Sends signal directly to specific thread

// Thread signal masks
#include <pthread.h>
int pthread_sigmask(int how, const sigset_t *set, sigset_t *oldset);
// Each thread has individual signal mask

items.title: 14.5 Windows Alternative: APCs
items.text: Windows doesn't natively support UNIX-style signals. Uses Asynchronous Procedure Calls (APCs): - Specify callback function executing asynchronously in context of specific user thread - Delivered when thread enters alertable wait state - Key difference: APC delivered directly to particular thread, not process

items.title: 14.6 Common POSIX/Linux Signals
items.text: Signal Number Description & Default Action SIGINT 2 Terminal interrupt (<Ctrl>+<C>). Terminate. SIGABRT 6 abort() called. Terminate with core dump. SIGKILL 9 Uncatchable, unignorable immediate termination. SIGSEGV 11 Segmentation fault (invalid memory). Core dump. SIGALRM 14 alarm() timer expired. Terminate. SIGSTOP 17/19/23 Uncatchable, unignorable pause. SIGCONT 18/19/25 Resume stopped process.

items.title: Simple (Legacy)
items.text:
#include <signal.h>
void (*signal(int sig, void (*handler)(int)))(int);

// Example
void handler(int sig) {
    printf("Caught signal %d\n", sig);
}
signal(SIGINT, handler);

items.title: Robust (Modern) — sigaction()
items.text:
#include <signal.h>

struct sigaction sa;
sa.sa_handler = handler;
sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
sa.sa_flags = 0;  // or SA_RESTART, SA_SIGINFO, etc.

sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);

items.title: Async-Signal-Safe Functions
items.text: Only these can be safely called from signal handlers: - write(), read(), open(), close() - fork(), exec(), exit(), _exit() - kill(), raise(), alarm() - sigaction(), sigprocmask(), sigpending() - NOT safe: printf(), malloc(), free(), pthread_mutex_lock(), etc.

items.title: 14.8 Signal Mask Operations
items.text:
#include <signal.h>

// Block signals
sigset_t set;
sigemptyset(&set);
sigaddset(&set, SIGINT);
sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, NULL);

// Unblock
sigprocmask(SIG_UNBLOCK, &set, NULL);

// Check pending
sigpending(&set);

items.title: In Multithreaded Programs
items.text:
#include <pthread.h>
#include <signal.h>

// Each thread has its own signal mask
pthread_sigmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, NULL);  // Block in this thread only

items.title: Timeout with alarm()
items.text:
void timeout_handler(int sig) {
    // Handle timeout
}

signal(SIGALRM, timeout_handler);
alarm(5);  // SIGALRM in 5 seconds
// ... do work ...
alarm(0);  // Cancel

items.title: Ignoring Signals
items.text: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);  // Ignore broken pipe (common in network code)

items.title: Restoring Default
items.text: signal(SIGINT, SIG_DFL);  // Restore default action

items.title: 14.10 Signal vs Other IPC
items.text: Mechanism Scope Use Case Signals Process/thread notification Async events, termination, timers Pipes/FIFOs Byte stream Data transfer between processes Sockets Bidirectional messages Local/remote communication Shared Memory Shared data High-speed data sharing Semaphores/Mutexes Synchronization Mutual exclusion, resource counting

items.title: 14.11 Key Takeaways
items.text:
• Signals = software interrupts for async/sync event notification
  • Lifecycle: Generation → Delivery → Handling
  • Synchronous = internal fault (delivered to faulting thread)
  • Asynchronous = external event (delivered to process/any thread)
  • Cannot catch/block: SIGKILL, SIGSTOP
  • Multithreaded delivery: 4 strategies; thread-specific for sync signals
  • Handler safety: Only async-signal-safe functions allowed
  • Modern API: sigaction() > signal(); pthread_kill() for thread-targeted
  • Windows: Uses APCs instead of signals

items.title: Topic 14 (Detailed): Signals & Signal Handling
items.text: Source: Lecture 13 (Unit 2) + Textbook Ch. 11 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stevens & Rago Ch. 10)

items.title: What is a Signal?
items.text:
A signal is a software interrupt — a notification to a process that an event has occurred.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SIGNAL LIFECYCLE                          │
│                                                              │
│  GENERATION → DELIVERY → HANDLING                           │
│       │            │            │                            │
│       ▼            ▼            ▼                            │
│  Event      Kernel marks    Process executes                │
│  occurs     signal pending  handler (or default)            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

items.title: Generation Sources
items.text: Source Examples Hardware exceptions Division by zero (SIGFPE), invalid memory (SIGSEGV), illegal instruction (SIGILL) Terminal Ctrl+C (SIGINT), Ctrl+Z (SIGTSTP), Ctrl+\ (SIGQUIT) Timers alarm() (SIGALRM), setitimer() Process events Child exit (SIGCHLD), pipe broken (SIGPIPE) Explicit kill(), raise(), sigqueue()

items.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous
items.text: Type Generated By Delivered To Synchronous Current instruction (fault) The faulting thread Asynchronous External event Process or any thread not blocking it Signal Type Typical Cause SIGSEGV Synchronous Invalid memory access SIGFPE Synchronous Division by zero, FP exception SIGILL Synchronous Illegal instruction SIGBUS Synchronous Bus error (misaligned access) SIGINT Asynchronous Ctrl+C SIGALRM Asynchronous Timer expiration SIGCHLD Asynchronous Child terminated SIGPIPE Asynchronous Write to closed pipe SIGUSR1/2 Asynchronous User-defined

items.title: 14.3 Signal Dispositions (Actions)
items.text:
Every signal has a disposition (what happens when delivered):

Disposition Meaning Default Kernel-defined action (Term, Core, Ign, Stop, Cont) Ignore Signal discarded (SIG_IGN) Catch User-defined handler function

items.title: Default Actions
items.text:
Signal Default Action Description SIGINT Terminate Terminal interrupt SIGTERM Terminate Termination request SIGKILL Terminate Uncatchable, unignorable SIGSTOP Stop Uncatchable, unignorable SIGQUIT Core dump Quit (Ctrl+) SIGSEGV Core dump Segmentation fault SIGFPE Core dump Arithmetic exception SIGCHLD Ignore Child stopped/terminated SIGPIPE Terminate Broken pipe SIGALRM Terminate Alarm clock

Critical: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (17/19/23) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored.

items.title: Legacy: signal()
items.text:
#include <signal.h>

// Simple but limited
void (*signal(int sig, void (*handler)(int)))(int);

// Example
void handler(int sig) {
    printf("Caught signal %d\n", sig);
}

signal(SIGINT, handler);  // Set handler
signal(SIGINT, SIG_DFL);  // Restore default
signal(SIGINT, SIG_IGN);  // Ignore

Limitations: - Not portable (System V vs BSD semantics) - Handler reset on delivery (System V) - No signal masking during handler

items.title: Modern: sigaction()
items.text:
#include <signal.h>

struct sigaction {
    void     (*sa_handler)(int);      // Handler (or SIG_DFL/SIG_IGN)
    void     (*sa_sigaction)(int, siginfo_t *, void *); // With info
    sigset_t sa_mask;                 // Signals blocked during handler
    int      sa_flags;                // SA_RESTART, SA_SIGINFO, etc.
    void     (*sa_restorer)(void);    // Obsolete
};

int sigaction(int signum, const struct sigaction *act, struct sigaction *oldact);

items.title: Complete Example
items.text:
#include <signal.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>

volatile sig_atomic_t got_signal = 0;

void handler(int sig, siginfo_t *info, void *ucontext) {
    // Async-signal-safe: only use safe functions!
    got_signal = 1;
    printf("Caught signal %d from PID %d\n", sig, info->si_pid);
}

int main() {
    struct sigaction sa;

    // Zero initialize
    memset(&sa, 0, sizeof(sa));

    // Use sa_sigaction (gets siginfo_t)
    sa.sa_sigaction = handler;

    // Block SIGTERM during handler
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sigaddset(&sa.sa_mask, SIGTERM);

    // Flags: SA_SIGINFO = use sa_sigaction, SA_RESTART = restart syscalls
    sa.sa_flags = SA_SIGINFO | SA_RESTART;

    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigaction");
        exit(1);
    }

    printf("Waiting for SIGINT (Ctrl+C)...\n");
    while (!got_signal) pause();  // Wait for signal

    printf("Signal received, exiting cleanly\n");
    return 0;
}

items.title: Common sa_flags
items.text: Flag Effect SA_RESTART Restart interrupted syscalls (read, write, etc.) SA_SIGINFO Use sa_sigaction (3 args) instead of sa_handler (1 arg) SA_NOCLDSTOP Don't get SIGCHLD when child stops SA_NOCLDWAIT Don't create zombies (auto-reap) SA_NODEFER Don't block signal during handler SA_RESETHAND Reset to SIG_DFL after handler runs (one-shot) SA_ONSTACK Use alternate signal stack

items.title: 14.5 Signal Sets & Blocking
items.text:
#include <signal.h>

sigset_t set;
sigemptyset(&set);      // Empty set
sigfillset(&set);       // All signals
sigaddset(&set, SIGINT); // Add signal
sigdelset(&set, SIGTERM); // Remove signal
sigismember(&set, SIGINT); // Test membership

// Block signals
sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, NULL);

// Unblock signals
sigprocmask(SIG_UNBLOCK, &set, NULL);

// Replace mask
sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &set, &oldset);

// Get pending signals
sigpending(&set);

items.title: Typical Pattern: Temporarily Block Signal
items.text:
sigset_t block_set, old_set;
sigemptyset(&block_set);
sigaddset(&block_set, SIGINT);

// Block SIGINT
sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &block_set, &old_set);

// Critical section (no SIGINT interruption)
do_critical_work();

// Restore old mask (unblocks SIGINT)
sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_set, NULL);

items.title: 14.6 Async-Signal-Safe Functions
items.text:
Only these can be safely called from a signal handler:

Category Functions I/O write, read, open, close, lseek Process fork, exec*, _exit, exit, kill, raise, alarm Signal sigaction, sigprocmask, sigpending, sigsuspend, sigwait Time sleep, nanosleep, clock_gettime Memory NONE (malloc/free NOT safe!)

NEVER use in handler: printf, malloc, free, pthread_mutex_lock, strcpy, strtok, etc.

items.title: Safe Handler Pattern
items.text:
volatile sig_atomic_t flag = 0;  // Atomic flag

void handler(int sig) {
    flag = 1;  // Only set atomic variable
}

int main() {
    signal(SIGINT, handler);
    while (!flag) {
        // Do work
    }
    // Handle signal in main context (can use printf, malloc, etc.)
    printf("Signal received!\n");
}

items.title: 1. Timeout with alarm()
items.text:
void timeout_handler(int sig) {
    // Handle timeout
}

void do_with_timeout(int seconds) {
    signal(SIGALRM, timeout_handler);
    alarm(seconds);  // SIGALRM in 'seconds'

    // Do work that might hang
    int result = slow_operation();

    alarm(0);  // Cancel alarm
    return result;
}

items.title: 2. Ignore SIGPIPE (Common in Network Code)
items.text:
signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);  // Prevent crash on broken pipe

// Or better:
struct sigaction sa = { .sa_handler = SIG_IGN };
sigaction(SIGPIPE, &sa, NULL);

items.title: 3. Wait for Signal (sigsuspend)
items.text:
sigset_t mask;
sigemptyset(&mask);
sigaddset(&mask, SIGUSR1);

// Wait for SIGUSR1
sigsuspend(&mask);  // Atomically unmask and wait

items.title: 4. Signal + Threads
items.text:
// Each thread has its own signal mask
pthread_sigmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, &oldset);  // Block in this thread

// Send signal to specific thread
pthread_kill(thread_id, SIGUSR1);

// Dedicated signal handling thread
void *signal_thread(void *arg) {
    sigset_t set;
    sigfillset(&set);
    pthread_sigmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, NULL);  // Block all in this thread

    while (1) {
        int sig;
        sigwait(&set, &sig);  // Wait for any signal
        handle_signal(sig);
    }
}

items.title: 14.8 Complete Signal Demo Program
items.text:
/*
 * File: signals_demo.c
 * Comprehensive signal handling demonstration
 * Compile: gcc -o signals_demo signals_demo.c
 */

#include <signal.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

volatile sig_atomic_t sigint_count = 0;
volatile sig_atomic_t sigusr1_count = 0;
volatile sig_atomic_t child_done = 0;

void sigint_handler(int sig) {
    sigint_count++;
    printf("\n[SIGINT] Count: %d\n", sigint_count);
    if (sigint_count >= 3) {
        printf("  Three SIGINTs - exiting\n");
        _exit(0);
    }
}

void sigusr1_handler(int sig) {
    sigusr1_count++;
    printf("[SIGUSR1] Count: %d\n", sigusr1_count);
}

void sigchld_handler(int sig) {
    int status;
    pid_t pid;
    while ((pid = waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG)) > 0) {
        if (WIFEXITED(status)) {
            printf("[SIGCHLD] Child %d exited with code %d\n", pid, WEXITSTATUS(status));
        } else if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) {
            printf("[SIGCHLD] Child %d killed by signal %d\n", pid, WTERMSIG(status));
        }
        child_done = 1;
    }
}

void setup_handlers() {
    struct sigaction sa = {0};

    // SIGINT: count, exit after 3
    sa.sa_handler = sigint_handler;
    sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;
    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);

    // SIGUSR1: count
    sa.sa_handler = sigusr1_handler;
    sigaction(SIGUSR1, &sa, NULL);

    // SIGCHLD: reap children
    sa.sa_handler = sigchld_handler;
    sa.sa_flags = SA_NOCLDSTOP | SA_RESTART;
    sigaction(SIGCHLD, &sa, NULL);
}

void child_process() {
    printf("[CHILD %d] Started, sleeping 2s\n", getpid());
    sleep(2);
    printf("[CHILD %d] Exiting with code 42\n", getpid());
    exit(42);
}

int main() {
    setup_handlers();

    printf("PID: %d\n", getpid());
    printf("Try: kill -SIGINT %d  (Ctrl+C)\n", getpid());
    printf("Try: kill -SIGUSR1 %d\n", getpid());
    printf("Try: kill -SIGCHLD %d (after child exits)\n", getpid());

    // Fork a child
    pid_t pid = fork();
    if (pid == 0) {
        child_process();
    }

    printf("\nParent waiting for signals...\n");

    // Main loop
    while (1) {
        if (sigint_count >= 3) break;
        if (child_done) break;
        pause();  // Wait for signal
    }

    printf("Exiting\n");
    return 0;
}

items.title: 14.9 Windows Alternative: APCs
items.text:
Windows doesn't have POSIX signals. Uses Asynchronous Procedure Calls (APCs):

POSIX Signal Windows APC Delivered to process Delivered to specific thread Handler runs in thread context Callback runs in thread's alertable wait kill(pid, sig) QueueUserAPC(callback, thread, data) 
// Windows APC example
DWORD WINAPI MyAPC(ULONG_PTR data) {
    printf("APC executed with data: %lu\n", data);
}

// Queue APC to thread
QueueUserAPC(MyAPC, thread_handle, 42);

// Thread must enter alertable wait:
SleepEx(INFINITE, TRUE);  // TRUE = alertable
WaitForSingleObjectEx(handle, INFINITE, TRUE);

items.title: 14.10 Complete Exam-Focused Summary
items.text: Concept Key Points Signal lifecycle Generation → Delivery → Handling Synchronous Internal fault (SIGSEGV, SIGFPE) → delivered to faulting thread Asynchronous External (SIGINT, SIGALRM) → delivered to process/any thread Cannot catch/block SIGKILL (9), SIGSTOP sigaction() > signal() Portable, masking, flags, siginfo_t SA_RESTART Restart interrupted syscalls SA_SIGINFO Use 3-arg handler (gets siginfo_t) Async-signal-safe Only: write, fork, exec, _exit, kill, sigaction, etc. sigprocmask Block/unblock signals in thread sigsuspend Atomically wait for signal Windows Uses APCs, not signals

items.title: 14.11 Common Pitfalls
items.text: Pitfall Wrong Correct printf in handler printf("caught\n"); Set atomic flag, handle in main malloc in handler malloc(100); Pre-allocate, or avoid mutex in handler pthread_mutex_lock(&m); Never block in handler longjmp from handler longjmp(buf, 1); Use siglongjmp if needed signal() portability signal(SIGINT, h); Use sigaction() Ignoring SIGCHLD signal(SIGCHLD, SIG_IGN); Use SA_NOCLDWAIT Missing SA_RESTART Interrupted syscalls fail Add SA_RESTART

items.title: Topic 15: Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.1 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stallings Ch. 7)

items.title: Logical vs Physical Address
items.text: Logical Address (CPU) → MMU → Physical Address (Memory)

items.title: Hardware Support
items.text:
• Base/Limit Registers: Simple relocation + protection
  • Base = starting physical address
  • Limit = range/size of logical address space
  • Legal: 0 ≤ Logical Address < Limit
  • Physical = Base + Logical Address

  • If Logical ≥ Limit → Hardware Trap (Addressing/Segmentation fault)

  • Memory Management Unit (MMU): Hardware for translation

  • Page Table Base Register (PTBR): Points to current process page table

items.title: Memory Allocation Strategies
items.text: Strategy Description First Fit Allocate first hole that is big enough (fastest) Best Fit Allocate smallest hole that is big enough (leaves smallest leftover) Worst Fit Allocate largest hole (leaves largest leftover; worst utilization)

items.title: Memory Protection
items.text:
• Valid/invalid bits in page tables
  • Read/Write/Execute permission bits

items.title: Shared Pages
items.text:
• Code sharing between processes
  • Copy-on-write (COW) for fork()

items.title: Dynamic Loading
items.text:
• Load routine only when called (not at startup)
  • Reduces memory footprint, faster startup

items.title: Dynamic Linking
items.text:
• Linking postponed until execution (shared libraries)
  • Single library copy in memory shared by multiple processes
  • Shared Libraries: .so files on Linux, .dll on Windows

items.title: 15.4 Memory-Mapped Files (mmap())
items.text:
#include <sys/mman.h>

void *mmap(void *addr, size_t len, int prot, int flags, int fd, off_t offset);
// Map file into memory — treats file I/O as memory access

munmap(void *addr, size_t len);  // Unmap

items.title: Parameters
items.text: Parameter Description addr Hint address (NULL = let kernel choose) len Length of mapping prot Protection: PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE, PROT_EXEC, PROT_NONE flags MAP_SHARED (changes visible to others, written to file) / MAP_PRIVATE (COW, changes not written to file) fd File descriptor from open() offset Offset into file (page-aligned)

items.title: Use Cases
items.text:
• Fast file I/O (memory access instead of read/write syscalls)
  • Shared memory between processes (MAP_SHARED + MAP_ANONYMOUS)
  • Loading executables (dynamic linker uses mmap)
  • Large data files (databases, video)

items.title: 15.5 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Base/Limit = simple relocation + protection
  2. MMU = hardware translation unit
  3. Dynamic Loading = load on demand
  4. Dynamic Linking = shared libraries at runtime
  5. mmap() = file I/O as memory access; MAP_SHARED vs MAP_PRIVATE
  6. First/Best/Worst Fit = contiguous allocation strategies

items.title: What is Memory?
items.text:
• Memory consists of a large array of bytes, each with its own address
  • Execution: Fetch instruction → Decode → Fetch operands → Execute → Store results
  • Memory unit sees stream of addresses; doesn't know how generated
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: Program Execution Requirements
items.text:
• Program must be brought from disk into memory, placed in ready queue
  • Main memory and registers: only storage CPU accesses directly
  • Register access: 1 CPU clock; Main memory: many cycles (stall)
  • Cache between registers and main memory speeds up access (no OS control)
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: 15.2 Address Translation & Hardware Support
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: Address Binding
items.text:
• Compile time: Absolute code; if start address changes → recompile (MS-DOS .COM)
  • Load time: Relocatable code; final binding at load time
  • Execution time: Process can move during execution; binding delayed until run time; needs hardware support (MMU)
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: Memory-Management Unit (MMU)
items.text:
• Hardware device mapping virtual → physical address at run time
  • Multiple methods: will be discussed

items.title: Logical vs Physical Address
items.text:
Logical Address (CPU) → MMU → Physical Address (Memory)
- Logical (virtual): Generated by CPU - Physical: Seen by memory unit - Same in compile/load-time binding; differ in execution-time binding
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: Base & Limit Registers (Protection & Relocation)
items.text:
Base register = relocation register = starting physical address
Limit register = range/size of logical address space
Legal: 0 ≤ Logical < Limit
Physical = Base + Logical
If Logical ≥ Limit → Hardware Trap (Addressing/Segmentation fault)
- Base/limit loaded only by OS via privileged instruction (kernel mode) - Prevents user programs from modifying OS or other users' memory

items.title: Dynamic Relocation (Relocation Register)
items.text:
• Value in relocation register added to every user address at time sent to memory
  • Example: base=14000, user address 0 → physical 14000; address 346 → 14346
  • User program deals with logical addresses; never sees real physical addresses

items.title: mmap() Lifecycle
items.text:
1. First access: Demand-paging fault; page-sized chunk read from disk
  2. Subsequent access: Memory accesses — no read()/write() overhead
  3. Deferred write-back: Modified pages paged to swap under memory pressure
  4. On close: Data written back to disk, unmapped
path: Topic 15 (Detailed): Main Memory — Hardware, Address Translation, Dynamic Loading/Linking, mmap

items.title: Advantages
items.text:
• High Performance: Bypasses read()/write() overhead
  • Zero-Copy I/O: Direct disk cache → user space
  • Random Access: Direct address access, no sequential reads
  • Efficient for Large Files: Demand paging loads only needed pages
  • Easy Programming: data[100] accesses file location
  • Sharing: Multiple processes map same file → share physical pages
  • IPC: Memory-mapped shared memory for fast IPC

items.title: Topic 16: Swapping & Fragmentation
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.2 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8)

items.title: 16.1 Swapping
items.text:
• Move processes between RAM and backing store (swap space)
  • Medium-term scheduler (swapper) manages this
  • Swap Out: Process → Disk (free memory)
  • Swap In: Disk → Process (resume execution)

items.title: 16.2 Fragmentation
items.text: Type Description Solution External Free memory holes scattered; total memory exists but non-contiguous Compaction, paging Internal Allocated block slightly larger than requested Paging (fixed-size frames)

items.title: 50% Rule (External Fragmentation)
items.text: For N allocated blocks under First Fit: ~0.5N blocks lost to fragmentation → roughly 1/3 of total memory becomes unusable

items.title: Compaction
items.text:
• Move all processes to one end → large free block
  • Expensive, needs dynamic relocation (base/limit registers)

items.title: 16.3 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Swapping = medium-term scheduler moves processes between RAM and disk
  2. External fragmentation = free but non-contiguous; solved by compaction or paging
  3. Internal fragmentation = allocated > requested; paging has internal frag on last page
  4. 50% rule = 0.5N blocks lost for N allocated blocks
  5. Compaction = move processes to create large contiguous free space

items.title: 16.4 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q73: Best Fit → smallest leftover hole
  • Q74: 50% rule → 0.5N blocks lost (1/3 memory unusable)
  • Q75: Paging eliminates external fragmentation but has internal fragmentation on last page

items.title: Topic 16 (Detailed): Swapping & Fragmentation
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.2 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8)

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Process swapped temporarily out of memory to backing store, then back for continued execution
  • Total physical memory space of processes can exceed physical memory
  • Backing store: Fast disk large enough for all memory images; direct access required

items.title: Swapping Variants
items.text: Variant Description Roll out, roll in Priority-based; lower-priority swapped out for higher-priority Standard Swapping disabled normally; enabled when memory > threshold

items.title: Swapping Details
items.text:
• Backing store: Fast disk, direct access to memory images
  • Transfer time: Major part of swap time; proportional to memory size
  • Ready queue: Processes with memory images on disk

items.title: Context Switch with Swapping
items.text:
Example: 100MB process, 50MB/sec disk
Swap out = 100/50 = 2 sec
Swap in = 2 sec
Total context switch = 4 seconds (just swapping)
- 3GB process → 60 seconds swap time! - Optimization: Swap only used memory via request_memory()/release_memory()

items.title: Swapping Constraints
items.text:
• Pending I/O: Can't swap out (I/O would go to wrong process) → double buffering
  • Standard swapping rarely used in modern OS; modified versions common
  • Swapping disabled normally; enabled when memory > threshold

items.title: Memory Layout
items.text: Low addr ──► [OS: interrupt vector, kernel] ──► [User Processes] ──► High addr

items.title: Hardware Support
items.text:
• Base register: Smallest physical address
  • Limit register: Logical address range (address < limit)
  • MMU: Maps logical → physical dynamically
  • Dispatcher: Loads base/limit registers during context switch

items.title: Memory Protection
items.text:
• Every CPU address checked against base/limit
  • Protects OS and other users' programs
  • Allows dynamic OS size (e.g., load device drivers on demand)

items.title: Fixed Partitions (IBM OS/360)
items.text:
• Memory divided into fixed-size partitions
  • One process per partition
  • Degree of multiprogramming = number of partitions
  • Internal fragmentation: allocated > requested

items.title: Variable Partitions (Modern)
items.text:
• Partitions sized to process needs
  • Hole = block of available memory
  • OS maintains table of allocated/free partitions
  • Process allocated from sufficiently large hole
  • On exit: partition freed, adjacent free holes combined

items.title: Example Problem
items.text:
Processes: 5=100MB, 8=400MB, 2=200MB, 9=200MB, 10=100MB
Process 5 terminates → can 11=200MB be accommodated?

items.title: 16.4 Dynamic Storage Allocation Strategies
items.text: Strategy Description Pros/Cons First Fit First hole big enough Fast; good utilization Best Fit Smallest hole big enough Smallest leftover; must search all Worst Fit Largest hole Largest leftover; poor utilization

items.title: Example
items.text:
Partitions: 300, 600, 350, 200, 750, 125 KB
Processes: 115, 500, 358, 200, 375 KB

items.title: 50% Rule (First Fit)
items.text:
• N allocated blocks → ~0.5N blocks lost to fragmentation
  • ~1/3 memory unusable: (0.5N)/(N+0.5N) = 1/3

items.title: 16.5 Fragmentation
items.text: Type Description Solution Internal Allocated > requested; unused within partition Paging (fixed frames) External Total free space exists but not contiguous Paging; Compaction

items.title: Compaction
items.text:
• Shuffle memory to create one large free block
  • Requires dynamic relocation (execution-time binding)
  • Problem: CPU overhead of moving 8GB RAM!
  • I/O issue: Latch job during I/O; use OS buffers

items.title: 16.6 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Swapping = medium-term scheduler moves processes between RAM and disk
  2. External fragmentation = free but non-contiguous; solved by paging
  3. Internal fragmentation = allocated > requested; paging has internal frag on last page
  4. 50% rule = 0.5N blocks lost for N allocated blocks
  5. Compaction = move processes to create large contiguous free space

items.title: 16.7 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q73: Best Fit → smallest leftover hole
  • Q74: 50% rule → 0.5N blocks lost (1/3 memory unusable)
  • Q75: Paging eliminates external fragmentation but has internal fragmentation on last page

items.title: Topic 17: Segmentation
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.3 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8)

items.title: Logical Address
items.text: <segment-number, offset>

items.title: Segment Table
items.text:
• Base + Limit per segment
  • Supports user view of memory (code, data, stack segments)

items.title: Characteristics
items.text: Aspect Details Division Unit Variable-size logical blocks (code, stack, heap) Programmer View Visible — matches modular programming Internal Fragmentation No External Fragmentation Yes (variable segments leave holes) Hardware Table Segment Table (Segment Base + Limit)

items.title: 17.2 Address Translation
items.text:
Logical:  s (segment #) | d (offset)
                │
                ▼
        Segment Table[s] → Base, Limit
                │
                ├── Check: d < Limit? → if not → Trap (Segmentation Fault)
                │
                ▼
           Physical = Base + d

items.title: 17.3 Segmentation vs Paging
items.text: Metric / Concept Paging Segmentation Division Unit Fixed-size blocks (pages / frames) Variable-size logical blocks (code, stack, heap) Programmer View Invisible (physical abstraction) Visible (logical modules) Internal Fragmentation Yes (on last page) No External Fragmentation No (pages map anywhere) Yes (variable segments leave holes) Hardware Table Page Table (Page → Frame) Segment Table (Segment Base + Limit)

items.title: 17.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Segmentation = variable-size logical units matching programmer view
  2. Logical address = <segment#, offset>
  3. Segment table = Base + Limit per segment
  4. External fragmentation = yes (unlike paging)
  5. Segmentation fault = offset ≥ limit

items.title: 17.5 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q82: Fundamental difference — paging fixed/transparent, segmentation variable/visible
  • Q83: Segmentation address translation — offset ≥ limit → trap (segmentation fault)

items.title: Topic 17 (Detailed): Segmentation
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.3 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8)

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Memory-management scheme supporting programmer's view of memory
  • Program = collection of segments (logical units):
  • Main program, procedure, function, method, object
  • Local/global variables, common block, stack, symbol table, arrays

items.title: Programmer's View
items.text:
Logical address = <segment-number s, offset d>
- Segment = logical unit (code, data, stack, etc.) - Addresses: segment name + offset within segment

items.title: Logical Address
items.text: <segment-number s, offset d>

items.title: Segment Table
items.text: Each entry contains: - Segment base: Starting physical address of segment - Segment limit: Length of segment

items.title: Registers
items.text:
• STBR (Segment Table Base Register): Points to segment table in memory
  • STLR (Segment Table Length Register): Number of segments used
  • Valid segment: s < STLR

items.title: 17.3 Address Translation
items.text:
Logical:  s (segment #) | d (offset)
                │
                ▼
        Segment Table[s] → Base, Limit
                │
                ├── Check: d < Limit? → if not → Trap (Segmentation Fault)
                │
                ▼
           Physical = Base + d

items.title: Example
items.text:
Segment Table:
Seg 0: Base=219, Limit=600
Seg 1: Base=2300, Limit=14
Seg 2: Base=90, Limit=100
Seg 3: Base=1327, Limit=580
Seg 4: Base=1952, Limit=96

Logical → Physical:
0,430  → 219+430=649        ✓
1,10   → 2300+10=2310       ✓
2,500  → Limit=100, offset=500 → TRAP!
3,400  → 1327+400=1727      ✓
4,112  → Limit=96, offset=112 → TRAP!

items.title: 17.3 Segmentation vs Paging
items.text: Metric / Concept Paging Segmentation Division Unit Fixed-size blocks (pages/frames) Variable-size logical blocks (code, stack, heap) Programmer View Invisible (physical abstraction) Visible (logical modules) Internal Fragmentation Yes (on last page) No External Fragmentation No (pages map anywhere) Yes (variable segments leave holes) Hardware Table Page Table (Page → Frame) Segment Table (Segment Base + Limit)

items.title: 17.4 Shared Segments
items.text:
• Two processes can have segments with same base address
  • Segments mapped to both → shared memory

items.title: 17.5 Linux Angle: Flat Memory Model
items.text:
• Legacy x86: Explicit segmentation registers (CS, DS, SS)
  • Modern Linux (x86-64): Flat memory model
  • Kernel sets all segment bases to 0x00000000
  • Limit = maximum addressable space
  • Effectively neutralizes segmentation

items.title: 17.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Segmentation = variable-size logical units matching programmer view
  2. Logical address = <segment#, offset>
  3. Segment table = Base + Limit per segment
  4. External fragmentation = yes (unlike paging)
  5. Segmentation fault = offset ≥ limit

items.title: 17.5 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:

  • Q83: Segmentation address translation — offset ≥ limit → trap (segmentation fault)

items.title: Topic 18: Paging
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.4 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stallings Ch. 7)

items.title: 18.1 Core Idea
items.text: Key Idea: Fixed-size frames (physical) + pages (logical) → No external fragmentation

items.title: 32-bit, 4KB Pages
items.text: Page Number (20 bits) | Page Offset (12 bits)

items.title: General Formula
items.text:
• Page size = 2^d bytes
  • Offset bits = d
  • Page number bits = address_bits - d

items.title: 18.3 Page Table
items.text: Maps page → frame

items.title: Page Table Entry (PTE)
items.text: | Frame # | Valid | Prot | Ref | Dirty | ...

items.title: PTE Bits
items.text: Bit Meaning Valid Page in memory? (1=yes, 0=on disk/not allocated) Protection Read/Write/Execute permissions Reference Page accessed recently (for LRU/Clock) Dirty Page modified (needs write-back on replacement)

items.title: Example: 32-bit, 4KB pages, 4-byte PTE
items.text:
Number of entries = 2^(32-12) = 2^20 = 1,048,576
Size = 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB per process

items.title: 2-Level Paging (32-bit, 4KB pages)
items.text:
Page Dir Index (10) | Page Table Index (10) | Offset (12)
  • Only allocate page tables for used regions
  • Reduces memory for sparse address spaces

items.title: 18.6 Inverted Page Table
items.text:
• One entry per physical frame (not per logical page)
  • Saves memory for 64-bit address spaces
  • Slower lookup (hash table)

items.title: 18.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Paging = fixed-size frames + pages → no external fragmentation
  2. Address split = Page Number | Offset
  3. Page Table = maps page → frame; PTE has Valid, Prot, Ref, Dirty bits
  4. 32-bit, 4KB → p=20 bits, d=12 bits; page table = 4 MB
  5. Multi-level = reduce memory for sparse addresses
  6. Inverted = one entry per frame; scales with physical RAM

items.title: 18.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q76: 32-bit, 4KB pages → p=20, d=12
  • Q77: Page table size = 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB
  • Q78: TLB = hardware cache for page translations
  • Q79: EAT = α(TLB+RAM) + (1-α)(TLB+2×RAM)
  • Q80: 2-level paging without TLB = 3 memory accesses
  • Q81: Inverted page table = one entry per physical frame

items.title: Topic 18 (Detailed): Paging
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.4 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stallings Ch. 7)

items.title: 18.1 Core Idea
items.text: Key Idea: Fixed-size frames (physical) + pages (logical) → No external fragmentation

items.title: Basic Method
items.text:
• Divide physical memory into fixed-size frames
  • Divide logical memory into same-size pages
  • Page size = frame size (hardware-defined)
  • Track all free frames
  • Run program of N pages → find N free frames → load
  • Page table translates logical → physical
  • Internal fragmentation still exists (last page)

items.title: Page Size
items.text:
• Hardware-defined: 512 bytes to 1 GB
  • Common: 4KB, 8KB
  • getconf PAGESIZE displays system page size

items.title: 32-bit, 4KB Pages
items.text: Page Number (20 bits) | Page Offset (12 bits)

items.title: General Formula
items.text:
• Page size = 2^d bytes
  • Offset bits = d
  • Page number bits = address_bits - d

items.title: 18.3 Page Table
items.text: Maps page → frame

items.title: Page Table Entry (PTE)
items.text: | Frame # | Valid | Prot | Ref | Dirty | ...

items.title: PTE Bits
items.text: Bit Meaning Valid Page in memory? (1=yes, 0=on disk/not allocated) Protection Read/Write/Execute permissions Reference Page accessed recently (for LRU/Clock) Dirty Page modified (needs write-back on replacement)

items.title: Example: 32-bit, 4KB pages, 4-byte PTE
items.text:
Number of entries = 2^(32-12) = 2^20 = 1,048,576
Size = 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB per process

items.title: 18.5 Paging Example (Silberschatz)
items.text:
Page size = 2,048 bytes
Process size = 72,766 bytes
Pages = 35 + 1,086 bytes
Internal fragmentation = 2,048 - 1,086 = 962 bytes
Worst case fragmentation = 1 frame - 1 byte

items.title: 18.6 Free Frames & Frame Table
items.text:
• OS manages physical memory via frame table
  • Tracks free/allocated frames
  • Page table used by CPU dispatcher for context switch
  • Paging increases context-switch time

items.title: 18.7 Two-Memory-Access Problem
items.text: Without TLB: every access needs 2 memory accesses (page table + data)

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Hardware cache for page table entries
  • TLB Hit: Translation in TLB → fast (bypass page table)
  • TLB Miss: Walk page table → slow (2+ memory accesses)

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Associative hardware cache (parallel lookup)
  • Stores recent <VPN, PPN> mappings
  • Typical size: 64-512 entries
  • ASID (Address Space ID): Distinguishes processes in TLB

items.title: Formula
items.text:
EAT = α × (t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α) × (t_TLB + 2 × t_RAM)
Where: - α = TLB hit ratio - t_TLB = TLB lookup time - t_RAM = Main memory access time

items.title: With 2-Level Paging on Miss
items.text: EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + 3×t_RAM)

items.title: 2-Level (32-bit, 4KB pages)
items.text:
p1 (10 bits) | p2 (10 bits) | d (12 bits)
    │            │           │
    ▼            ▼           ▼
Page Dir    Page Table    Frame
- Only allocate page tables for used regions - Reduces memory for sparse address spaces

items.title: 64-bit Systems
items.text:
• 2-level insufficient → 3, 4, or 5-level paging
  • Linux x86-64: 4-level (PML4 → PDPT → PD → PT)

items.title: 18.10 Inverted Page Table
items.text:
• One entry per physical frame (not per logical page)
  • Used in 64-bit systems (PowerPC, UltraSPARC)
  • Lookup via hash table (slower than direct indexing)
  • Saves enormous memory for sparse 64-bit address spaces

items.title: TLB vs CPU Cache
items.text: Aspect TLB CPU Cache Purpose Speed up address translation Speed up memory access Timing At MMU translation At CPU memory access

items.title: Memory Protection
items.text:
• Protection bits per frame (read-only, read-write, execute-only)
  • Valid/Invalid bit: valid = in address space; invalid = not in space / on disk
  • PTLR (Page Table Length Register) alternative

items.title: Valid/Invalid Bit
items.text:
• valid = page in memory (memory resident)
  • invalid = page on disk / not in address space
  • Demand Paging: mark invalid intentionally to trigger page fault

items.title: Shared Pages
items.text:
• Code sharing: Read-only (reentrant) code shared (text editors, compilers)
  • COW: fork() shares pages read-only; write triggers copy

items.title: Problem 1
items.text:

t_TLB = 5 ns, t_RAM = 100 ns
2-level paging
Calculate EAT.

items.title: Problem 2
items.text:
32-bit, 4KB pages, TLB size 64
Process accesses 1000 pages, TLB hit 95%
Memory accesses saved?

items.title: Problem 3
items.text:
3-level paging, no TLB
Memory accesses for one translation?

items.title: 18.12 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Paging = fixed-size frames + pages → no external fragmentation
  2. Address split = Page Number | Offset
  3. Page Table = maps page → frame; PTE has Valid, Prot, Ref, Dirty bits
  4. 32-bit, 4KB → p=20 bits, d=12 bits; page table = 4 MB
  5. Multi-level = reduce memory for sparse addresses
  6. Inverted = one entry per frame; scales with physical RAM
  7. TLB = hardware associative cache for page translations
  8. EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + k×t_RAM)

items.title: 18.13 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q76: 32-bit, 4KB pages → p=20, d=12
  • Q77: Page table size = 2^20 × 4 bytes = 4 MB
  • Q78: TLB = hardware cache for page translations
  • Q79: EAT = α(TLB+RAM) + (1-α)(TLB+2×RAM)
  • Q80: 2-level paging without TLB = 3 memory accesses
  • Q81: Inverted page table = one entry per physical frame

items.title: Topic 19: Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.5 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 8 (Silberschatz Ch. 8, Stallings Ch. 7)

items.title: 2-Level (32-bit, 4KB pages)
items.text:
p1 (10 bits) | p2 (10 bits) | d (12 bits)
    │            │           │
    ▼            ▼           ▼
Page Dir    Page Table    Frame

Without TLB: 1 memory access requires 3 physical memory accesses (outer table, inner table, data frame)

items.title: 19.2 Inverted Page Table
items.text:
• One entry per physical frame (not per logical page)
  • Used in 64-bit systems (PowerPC, UltraSPARC)
  • Lookup via hash table (slower than direct indexing)
  • Saves enormous memory for sparse 64-bit address spaces

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Hardware cache for page table entries
  • TLB Hit: Translation in TLB → fast (bypass page table)
  • TLB Miss: Walk page table → slow (2+ memory accesses)

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Associative hardware cache (parallel lookup)
  • Stores recent <VPN, PPN> mappings
  • Typical size: 64-512 entries

items.title: Formula
items.text:
EAT = α × (t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α) × (t_TLB + 2 × t_RAM)

Where: - α = TLB hit ratio - t_TLB = TLB lookup time - t_RAM = Main memory access time

items.title: With 2-Level Paging on Miss
items.text:
EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + 3×t_RAM)
(outer page table + inner page table + data frame)

items.title: 19.5 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Multi-level paging = reduces page table memory; 2-level = 3 memory accesses without TLB
  2. Inverted page table = one entry per physical frame; scales with RAM not virtual space
  3. TLB = hardware associative cache for page translations
  4. EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + k×t_RAM) where k = page table levels + 1

items.title: 19.6 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:

  • Q79: EAT calculation with given hit ratio, TLB time, RAM time
  • Q80: 2-level paging without TLB = 3 memory accesses
  • Q81: Inverted page table = one entry per physical frame

items.text:
• Protection bit per frame: read-only / read-write
  • Execute-only bits possible

items.title: Valid/Invalid Bit
items.text:
• Valid (1): Page in address space, legal
  • Invalid (0): Page not in address space / on disk
  • Alternative: PTLR (Page Table Length Register)

items.title: 19.5 Valid/Invalid Bit & Demand Paging
