items.title: Demand Paging
items.text:
• Mark pages invalid intentionally
  • Page fault triggers OS to load page
  • Pure demand paging: start process with no pages in memory
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Shared Pages
items.text:
• Code sharing: Read-only (reentrant) code shared (text editors, compilers)
  • Reentrant code: Non-self-modifying, reusable simultaneously
  • Example: 40 users, 150KB code + 50KB data → 8,000KB without sharing → 2,150KB with sharing
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.6 Page Table Structures
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Problem: Page Table Size
items.text:
32-bit, 4KB pages:
Entries = 2^20 = 1,048,576
4-byte PTE → 4 MB per process
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.7 Hierarchical (Multi-Level) Page Tables
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 2-Level Paging (32-bit, 4KB)
items.text:
p1 (10 bits) | p2 (10 bits) | d (12 bits)
    │            │           │
    ▼            ▼           ▼
Page Dir    Page Table    Frame
- Only allocate page tables for used regions - Reduces memory for sparse address spaces
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 64-bit Systems
items.text:
• 2-level insufficient → 3, 4, or 5-level paging
  • Linux x86-64: 4-level (PML4 → PDPT → PD → PT)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.8 Hashed Page Tables
items.text:
• Hash function on virtual page number
  • Handle collisions via chaining
  • Used when address space > physical memory
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.7 Inverted Page Table
items.text:
• One entry per physical frame (not per logical page)
  • Used in 64-bit systems (PowerPC, UltraSPARC)
  • Lookup via hash table (slower than direct indexing)
  • Saves enormous memory for sparse 64-bit address spaces
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Inverted PTE Structure
items.text:
struct {
    int pid;        // Owning process
    int vpn;        // Virtual page number
    int frame;      // Physical frame
    // ... protection, ref, dirty bits
}
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Lookup
items.text: hash(pid, vpn) → bucket → linear search for (pid, vpn) match
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text: Pros Cons Scales with RAM (not virtual space) Hash lookup slower than array index One table for all processes Collisions → chain traversal Saves massive memory for 64-bit Need separate per-process table for TLB shootdowns
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.8 TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Hardware cache for page table entries
  • TLB Hit: Translation in TLB → fast
  • TLB Miss: Walk page table → slow (2+ memory accesses)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Associative hardware cache (parallel lookup)
  • Stores recent <VPN, PPN> mappings
  • Typical size: 64-512 entries
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.9 Effective Access Time (EAT)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Formula
items.text:
EAT = α × (t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α) × (t_TLB + 2 × t_RAM)
Where: - α = TLB hit ratio - t_TLB = TLB lookup time - t_RAM = Main memory access time
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Example
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: With 2-Level Paging on Miss
items.text:
EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + 3×t_RAM)
(outer page table + inner page table + data frame)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Practice Problems
items.text:
1. TLB hit ratio = 90%, t_TLB=10ns, t_RAM=100ns, 2-level paging → EAT?
  2. 32-bit, 4KB pages, TLB size 64, 1000 accesses, 95% hit → memory accesses saved?
  3. 3-level paging, no TLB → memory accesses for one translation?
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.9 TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Hardware cache for page table entries
  • TLB Hit: Translation in TLB → fast (bypass page table)
  • TLB Miss: Walk page table → slow (2+ memory accesses)
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Associative hardware cache (parallel lookup)
  • Stores recent <VPN, PPN> mappings
  • Typical size: 64-512 entries
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: 19.10 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Multi-level paging = reduces page table memory; 2-level = 3 memory accesses without TLB
  2. Inverted page table = one entry per physical frame; scales with RAM not virtual space
  3. TLB = hardware associative cache for page translations
  4. EAT = α(t_TLB + t_RAM) + (1-α)(t_TLB + k×t_RAM) where k = page table levels + 1
path: Topic 19 (Detailed): Page Table Structures, TLB & Effective Access Time (EAT)

items.title: Topic 20: Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.6 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 9 (Silberschatz Ch. 9, Stallings Ch. 8)

items.title: Core Philosophy
items.text:
Pages loaded into physical memory only when referenced (lazy loading)

  • Valid/Invalid bit in PTE:
  • Valid (1) = page in memory
  • Invalid (0) = page on disk or not allocated

items.title: 20.2 Page Fault Handling
items.text:
1. Process accesses invalid page → Page Fault Trap
2. OS checks: Valid access? (within VMA, permissions OK?)
3. Find free frame (or victim via replacement)
4. If victim dirty → Write to swap
5. Read requested page from disk into frame
6. Update PTE (frame #, valid=1)
7. Restart faulting instruction

items.title: 20.3 Minor vs Major Page Fault
items.text: Type Description Latency Minor Page already in RAM (shared library, free list, COW copy) — zero disk I/O Microseconds Major Page must be read from disk Milliseconds

items.title: fork() with COW
items.text:
1. fork() shares all pages read-only (COW)
  2. Parent/child can read freely
  3. On write attempt → Page Fault (protection violation)
  4. OS allocates new frame, copies page, marks read-write
  5. Restarts instruction
// COW example
pid = fork();
// Parent and child share ALL pages (read-only)
// Child calls exec() → new program loaded (no COW needed for that)
// Or child modifies variable → COW triggers → private copy made

items.title: 20.5 Dirty Bit (Modify Bit)
items.text: Value Meaning 0 (Clean) Page not modified → overwrite immediately on replacement 1 (Dirty) Page modified → must write back to disk before replacement (doubles fault time)

items.title: 20.6 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Demand Paging = load pages on reference (lazy loading)
  2. Page Fault = trap → check validity → find frame → read from disk → update PTE → restart
  3. Minor Fault = resolves in RAM (COW, shared lib); Major Fault = disk I/O
  4. COW = fork() shares pages read-only; write triggers private copy
  5. Dirty Bit = if 0, no disk write needed on replacement

items.title: 20.7 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q84: Demand paging = load pages on reference (lazy loading)
  • Q85: Page fault handling — MMU generates trap to OS first
  • Q86: COW fork — protection violation trap → OS copies page → restarts instruction
  • Q87: Minor vs Major fault — minor = no disk I/O; major = disk read
  • Q88: Dirty bit = if 0, no write-back needed on replacement

items.title: 20.1 Background: Virtual Memory
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Virtual Memory: Separation of user logical memory from physical memory
  • Allows programs larger than physical memory
  • Only part of program needs to be in memory
  • More programs can run concurrently
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.title: Virtual Address Space
items.text:
Stack: starts at MAX address, grows DOWN
Heap:  starts at low address, grows UP
Hole:  Unused space between stack and heap
- No physical memory needed until heap/stack grows to new page - Enables sparse address spaces with holes for growth - System libraries shared via mapping into virtual address space - Shared memory via mapping pages read-write - Pages shared during fork() → speeds process creation
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.text:

Without sharing: 40 × 200KB = 8,000 KB
With code sharing: 150KB + 40 × 50KB = 2,150 KB

items.title: 20.6 Complete Page Fault Flow
items.text:
CPU accesses page
       │
       ▼
MMU checks PTE Valid bit
       │
       ├── Valid=1 → Physical address → Memory access (fast)
       │
       └── Valid=0 → PAGE FAULT TRAP
                        │
                        ▼
              OS Page Fault Handler
                        │
                        ├── Check: Valid access? (VMA, permissions)
                        │
                        ├── Find free frame (or victim via replacement)
                        │
                        ├── If victim dirty → Write to swap
                        │
                        ├── Read page from disk into frame
                        │
                        ├── Update PTE (frame#, valid=1)
                        │
                        └── Restart faulting instruction

items.text: Aspect Minor Fault Major Fault Source Page in RAM (COW, shared lib, zero-fill) Page on disk Disk I/O None Required Latency Microseconds Milliseconds Example COW copy, shared library, zero-fill First access, swapped out

items.title: 20.8 Copy-on-Write (COW) Details
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.title: Mechanism
items.text:
Hardware Enforcement: OS marks PTEs for BOTH processes as Read-Only
The Trap: If either process writes → MMU triggers protection fault
OS Response: Intercepts trap → allocates new frame → copies data →
             updates PTE to Read/Write → restarts instruction
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.title: COW & fork()
items.text:
Parent forks Child
    │
    ├── Both share ALL pages (Read-Only, COW)
    │
    ├── Child calls exec()
    │     └── New address space loaded; COW pages discarded
    │
    └── Child modifies variable
          └── COW triggers → private copy made

4. Update page/frame tables
5. Restart instruction

items.title: The Problem
items.text: • Should OS wait for 0 free frames before replacing?
path: Topic 20 (Detailed): Virtual Memory — Demand Paging, Page Faults, Copy-on-Write

items.title: Linux Solution: kswapd (Kernel Swap Daemon)
items.text:
• Watermarks: "high" and "low" free memory thresholds
  • When free memory < low watermark → kswapd wakes up
  • Proactively evicts inactive pages in background
  • Builds pool of free frames → programs rarely wait synchronously

items.title: 21.1 Page Replacement Problem
items.text:
When page fault occurs and no free frames exist, OS must choose a victim frame to evict.

Page Fault → No free frames → Choose victim → Write if dirty → Read new page → Update PTE → Restart

Goal: Minimize page faults.

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
• Circular list of frames with reference bit (R)
  • Hand sweeps around:
  • If R=0 → victim (replace)
  • If R=1 → R=0, give second chance, advance hand
path: Topic 21 (Detailed): Page Replacement, Frame Allocation, Thrashing

items.title: Trace: 3 Frames
items.text:
Initial: all R=0

Ref 1: [1@R=1]           Fault, set R=1
Ref 2: [1@1, 2@1]        Fault, set R=1
Ref 3: [1@1, 2@1, 3@1]   Fault, set R=1
Ref 4: Hand at 1@1→R=1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 2@1→R=1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 3@1→R=1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 1@0→VICTIM! Replace with 4@1
       Frames: [4@1, 2@0, 3@0]
Ref 1: Hand at 2@0→VICTIM! Replace with 1@1
       Frames: [4@1, 1@1, 3@0]
Ref 2: Hand at 3@0→VICTIM! Replace with 2@1
       Frames: [4@1, 1@1, 2@1]
Ref 5: Hand at 4@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 1@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 2@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 4@0→VICTIM! Replace with 5@1
       Frames: [5@1, 1@0, 2@0]
Ref 1: Hit! Set R=1 → [5@1, 1@1, 2@0]
Ref 2: Hit! Set R=1 → [5@1, 1@1, 2@1]
Ref 3: Hand at 5@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 1@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 2@1→set 0, advance
       Hand at 5@0→VICTIM! Replace with 3@1

items.title: 22.1 NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) Architecture
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: The Problem: UMA Doesn't Scale
items.text:
UMA (Uniform Memory Access):
        CPU 0          CPU 1          CPU 2          CPU 3
          │              │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
              ┌───────────────────┐
              │   SHARED MEMORY   │  (Single bus, uniform latency)
              └───────────────────┘

Problem: Bus contention → latency increases with CPU count
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: NUMA Solution
items.text:
NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access):
         NODE 0                          NODE 1
    ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────┐
    │  CPU 0  CPU 1    │           │  CPU 2  CPU 3    │
    │       │          │           │       │          │
    │  ┌────┴────┐     │           │  ┌────┴────┐     │
    │  │ LOCAL   │     │  INTERCONNECT  │ LOCAL   │     │
    │  │  MEM    │     │                │  MEM    │     │
    │  └─────────┘     │                └─────────┘     │
    └──────────────────┘           └──────────────────┘

Local access:  ~100ns (direct on node's bus)
Remote access: ~200-400ns (traverse interconnect)

items.title: Key Characteristics
items.text: Aspect UMA NUMA Memory latency Uniform Varies by CPU-memory distance Scalability Limited (~8-16 CPUs) High (64+ CPUs) Programming model Simple Requires NUMA awareness OS support Standard NUMA-aware scheduler/allocator

items.title: 22.2 Memory Locality & First-Touch Policy
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: First-Touch Policy
items.text:
When a page is first WRITTEN (not just allocated):
1. OS allocates physical frame on the CURRENT NODE
2. Page stays on that node unless migrated

Example:
Process on Node 0 calls malloc(100MB)
  → Pages marked "not present"
Process writes to page 0 on Node 0
  → Page fault → allocated on Node 0
Process migrates to Node 1, writes to page 1
  → Page fault → allocated on Node 1
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Code Example: First-Touch Matters
items.text:
// BAD: All memory allocated on master thread's node
double *array = malloc(N * sizeof(double));
#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    array[i] = 0.0;  // All pages allocated on master's node!
}

// GOOD: Each thread touches its own pages
double *array = malloc(N * sizeof(double));
#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    array[i] = 0.0;  // Each thread's pages allocated on its node
}

#include <numaif.h>

// Allocate on specific node
void *ptr = numa_alloc_onnode(size, node);

// Allocate interleaved across nodes
void *ptr = numa_alloc_interleaved(size, nodemask);

// Set preferred node for current thread
numa_set_preferred(node);

// Get current node
int node = numa_node_of_cpu(sched_getcpu());

// Move pages between nodes

items.title: 22.3 NUMA-Aware Scheduler
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Goals
items.text:
1. Prefer local memory — Keep processes on nodes where their memory resides
  2. Balance load — Don't overload one node while others idle
  3. Minimize migrations — Moving processes is expensive (cache cold, remote memory)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Scheduler Policies
items.text:
Linux CFS NUMA Balancing:
1. Task NUMA group tracking
   - Track which nodes a task's memory is on
   - Periodic NUMA hinting faults to detect access patterns

2. Load balancing with NUMA cost
   - Calculate "imbalance" including remote memory penalty
   - Prefer same-node migration
   - Cross-node only for severe imbalance

3. Wake-up affinity
   - Wake task on same node as waker (shared data likely)
   - Or on node where task's memory resides

items.title: 22.4 Clock Page Replacement — Complete Implementation

items.title: Basic Clock (Second-Chance)
items.text:
Data Structure:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Circular list of frames with reference bit (R)    │
│                                                     │
│  Frame 0: Page 5, R=1  ← hand                      │
│  Frame 1: Page 2, R=0                               │
│  Frame 2: Page 7, R=1                               │
│  Frame 3: Page 1, R=0                               │
│  Frame 4: Page 9, R=1                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Algorithm:
1. Hand points to next frame to examine
2. If R=0 → VICTIM (replace)
3. If R=1 → R=0 (second chance), advance hand
4. Repeat until victim found

items.title: Clock State Machine
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: 22.5 Enhanced Clock (With Dirty Bit)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: 4 Priority Classes
items.text: Priority (Ref, Dirty) Name Action 1 (Best) (0, 0) Clean, unreferenced Replace immediately (no I/O) 2 (0, 1) Dirty, unreferenced Write to disk, then replace 3 (1, 0) Referenced, clean Clear R, give second chance 4 (Worst) (1, 1) Referenced, dirty Clear R, give second chance
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Multi-Pass Algorithm
items.text:
Pass 1: Scan for (0,0) — replace immediately if found
Pass 2: Scan for (0,1) — clear R, advance; if completes → write dirty, replace
Pass 3: Scan for (1,0) — clear R, advance
Pass 4: Scan for (1,1) — clear R, advance
Repeat from Pass 1
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Why (0,0) First?
items.text:
• No disk write needed → fastest replacement
  • Clean page → can be overwritten immediately
  • Unreferenced → unlikely to be needed soon
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Enhanced Clock Replacement

items.title: Why (1,1) Last?
items.text:
• Recently used → likely to be used again
  • Modified → requires disk write before replacement
  • Maximum cost to replace

items.title: 22.6 Complete Enhanced Clock Implementation
items.text:
/*
 * File: enhanced_clock.c
 * Complete Enhanced Clock with 4-pass algorithm
 * Compile: gcc -o enhanced_clock enhanced_clock.c
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#define MAX_FRAMES 10

typedef struct {
    int page;        // Page number (-1 = empty)
    int ref_bit;     // Reference bit (R)
    int dirty_bit;   // Dirty bit (D)
} Frame;

Frame frames[MAX_FRAMES];
int n_frames;
int hand = 0;

// Priority: (R,D) pairs in order of preference
// Pass 0: (0,0) - best
// Pass 1: (0,1)
// Pass 2: (1,0)
// Pass 3: (1,1) - worst

int find_victim() {
    for (int pass = 0; pass < 4; pass++) {
        int start_hand = hand;
        bool found = false;

        do {
            int r = frames[hand].ref_bit;
            int d = frames[hand].dirty_bit;
            bool match = false;

            // Check if this frame matches current pass priority
            if (pass == 0 && r == 0 && d == 0) match = true;
            else if (pass == 1 && r == 0 && d == 1) match = true;
            else if (pass == 2 && r == 1 && d == 0) match = true;
            else if (pass == 3 && r == 1 && d == 1) match = true;

            if (match) {
                // Victim found!
                int victim = hand;
                hand = (hand + 1) % n_frames;
                return victim;
            } else {
                // Not a match - clear reference bit, advance hand
                frames[hand].ref_bit = 0;
                hand = (hand + 1) % n_frames;
            }
        } while (hand != start_hand);
    }

    // Should never reach here (pass 3 always matches)
    int victim = hand;
    hand = (hand + 1) % n_frames;
    return victim;
}

void access_page(int page, int is_write) {
    // Check if page already in memory
    for (int i = 0; i < n_frames; i++) {
        if (frames[i].page == page) {
            // HIT
            frames[i].ref_bit = 1;
            if (is_write) frames[i].dirty_bit = 1;
            printf("Hit: Page %d (R=%d, D=%d)\n", page, frames[i].ref_bit, frames[i].dirty_bit);
            return;
        }
    }

    // PAGE FAULT
    printf("Fault: Page %d\n", page);

    // Find free frame
    for (int i = 0; i < n_frames; i++) {
        if (frames[i].page == -1) {
            frames[i].page = page;
            frames[i].ref_bit = 1;
            frames[i].dirty_bit = is_write ? 1 : 0;
            printf("  Loaded into free frame %d (R=%d, D=%d)\n", i, frames[i].ref_bit, frames[i].dirty_bit);
            return;
        }
    }

    // Need replacement - use enhanced clock
    int victim = find_victim();

    if (frames[victim].dirty_bit) {
        printf("  [DISK WRITE] Frame %d (page %d) was dirty\n", victim, frames[victim].page);
    }

    frames[victim].page = page;
    frames[victim].ref_bit = 1;
    frames[victim].dirty_bit = is_write ? 1 : 0;
    printf("  Replaced frame %d with page %d (R=%d, D=%d)\n", victim, page, frames[victim].ref_bit, frames[victim].dirty_bit);
}

void print_frames() {
    printf("Frames: ");
    for (int i = 0; i < n_frames; i++) {
        if (frames[i].page == -1) printf("[empty] ");
        else printf("[P%d R%d D%d] ", frames[i].page, frames[i].ref_bit, frames[i].dirty_bit);
    }
    printf("  (hand=%d)\n", hand);
}

int main() {
    // Reference string from slides
    int refs[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    int n_refs = 12;

    n_frames = 3;
    for (int i = 0; i < n_frames; i++) frames[i].page = -1;

    printf("=== Enhanced Clock (3 frames) ===\n");
    printf("Reference string: ");
    for (int i = 0; i < n_refs; i++) printf("%d ", refs[i]);
    printf("\n\n");

    for (int i = 0; i < n_refs; i++) {
        access_page(refs[i], 0); // All reads for simplicity
        print_frames();
    }

    return 0;
}

items.title: Challenge: Page Replacement Across NUMA Nodes
items.text:
Problem:
- Page replacement chooses victim globally
- Victim might be on remote node
- Evicting remote page = remote disk I/O (slow)
- Allocating replacement page on local node = good

Solution: NUMA-aware page replacement
1. Prefer local victims
2. If no local victim, consider remote with penalty
3. Allocate replacement on requesting node

items.title: Migrate-on-Fault
items.text:
When process on Node 0 accesses page on Node 1:
1. Page fault (page present but remote)
2. Option A: Migrate page to Node 0
   - Allocate local frame
   - Copy content
   - Update PTE
   - Free remote frame
3. Option B: Keep remote, track NUMA hint
   - Increment NUMA fault counter
   - If threshold exceeded → migrate

items.title: Topic 22: NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement
items.text: Source: Lecture 3.8 (Unit 3) + Textbook Ch. 9 (Silberschatz Ch. 9)

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
• Memory access latency varies by CPU-memory distance
  • Each CPU has "local" memory (fast) and "remote" memory (slow)
  • Multiple nodes: each with CPUs + local RAM, connected via interconnect

items.title: Memory Locality
items.text: Access Type Latency Local ~100ns (direct on CPU's local bus) Remote ~200-400ns (traverse interconnect)

items.title: First-Touch Policy
items.text:
• Page allocated on node where first touched
  • OS tries to allocate on same node as accessing thread

items.title: OS Scheduler Support
items.text:
• Prefers same-node migration
  • Cross-node only for severe imbalance
  • Tracks NUMA topology

items.title: Basic Algorithm
items.text:
• Circular list of frames with reference bit
  • Hand sweeps around:
  • If ref=0 → victim (replace)
  • If ref=1 → ref=0, give second chance, advance hand
Frame:  [P1,1] [P2,0] [P3,1] [P4,1] [P5,0]
              ↑ hand

items.title: Logic
items.text:
while (true):
    if frame[hand].ref == 0:
        victim = hand
        break
    else:
        frame[hand].ref = 0  // second chance
        hand = (hand + 1) % N

items.title: 4 Priority Classes (Best → Worst)
items.text: Priority (Ref, Dirty) Reason 1 (Best) (0, 0) Not referenced, clean → no write-back 2 (0, 1) Not referenced, dirty → needs write-back 3 (1, 0) Referenced, clean → recently used 4 (Worst) (1, 1) Referenced and dirty

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
1. Scan for (0,0) — if found, replace
  2. If not found, scan for (0,1) — clear ref, advance
  3. If not found, scan for (1,0) — clear ref, advance
  4. If not found, scan for (1,1) — clear ref, advance
  5. Repeat from step 1

Linux uses variant of enhanced clock.

items.title: 22.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. NUMA = local memory fast, remote memory slow; scheduler must be NUMA-aware
  2. First-touch = page allocated on node where first accessed
  3. Clock Algorithm = circular + ref bit; ref=1 → reset to 0, advance; ref=0 → replace
  4. Enhanced Clock = 4 classes by (ref, dirty); (0,0) evicted first (no write-back)
  5. Linux = uses enhanced clock variant

items.title: 22.5 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text:
• Q100: NUMA — local memory on CPU's local bus, lower latency than remote across interconnect
  • Q93: Clock — ref=1 → reset to 0, advance hand; ref=0 → replace
  • Q94: Enhanced Clock — (0,0) highest priority candidate for replacement

items.title: 22.1 NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
• Memory access latency varies by CPU-memory distance
  • Each CPU has "local" memory (fast) and "remote" memory (slow)
  • Multiple nodes: each with CPUs + local RAM, connected via interconnect
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: NUMA Components
items.text: Component Description Processors (CPUs) Execute processes; access local & remote memory Local Memory Directly connected to CPU; lowest access latency Remote Memory Connected to another CPU; accessed via interconnect High-Speed Interconnect Transfers data between nodes Memory Controller Handles requests, manages data transfer OS Schedules processes, allocates memory for locality
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.2 Memory Locality
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Tendency of program to access same/nearby memory locations repeatedly
  • Basis for efficient memory hierarchy (registers → cache → RAM → virtual memory)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Benefits
items.text:
• Reduces memory access time
  • Increases CPU cache hit rate
  • Decreases cache misses
  • Improves virtual memory/paging efficiency
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Types of Locality
items.text: Type Description Applications Temporal If location accessed, likely accessed again soon CPU cache stores recent data; frequent instructions in instruction cache Spatial If location accessed, nearby locations likely next Cache loads entire cache line; sequential file reading
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.3 NUMA Memory Latency
items.text: Access Type Latency Local ~100ns (direct on CPU's local bus) Remote ~200-400ns (traverse interconnect)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.4 First-Touch Policy
items.text:
• Page allocated on node where first touched
  • OS tries to allocate on same node as accessing thread
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Example
items.text:
// BAD: All memory on master thread's node
double *a = malloc(N * sizeof(double));
#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = 0.0;

// GOOD: Each thread touches its pages
double *a = malloc(N * sizeof(double));
#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) a[i] = 0.0;  // Each thread touches its pages
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.5 NUMA-Aware OS Support
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Linux APIs
items.text:
#include <numa.h>

// Allocate on specific node
void *ptr = numa_alloc_onnode(size, node);

// Allocate interleaved across nodes
void *ptr = numa_alloc_interleaved(size, nodemask);

// Set preferred node for current thread
numa_set_preferred(node);

// Get current node
int node = numa_node_of_cpu(sched_getcpu());

// Move pages between nodes
move_pages(pid, count, pages, nodes, status, flags);
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Scheduler Support
items.text:
• Prefers same-node migration
  • Cross-node only for severe imbalance
  • Tracks NUMA topology
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.5 NUMA + Page Replacement
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Challenge
items.text:
• Global replacement may choose remote victim
  • Evicting remote page = remote disk I/O (slow)
  • Allocating replacement on local node = good
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Solution: NUMA-Aware Replacement
items.text:
1. Prefer local victims
  2. If no local victim, consider remote with penalty
  3. Allocate replacement on requesting node
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Linux Implementation
items.text:
• Per-zone LRU lists (each NUMA node has own LRU)
  • kswapd runs per node
  • Global direct reclaim considers NUMA distance
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Migrate-on-Fault
items.text:
Process on Node 0 accesses page on Node 1:
1. Page fault (page present but remote)
2. Option A: Migrate page to Node 0
   - Allocate local frame
   - Copy content
   - Update PTE
   - Free remote frame
3. Option B: Keep remote, track NUMA hint
   - Increment NUMA fault counter
   - If threshold exceeded → migrate
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.6 Clock Page Replacement (Second-Chance)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Basic Algorithm
items.text:
• Circular list of frames with reference bit (R)
  • Hand sweeps around:
  • If R=0 → victim (replace)
  • If R=1 → R=0, give second chance, advance hand
Frame:  [P1,1] [P2,0] [P3,1] [P4,1] [P5,0]
              ↑ hand
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Logic
items.text:
while (true):
    if frame[hand].ref == 0:
        victim = hand
        break
    else:
        frame[hand].ref = 0  // second chance
        hand = (hand + 1) % N
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.7 Enhanced Clock (Second-Chance with Dirty Bit)
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 4 Priority Classes (Best → Worst)
items.text: Priority (Ref, Dirty) Reason 1 (Best) (0, 0) Not referenced, clean → no write-back 2 (0, 1) Not referenced, dirty → needs write-back 3 (1, 0) Referenced, clean → recently used 4 (Worst) (1, 1) Referenced and dirty
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
1. Scan for (0,0) — if found, replace
  2. If not found, scan for (0,1) — clear ref, advance
  3. If not found, scan for (1,0) — clear ref, advance
  4. If not found, scan for (1,1) — clear ref, advance
  5. Repeat from step 1

Linux uses variant of enhanced clock.
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.6 Clock Algorithm Example (Trace)
items.text:
Reference String: 1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 1 Frames: 3 Initial: all R=0

Step Ref Frame States (Page, R) Action 1 1 [1,0], [-,0], [-,0] Fault, set R=1 2 2 [1,1], [2,1], [-,0] Fault, set R=1 3 3 [1,1], [2,1], [3,1] Fault, set R=1 4 2 [1,1], [2,1], [3,1] Hit, set R=1 5 4 Hand: 1@1→0, 2@1→0, 3@1→0, 1@0→VICTIM! → [4,1], [2,0], [3,0] Fault 6 1 Hand: 2@0 → VICTIM! → [4,1], [1,1], [3,0] Fault
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.7 Enhanced Clock Algorithm Details
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Multi-Pass Algorithm
items.text:
Pass 1: Scan for (0,0) — replace immediately if found
Pass 2: Scan for (0,1) — clear ref, advance; if completes → write dirty, replace
Pass 3: Scan for (1,0) — clear ref, advance
Pass 4: Scan for (1,1) — clear ref, advance
Repeat from Pass 1
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Why (0,0) First?
items.text:
• No disk write needed → fastest replacement
  • Clean page → can be overwritten immediately
  • Unreferenced → unlikely to be needed soon
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: Why (1,1) Last?
items.text:
• Recently used → likely to be used again
  • Modified → requires disk write before replacement
  • Maximum cost to replace
path: Topic 22 (Detailed): NUMA, Memory Locality & Clock Page Replacement

items.title: 22.8 Complete Exam-Focused Summary
items.text: Concept Key Points NUMA Local memory ~100ns, remote ~200-400ns First-touch Page allocated on node where first written NUMA scheduler Prefers same-node migration; cross-node for severe imbalance Clock Algorithm Circular + R bit; R=1→reset to 0, advance; R=0→replace Enhanced Clock 4 passes by (R,D): (0,0)>(0,1)>(1,0)>(1,1) Pass 0: (0,0) Best - no I/O needed Pass 3: (1,1) Worst - recently used + dirty Linux Uses enhanced clock variant

items.title: 23.1 Overview: File System & Directory
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: What is a File System?
items.text:
• Directory: A collection of nodes containing information about all files
  • Both directory structure and files reside on disk
  • Maps logical file names → physical disk locations
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Disk Structure
items.text:
• Disk partitions: Disk can be subdivided into partitions
  • RAID: Disks/partitions can be RAID protected against failure
  • Raw vs Formatted: Disk/partition can be used raw (no file system) or formatted with a file system
  • Partitions = minidisks, slices
  • Volume: Entity containing file system; each volume tracks its file system info in device directory or volume table of contents
  • Special-purpose FS: Many special-purpose FS coexist with general-purpose FS
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: LVM (Logical Volume Manager)
items.text:
Physical Volumes → Partitions → Logical Volumes → File Systems
/dev/sdb1        /dev/sdb1    /home (ext3)  /data (xfs)
/dev/sdc2        /dev/sdc2
- Physical volumes → Partitions → Logical Volumes → File Systems - Allows flexible volume management across multiple physical disks
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.2 Disk Structure
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Disk Organization
items.text:
• Platters: Rigid disks coated with magnetic material
  • Tracks: Concentric circles on each surface
  • Sectors: Smallest addressable unit (typically 512 bytes or 4KB)
  • Cylinders: Set of tracks at same radius across all platters
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Disk Addressing
items.text: Logical Block Address (LBA) = (Cylinder × Heads × Sectors/Track) + (Head × Sectors/Track) + Sector
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Disk Controller
items.text:
• Hardware interface between CPU and disk
  • Manages: seek time, rotational latency, transfer time
  • Handles bad block mapping, caching
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.3 Directory Structure
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Operations on Directory
items.text: Operation Description Search Locate file by name Create Add new file entry Delete Remove file entry List Display directory contents Rename Change file name Traverse Walk directory tree

items.title: 23.4 Directory Organization Principles
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Design Goals
items.text: Goal Description Efficiency Locate file quickly Naming Convenient to users; allow same name for different files Grouping Logical grouping by properties (all Java programs, all games)

items.title: 23.5 Single-Level Directory
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Single directory for all users
  • All files in one directory
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Problems
items.text:
Problem Description Naming No two files can have same name Grouping Cannot group files logically 
Directory: cat, bo, a, test, da, mail, cont, hex, record
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.6 Two-Level Directory
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Separate directory for each user
  • Path name: /user/file
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Advantages
items.text:
• Different users can have same file name
  • Efficient searching (smaller per-user directory)
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• No grouping capability (all files of user in one directory)
User1: [file1, file2, file3]
User2: [file1, file4, file5]

items.title: 23.7 Tree-Structured Directories (Most Common)
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Root directory at top
  • Every file has a unique path from root
  • Supports subdirectories to arbitrary depth
Root
├── home
│   ├── user1
│   │   ├── docs
│   │   └── projects
│   └── user2
├── bin
├── etc
└── var

items.title: Features
items.text: Feature Description Efficient searching Path-based lookup Grouping Logical grouping by properties Current directory Working directory (.) Path names Absolute (/home/user/file) or relative (../file)

items.text: Command Action mkdir <dir> Create subdirectory in current directory rm <file> Delete file rm -r <dir> Delete directory + entire subtree cd <path> Change current directory pwd Print working directory

items.text:

rm -r mail

items.title: 23.8 Acyclic-Graph Directories
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Motivation
items.text:
• Share subdirectories and files between users
  • Same file/subdirectory in multiple directories
  • Example: Two programmers working on joint project
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Directed acyclic graph (no cycles)
  • Same file/subdirectory appears in multiple directories
  • Aliasing: Two different names (paths) for same file
User A: /home/a/project/src
User B: /home/b/project/src
         ↓ (same physical file)
Shared: /shared/project/src
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Aliasing Problems
items.text: Issue Description Dangling pointer If A deletes, B's pointer becomes invalid Multiple copies Confusion about which is "real"
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Solutions for Dangling Pointers
items.text: Solution Description Backpointers Maintain pointers from file to all directories referencing it Daisy chain Chain of backpointers Entry-hold-count Reference count; delete when count = 0 New directory entry type Special link entries

path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Link Operations
items.text: Operation Hard Link Symbolic Link Create ln file link ln -s file link Delete original Link still works Becomes dangling Cross filesystem No Yes Directory Usually not allowed Allowed
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.10 General Graph Directory
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Allows cycles within directory structure
  • Multiple directories can be derived from more than one parent
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Advantages
items.text:
• Maximum flexibility in sharing
  • Complex relationships modeled naturally
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Disadvantages
items.text: Disadvantage Description Costly More complex traversal Garbage collection Need to traverse entire FS to find accessible objects Cycles Can cause infinite loops in traversal
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Cycle Prevention
items.text: Method Description Link restriction Allow only links to files, not subdirectories Cycle detection Run cycle detection algorithm on each new link Garbage collection Periodic full traversal to mark accessible objects
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.11 File System Mounting
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Mount: Attach a filesystem to directory tree at mount point
  • Unmount: Detach filesystem
Before mount:          After mount /dev/sdb1 on /mnt/data:
/mnt/data (empty)      /mnt/data → shows /dev/sdb1 contents

items.text:
• OS maintains table of mounted filesystems
  • Contains: device, mount point, filesystem type, options

items.title: 23.12 File Sharing & Protection
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Access Control
items.text: Method Description Access Control List (ACL) Per-file list of users + permissions Permission Bits Owner/Group/Other (rwx) Capabilities Unforgeable tokens granting specific access
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: Remote File Systems
items.text:
• NFS: Network File System (Unix)
  • SMB/CIFS: Server Message Block (Windows)
  • AFS: Andrew File System
path: Topic 23: File System — Directory & Disk Structure

items.title: 23.12 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Directory = logical organization of files; maps names → metadata
  2. Disk = physical storage; partitioned → volumes → file systems
  3. Tree-structured directories = most common; supports hierarchy, grouping
  4. Acyclic-graph = enables sharing; requires cycle prevention
  5. Links = hard (same inode) vs symbolic (path pointer)
  6. Mounting = attaches filesystem to directory tree
  7. Protection = ACLs, permission bits, capabilities

items.title: 24.1 File Concept
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• File: Logical storage unit; a sequence of bits, bytes, lines, or records
  • Meaning: Defined by file's creator and user
  • Content: Source/executable programs, numeric/text data, photos, music, video, etc.
  • Storage: Data must be in files to be written to disk
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: File vs Disk
items.text: File (Logical) Disk (Physical) Abstract view Hardware storage Sequence of bits/bytes/records Magnetic/optical media User-defined meaning Block/sector organization
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: File Data Types
items.text: Type Examples Numeric Integers, floats, scientific data Alphabetic Text documents, source code Alphanumeric Mixed text/numbers Binary Executables, images, audio, video, compressed files
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.2 File Attributes
items.text: Attribute Description Name Human-readable identifier (only human-readable part) Identifier Unique tag (number) within file system Type Needed for systems supporting different types Location Pointer to file location on device Size Current file size (bytes, blocks) Protection Access controls (read/write/execute) Time/Date/User Creation, modification, access timestamps; owner ID
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Attribute Storage
items.text:
• All file metadata stored in directory structure on disk
  • Directory entry maps filename → attributes + location
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.3 File Operations
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Basic Operations
items.text: Operation Description Create Allocate space, make directory entry Write Write at write pointer location; advance pointer Read Read at read pointer location; advance pointer Reposition (Seek) Move file pointer via lseek(); no I/O Delete Remove directory entry; free space Truncate Erase contents, keep attributes; set size to 0 Append Add data at end of file Open open() system call; creates open file table entry Close Release resources; decrement open count
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: File Pointers & Open File Table
items.text: Component Purpose File Pointer Per-process pointer to last read/write location Open File Table Tracks all open files system-wide File-Open Count Reference count; removes entry when count = 0
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Open File Information
items.text: Information Description File Pointer Current read/write position File-Open Count Number of processes with file open Disk Location Physical location on disk Access Rights Permissions for this open instance
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.4 File Locking
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Concurrency control for shared files
  • Similar to reader-writer locks
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Lock Types
items.text: Lock Type Behavior Similar To Shared Lock Multiple processes can hold concurrently Reader lock Exclusive Lock Only one process can hold Writer lock
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Locking Modes
items.text:
Mode Behavior Mandatory OS enforces; access denied if lock conflict Advisory Processes check locks voluntarily; OS doesn't enforce 
Mandatory: OS blocks access if lock conflict
Advisory:  Processes check lock status; cooperation required
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Classification by Extension/Content
items.text: Type Extensions Description Executable .exe, .com, .bin Ready-to-run machine code Object .obj, .o Compiled, not linked Source Code .c, .cc, .java, .pas, .asm, .a Source code in various languages Batch/Script .bat, .sh Commands for interpreter Text/Document .txt, .wp, .tex, .rtf, .doc Textual data, word processor formats Library .lib, .a, .so, .dll Libraries of routines Print/View .ps, .pdf, .jpg Formatted for printing/viewing Archive .arc, .zip, .tar Grouped files, often compressed Multimedia .mpeg, .mov, .rm, .mp3, .avi Audio/video
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.text: Approach Description OS-recognized OS understands types; enforces rules Program-decided Application interprets structure (Unix/Linux)

items.title: 24.5 File Structure
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Internal Structure Options
items.text: Structure Description None Sequence of words/bytes (byte stream) Simple Record Fixed or variable length records Lines Text lines (terminated by newline) Fixed Length All records same size Variable Length Records vary in size Complex Formatted documents, relocatable load files
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Simulating Complex Structures
items.text:
• Can simulate complex structures with byte stream + control characters
  • Who decides structure: OS (some systems) or Program (Unix-like)
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.6 Access Methods
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 1. Sequential Access
items.text:
read next    → read next record, advance pointer
write next   → write at current position, advance
reset        → rewind to beginning
- Simplest: Process records in order - Use case: Text files, logs, sequential data processing
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 2. Direct Access (Relative Access)
items.text:
read n       → read record n
write n      → write record n
position to n → move to record n
read next    → read record n+1
write next   → write record n+1
- Fixed-length logical records (key requirement) - n = relative block number (index from start) - Random access to any record
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Comparison
items.text: Aspect Sequential Direct Access Pattern In order Any order Record Size Variable Fixed Seek No Yes (position to n) Use Case Text, logs Databases, indexes
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.6 Simulation of Sequential on Direct Access
items.text:
// Direct access file simulating sequential
int cp = 0;  // current position

// Read next
read(cp);
cp = cp + 1;

// Write next
write(cp);
cp = cp + 1;
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: Systems Support
items.text: System Access Support Some Sequential only Some Direct only Most Both
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. File = logical storage unit (bits/bytes/records); meaning defined by creator
  2. Attributes = name, ID, type, location, size, protection, timestamps
  3. Operations = create, read, write, seek, delete, truncate, open, close
  4. File Pointer = per-process position; Open File Table = system-wide tracking
  5. Locking = shared (readers) vs exclusive (writers); mandatory vs advisory
  6. File Types = OS-recognized vs program-decided; extensions indicate type
  7. Access Methods = Sequential (stream) vs Direct (random, fixed records)
  8. Simulation = Sequential on direct via position counter
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 24.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer File attributes Name, ID, type, location, size, protection, time/date/user File operations Create, read, write, seek, delete, truncate, open, close Open file table Tracks open files; per-process file pointer + open count Shared vs Exclusive lock Shared = multiple readers; Exclusive = single writer Mandatory vs Advisory Mandatory = OS enforces; Advisory = cooperation required File types Executable, object, source, batch, text, library, archive, multimedia Sequential access read next, write next, reset Direct access read n, write n, position to n (fixed-length records) Simulating sequential on direct Maintain position counter (cp); increment after each read/write
path: Topic 24: File System — File Concept & Operations

items.title: 25.1 File System Mounting
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Mount: Attach a filesystem to directory tree at a mount point
  • Filesystem must be mounted before it can be accessed
  • Unmount: Detach filesystem
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: 25.5 File Protection
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Access Types
items.text: Access Description Read View file contents Write Modify file contents Execute Run as program Append Add to end only Delete Remove file List List directory contents
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Protection Goal
items.text: File owner/creator controls: - What can be done (which operations) - By whom (which users/groups)

path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Three Classes of Users
items.text: Class Symbol Permissions Owner u Set by creator Group g Users in file's group Others o Everyone else
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Permission Bits
items.text: Permission Binary Octal Meaning Read 100 4 View contents Write 010 2 Modify Execute 001 1 Run/Traverse
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.text: Class Permissions Binary Octal Owner RWX 111 7 Group RW- 110 6 Others --X 001 1
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Example: chmod 761 game
items.text:
Owner (7):  RWX (read, write, execute)
Group (6):  RW- (read, write)
Others (1): --X (execute only)
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: 25.6 Groups & Access Control
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Group Management
items.text:
# Create group
groupadd G

# Add users to group
usermod -a -G G user1
usermod -a -G G user2

# Change file group
chgrp G game

# Set permissions
chmod 761 game
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Group Benefits
items.text:
• Simplify management: Grant access to multiple users at once
  • Project-based access: Add project members to group
  • Hierarchical: Users can belong to multiple groups
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: 25.6 Advanced Access Control
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Access Control Lists (ACLs)
items.text:
• Per-file list of users + specific permissions
  • More granular than owner/group/others
  • setfacl, getfacl commands
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Capabilities
items.text:
• Unforgeable tokens granting specific access rights
  • More flexible than ACLs
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
items.text:
• System-enforced policies (e.g., SELinux, AppArmor)
  • Cannot be overridden by users
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: 25.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Mounting = attach filesystem at mount point; unmount to detach
  2. NFS/CIFS = standard network file sharing protocols
  3. Protection = owner controls what/by whom; types: read, write, execute, append, delete, list
  4. Unix Permissions = owner/group/others × read/write/execute (rwx = 7)
  5. Groups = simplify multi-user access management
  6. ACLs = finer-grained control beyond owner/group/others
path: Topic 25: File System — Mounting, Sharing & Protection

items.title: 25.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer Mounting Filesystem must be mounted before access; attaches at mount point NFS vs CIFS NFS = Unix standard; CIFS = Windows standard Unix permissions Owner/Group/Others × rwx = 3×3 bits = 9 bits chmod 761 Owner: rwx, Group: rw-, Others: --x Groups Simplify multi-user access; chgrp, chmod Access types Read, Write, Execute, Append, Delete, List MAC vs DAC MAC = system-enforced (SELinux); DAC = user-controlled

items.title: Topic 26: Shell Programming — AWK & SED
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.13.1 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 10 (Stevens & Rago Ch. 9, 10)

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Process text files: log analysis, data extraction, report generation
  • Data extraction & transformation: parse, filter, reformat text

items.title: Common Tools
items.text: Tool Type Primary Use awk Programming language Data processing, field manipulation sed Stream editor Text editing, line-based transformations

items.title: What is AWK?
items.text:
• Scripting language for pattern scanning and processing
  • Works line-by-line on input files
  • Pattern → Action paradigm

items.title: Use Cases
items.text: Use Case Description Data filtering Select lines matching pattern Report generation Format and summarize data Data extraction Pull specific fields from structured text

items.title: How AWK Works
items.text: Input File → Read line by line → Split into fields → Apply Pattern → Action → Output

items.title: AWK Processing Model
items.text:
For each line in input:
    1. Read line
    2. Split into fields ($1, $2, $3... $NF)
    3. Test pattern condition
    4. If true → execute action
    5. Repeat for next line

items.title: Basic Syntax
items.text: awk 'pattern {action}' file

items.title: Components
items.text: Part Description pattern Condition to match (regex, comparison, etc.) action Code to execute when pattern matches file Input file(s)

items.title: Simple Example
items.text:
# Print first and fourth fields of each line
awk '{print $1,$4}' employee.txt

items.title: Field Access
items.text: Variable Meaning $1, $2, ... Field 1, 2, etc. $0 Entire line $NF Last field NF Number of fields in current line

items.title: Built-in Variables
items.text: Variable Meaning NR Number of records (lines) processed NF Number of fields in current line FS Field separator (default: whitespace) OFS Output field separator RS Record separator (default: newline) ORS Output record separator

items.title: Conditionals
items.text:
if (condition) { action }
if (condition) { action } else { action }

items.title: Operators
items.text: Type Operators Comparison ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= Logical &&, \|\|, ! Regex Match ~, !~

items.title: Example 1: Print Selected Columns
items.text:
# Print 1st and 4th fields
awk '{print $1,$4}' file.txt

items.title: Example 2: Pattern Matching
items.text:
# Print lines containing "manager"
awk '/manager/ {print}' file.txt

items.title: Example 3: Count Lines
items.text:
# Print total number of lines
awk 'END {print NR}' file.txt

items.title: Example 4: Conditional Processing
items.text:
# Print lines where 3rd field > 100
awk '$3 > 100 {print $1, $3}' data.txt

# Print lines where 1st field starts with "error"
awk '$1 ~ /^error/ {print}' log.txt

items.title: Example 5: Arithmetic & Reporting
items.text:
# Sum 3rd column
awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum}' data.txt

# Average of 2nd column
awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum/NR}' data.txt

# Max of 4th column
awk 'BEGIN {max=0} $4 > max {max=$4} END {print max}' data.txt

items.title: Example 6: Field Separator
items.text:
# CSV file (comma-separated)
awk -F',' '{print $1, $3}' data.csv

# Colon-separated (like /etc/passwd)
awk -F':' '{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd

items.title: What is SED?
items.text:
• Stream Editor for text transformation
  • Single pass through input
  • Pipeline-friendly: command | sed '...' | command

items.title: Syntax
items.text: sed 'command' file

items.title: Basic Example
items.text:
# Replace first "hello" with "world" on each line
sed 's/hello/world/' file.txt

items.title: 26.7 SED — Common Operations
items.text: Command Syntax Description Substitute s/old/new/ Replace first occurrence per line Substitute Global s/old/new/g Replace all occurrences per line Delete d Delete line Print p Print line (with -n to suppress default) Insert i\text Insert before line Append a\text Append after line

items.title: Example 1: Substitute (Replace)
items.text:
# Replace first "hello" with "world" per line
sed 's/hello/world/' file.txt

# Replace ALL "hello" with "world" per line
sed 's/hello/world/g' file.txt

# Case-insensitive
sed 's/hello/world/gi' file.txt

items.title: Example 2: Delete Lines
items.text:
# Delete line 2
sed '2d' file.txt

# Delete lines 4-6
sed '4,6d' file.txt

# Delete lines matching pattern
sed '/error/d' file.txt

items.title: Example 3: Print Specific Lines
items.text:
# Print only line 2 (suppress default output with -n)
sed -n '2p' file.txt

# Print lines 2-5
sed -n '2,5p' file.txt

items.title: Example 4: Range Operations
items.text:
# Delete lines 4-6
sed '4,6d' file.txt

# Print lines between patterns
sed -n '/start/,/end/p' file.txt

items.title: Example 5: In-Place Editing
items.text:
# Modify file in-place (backup with .bak)
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file.txt

# In-place without backup
sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt

items.title: 26.8 AWK vs SED Comparison
items.text: Feature AWK SED Type Programming language Stream editor Focus Data processing Text editing Works On Fields (columns) Lines Complexity Higher (full language) Simpler Variables Yes (NR, NF, custom) Limited Arithmetic Yes No Conditionals Full if/else/while Limited Best For Reports, data extraction, math Line edits, substitutions, deletions

items.title: When to Use Which
items.text: Scenario Tool Column extraction, math, reports AWK Line deletion, substitution, simple edits SED Complex data processing AWK Simple search/replace in pipeline SED

items.title: Example: Process Log File
items.text:
# Extract IP addresses and count occurrences (AWK)
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

# Same with AWK only
awk '{ip[$1]++} END {for (i in ip) print ip[i], i}' access.log

items.title: Example: Clean CSV with SED then Process with AWK
items.text:
# Remove quotes from CSV, then process
sed 's/"//g' data.csv | awk -F',' '{print $2, $5}'

items.title: 26.10 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. AWK = field-oriented programming language; NR/NF, math, conditionals
  2. SED = stream editor; line-oriented; substitute, delete, print
  3. AWK syntax: awk 'pattern {action}' file
  4. SED syntax: sed 'command' file
  5. AWK fields: $1, $2...$NF; built-ins: NR, NF, FS, OFS
  6. SED commands: s/old/new/g, d, p, 2d, 4,6d, -n '2p'
  7. AWK vs SED: AWK = data processing/math; SED = text editing

items.title: 26.11 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer AWK field separator -F',' or -F':' NR vs NF NR = record number (line); NF = field count SED substitute s/old/new/g (g = global) SED delete line 2 sed '2d' file SED print line 3 only sed -n '3p' file AWK vs SED AWK = programming language, fields; SED = stream editor, lines AWK END block Executes after all input processed

items.title: Problem 1: AWK Column Extraction
items.text:
# /etc/passwd format: user:pass:uid:gid:gecos:home:shell
# Extract username and home directory
awk -F':' '{print $1, $6}' /etc/passwd

items.title: Problem 2: SED Line Deletion
items.text:
# Delete lines 10-20 and all lines containing "debug"
sed -e '10,20d' -e '/debug/d' log.txt

items.title: Problem 3: AWK Sum & Average
items.text:
# File: value1 value2 value3 (space-separated)
# Print sum of column 2 and average of column 3
awk '{sum2+=$2; sum3+=$3} END {print "Sum:", sum2, "Avg:", sum3/NR}' data.txt

items.title: Problem 4: SED In-Place Edit
items.text:
# Replace all "TODO" with "DONE" in all .c files
sed -i 's/TODO/DONE/g' *.c

items.title: Problem 5: Combined Pipeline
items.text:
# Count unique IP addresses in web log
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq | wc -l

items.title: What is a Device Driver?
items.text:
• Definition: Specialized software component enabling OS to communicate with and control a hardware device
  • Role: Translator between OS and hardware
  • Benefit: OS doesn't need to understand internal hardware details
  • Interface: Provides standard interface for OS to access device
path: Topic 27: Device Drivers, Flash Storage & File System Implementation

items.text: Device Driver Keyboard Keyboard Driver Mouse Mouse Driver Printer Printer Driver HDD/SSD Disk/Storage Driver Network Card Network Card Driver USB USB Driver

items.title: Topic 28: File System — Allocation Methods
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.4 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 11 (Silberschatz Ch. 11, Stallings Ch. 12)

items.title: What is an Allocation Method?
items.text:
• Determines how disk blocks are assigned to files
  • Affects: performance, fragmentation, access speed, space utilization

items.title: Three Main Methods
items.text: Method Description Contiguous File = contiguous blocks Linked File = linked list of blocks Indexed File = index block with pointers

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Each file occupies contiguous blocks on disk
  • Directory entry stores: starting block + length (in blocks)

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Best performance Sequential & direct access both fast Simple Only starting block + length needed Direct access Block K = start + K Sequential access Natural, no seeks

items.title: Address Translation
items.text:
Logical Address = Block # (Q) + Offset (R)
Block to access = Start Block + Q
Offset in block = R

items.title: Example
items.text:
File starts at block 100, length = 5 blocks
Block 0 → Physical 100
Block 1 → Physical 101
Block 2 → Physical 102
...
Block K → Physical (100 + K)

items.title: 28.3 Contiguous Allocation Problems
items.text: Problem Description External Fragmentation Free space scattered in small chunks Finding Space First-fit / Best-fit / Worst-fit needed File Size Known Must know final size at creation Compaction Required to reclaim space; offline (downtime) or online

items.title: Compaction
items.text:
• Offline: System down; move all files to consolidate free space
  • Online: System running; complex, affects performance

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Each file = linked list of blocks
  • Each block contains pointer to next block
  • Directory entry: pointer to first block

items.title: Structure
items.text:
Directory Entry → Block 1 → Block 2 → Block 3 → ... → NULL
                    ↓           ↓           ↓
                 Data+ptr   Data+ptr   Data+ptr

items.title: Space Overhead
items.text: Parameter Calculation Block size 512 bytes Pointer size 4 bytes Usable data 508 bytes per block Overhead ~0.8% per block

items.title: Clustering
items.text:
• Group blocks into clusters (e.g., 4 blocks = 2KB)
  • Allocate clusters instead of individual blocks
  • Reduces pointer overhead

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description No external fragmentation Any free block can be used No compaction needed Free blocks anywhere Dynamic growth File can grow as long as free blocks exist Simple Only first block in directory

items.title: Disadvantages
items.text: Disadvantage Description No direct access Must traverse from start (O(n) seeks) Sequential only Efficient for sequential, poor for random Space overhead Pointer in each block Reliability Broken pointer → rest of file lost No caching benefit Can't cache intermediate blocks effectively

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• FAT = variation of linked allocation
  • Table at start of volume indexed by block number
  • Like linked list but faster (cached in memory)

items.title: FAT Entry Values
items.text: Value Meaning 0 Free/unused block 1...N-1 Next block in chain EOF End of file (special marker)

items.title: FAT Operation
items.text:
To allocate new block to file:
1. Find first 0 in FAT
2. Replace previous EOF with new block address
3. Set new block to EOF

items.title: Directory Entry
items.text: Filename | Start Block | Size | Attributes

items.title: FAT Advantages
items.text: Benefit Description Faster traversal FAT cached in memory No disk seeks for traversal Table in RAM Simple allocation Scan FAT for 0

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Index block = special block with pointers to all file blocks
  • Each file has its own index block
  • Directory entry points to index block

items.title: Structure
items.text:
Directory Entry → Index Block → [Block 1, Block 2, Block 3, ...]
                                    ↓         ↓         ↓
                                Block 1   Block 2   Block 3

items.title: Address Translation
items.text: Index Block[i] = Physical address of i-th file block

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Direct access Index block gives direct block pointers No external fragmentation Any free block usable Fast random access O(1) block access via index

items.title: Disadvantages
items.text: Disadvantage Description Pointer overhead Index block full of pointers Small files waste 2-block file needs full index block Index block size limit Max file size limited by index block capacity

items.title: Overhead Comparison
items.text: Method Per-block Overhead Linked 1 pointer per block Indexed 1 pointer per block IN index block

items.title: 1. Linked Index Blocks
items.text:
• Index blocks linked together for large files
  • First index block points to next index block

items.title: 2. Multi-level Index (Unix inode style)
items.text: Index Block → Indirect Block → Double Indirect → Triple Indirect

items.title: 2. Combined Scheme (Unix inode)
items.text:
inode:
  12 Direct pointers
  1 Single indirect pointer
  1 Double indirect pointer
  1 Triple indirect pointer

items.title: 28.8 Allocation Method Comparison
items.text: Aspect Contiguous Linked Indexed Direct Access ✅ Excellent ❌ Poor ✅ Excellent Sequential Access ✅ Excellent ✅ Good ✅ Good External Fragmentation ❌ Severe ✅ None ✅ None Internal Fragmentation ❌ Last block ⚠️ Per-block pointer ⚠️ Index block Space Overhead None 1 ptr/block Index block File Growth Difficult Easy Easy File Deletion Creates holes Easy Easy Max File Size Disk size Disk size Index block capacity Reliability Good Poor (broken link) Good (index damage = loss)

items.title: Bit Vector (Bitmap)
items.text:
• One bit per block: 1 = free, 0 = allocated
  • Size: N blocks → N bits = N/8 bytes
  • Example: 1TB disk, 4KB blocks = 2^30 blocks = 2^27 bits = 128 MB bitmap

items.title: Linked List
items.text:
• Link all free blocks together
  • First free block in superblock

items.title: Grouping
items.text:
• Store addresses of N free blocks in first free block
  • Reduces list traversal

items.title: Counting
items.text:
• Store (start block, count) for contiguous free runs
  • Efficient for contiguous free space

items.title: 28.10 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Contiguous = best performance, but external fragmentation
  2. Linked = no external frag, but no direct access
  3. FAT = linked + cached table for speed
  4. Indexed = direct access, no external frag, index overhead
  5. Unix inode = combined direct/indirect indexing
  6. Free space = bitmap, linked list, grouping, or counting

items.title: 28.11 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer Contiguous allocation Start block + length; direct access = start + offset External fragmentation Contiguous suffers; linked/indexed don't Linked allocation No direct access; pointer overhead; no external frag FAT Table in memory; 0=free; chain of blocks Indexed allocation Index block with pointers; direct access Small files + indexed Wasteful (index block per file) Unix inode 12 direct + 1 indirect + 1 double + 1 triple indirect External fragmentation Contiguous only; solved by paging/compaction

items.title: Problem 1: Contiguous Allocation
items.text:

items.title: Problem 2: Linked Allocation
items.text:

items.text:

items.title: Problem 5: Unix Inode
items.text:
12 direct + 1 indirect + 1 double + 1 triple indirect.
Block size 4KB, pointer 8 bytes.
Max file size?

items.title: 29.1 Free Space Management
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Purpose
items.text:
• Reuse disk space from deleted files for new files
  • Free-space list tracks all free disk blocks
  • On file create: search free list, allocate, remove from list
  • On file delete: add blocks back to free list

items.text: Method Space Search Speed Best For Bit Vector N/8 bytes Fast (bit ops) General purpose Linked List N pointers Slow (I/O) Few free blocks Grouping N/n pointers Fast Large free space Counting 2×runs Fast (tree) Contiguous free space

items.title: 29.3 Buffer Cache vs Page Cache
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Buffer Cache (Traditional)
items.text:
• Separate memory section for file system blocks
  • Caches file-system-oriented blocks
  • Separate from virtual memory
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Page Cache (Modern)
items.text:
• Virtual memory techniques to cache file data as pages
  • Unified virtual memory: single cache for process pages + file data
  • Used by: Linux, Windows, Solaris
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Comparison
items.text: Aspect Buffer Cache Page Cache Granularity FS blocks (e.g., 4KB) VM pages (e.g., 4KB) Integration Separate from VM Unified with VM Efficiency Lower Higher (VM integration) Systems Traditional Unix Linux, Windows, Solaris
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Unified Virtual Memory
items.text:
Process Pages ←→ Page Cache ←→ Disk
- Single page cache for both process memory and file data - Eliminates double buffering - Better memory utilization
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: 29.3 I/O Without vs With Unified Buffer Cache
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Without Unified Cache
items.text:
read()/write() → Buffer Cache → Disk
mmap() → Page Cache → Disk
- Two separate caches → double buffering - Data copied between caches
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: With Unified Buffer Cache
items.text:
read()/write()/mmap() → Unified Page Cache → Disk
- Single cache for all I/O - No double buffering - Better memory utilization
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: 29.3 Sequential Access Optimization
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Free-Behind
items.text:
• When: Sequential read
  • Action: Remove page from buffer after next page requested
  • Rationale: Previous pages unlikely to be reused
  • Benefit: Frees buffer space for new pages
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: Read-Ahead
items.text:
• When: Sequential read detected
  • Action: Read requested page + several subsequent pages
  • Rationale: Next pages likely needed soon
  • Benefit: Single disk transfer for multiple pages

items.title: Comparison

items.title: 29.4 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Free Space Methods: Bit vector (fast), Linked list (simple), Grouping (fast traversal), Counting (contiguous runs)
  2. Bit Vector = best general purpose; Counting = best for contiguous allocation
  3. Buffer Cache → Page Cache → Unified VM = evolution of I/O caching
  4. Unified VM = single cache for process pages + file data
  5. Free-behind = evict read pages during sequential access
  6. Read-ahead = prefetch sequential pages
  7. Performance = keep data/metadata close; use cache effectively
path: Topic 29: File System — Free Space Management, Efficiency & Performance

items.title: 30.1 Magnetic Disk Structure
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Physical Organization
items.text: Component Description Platter Flat circular disk (1.8"-3.5" diameter); both sides coated with magnetic material Track Concentric circle on platter surface Sector Smallest addressable unit (typically 512B or 4KB) Cylinder Set of tracks at same radius across all platters Head Read/write element on actuator arm Arm Moves all heads together as a unit
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Disk Geometry
items.text:
Platter (top & bottom surfaces)
    ↓
Track (concentric circle)
    ↓
Sector (smallest addressable unit, 512B/4KB)
    ↓
Cylinder = all tracks at same radius across platters
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Disk Addressing (CHS)
items.text:
Cylinder (C) = Arm position
Head (H)     = Platter surface (0 or 1 per platter)
Sector (S)   = Sector number within track

LBA = (C × Heads × Sectors/Track) + (H × Sectors/Track) + S
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: 30.2 Disk Performance Metrics
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Disk Latency Components
items.text:
Disk Latency = Seek Time + Rotational Latency + Transfer Time
Component Description Typical Value Seek Time Move arm to target cylinder 3-10 ms (avg) Rotational Latency Wait for sector to rotate under head 0.5 × Rotation Period (2-4 ms at 7200 RPM) Transfer Time Data transfer rate 50-200 MB/s
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Total Latency Formula
items.text: Disk Latency = Seek Time + Rotational Latency + (Bytes / Transfer Rate)
path: Topic 30: Mass Storage Structure — Disk Structure & SSD

items.title: Disk Speed
items.text:
• Rotation: 5,400 - 15,000 RPM (typically 7,200 RPM)
  • Rotation Period: 8.33 ms (7200 RPM)
  • Average Rotational Latency: 4.17 ms (half rotation)

items.text:

items.title: Air Bearing
items.text:
• Head flies on air cushion (nanometers above surface)
  • Generated by platter rotation

items.title: 30.6 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Disk Structure: Platters → Tracks → Sectors → Cylinders
  2. Disk Latency = Seek + Rotational Latency + Transfer
  3. Seek Time = Arm movement to cylinder (3-10 ms)
  4. Rotational Latency = 0.5 × rotation period (2-4 ms at 7200 RPM)
  5. SSD = No seek/rotational latency; NAND flash; limited write cycles
  6. Tape = Sequential only; backup/archival; high capacity, low cost
  7. Interfaces: SATA, SAS, NVMe, Fiber Channel
