items.title: Topic 31: Disk Scheduling & Disk Management
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.7 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 12 (Silberschatz Ch. 12, Stallings Ch. 13)

items.title: Goals
items.text: Goal Description Minimize Seek Time Seek time ∝ seek distance Maximize Disk Bandwidth Total bytes transferred / total time (first request to last completion)

items.title: Why Scheduling Matters
items.text:
• Multiple I/O requests from: OS, system processes, user processes
  • Requests queued per disk/device
  • Idle disk → immediate service
  • Busy disk → requests queued
  • Optimization only matters when queue exists

items.title: I/O Request Structure
items.text: Field Description Mode Input (read) or Output (write) Disk Address Cylinder/track/sector or LBA Memory Address Buffer in RAM Sector Count Number of sectors to transfer

items.title: Reference Queue
items.text:
Queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67
Head starts at: 53
Cylinders: 0-199

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
• Service requests in arrival order
  • No optimization

items.title: Characteristics
items.text: Property Value Total Movement 640 cylinders Fairness ✅ Perfect Performance ❌ Poor (no optimization)

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
• Select request with minimum seek time from current head position
  • Form of SJF scheduling

items.title: Characteristics
items.text: Property Value Total Movement 236 cylinders (vs 640 FCFS) Throughput ✅ Better than FCFS Starvation ❌ Possible (requests far from head) Fairness ❌ Poor

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
• Arm moves from one end to other
  • Services requests in current direction
  • At end → reverse direction
  • Also called: Elevator Algorithm

items.title: Characteristics
items.text: Property Value Total Movement 236 cylinders Starvation None (all requests eventually served) Variance ⚠️ Ends wait longer if uniform density

items.title: Algorithm
items.text:
• Head moves from one end to other
  • At end → immediately returns to start (no service on return)
  • Cylinders treated as circular list (wraps around)

items.title: Characteristics
items.text: Property Value Total Movement 382 cylinders Wait Time More uniform than SCAN Return Trip No service (fast return)

items.title: LOOK (Improved SCAN)
items.text:
• Arm goes only to last request in current direction
  • Reverses immediately (no travel to physical end)

items.title: C-LOOK (Improved C-SCAN)
items.text:
• Goes to last request in direction
  • Jumps to first request in opposite direction

items.title: C-LOOK Trace
items.text:
Head at 53, direction ↑
53 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183 (last request)
→ Jump to 14 (first request in other direction)
→ 37
End at 37

Movements:
53→65   = 12
65→67   = 2
67→98   = 31
98→122  = 24
122→124 = 2
124→183 = 59
183→14  = 169 (jump)
14→37   = 23
Total = 322 cylinders

items.title: 31.5 Algorithm Comparison
items.text:
Algorithm Total Movement Starvation Fairness Complexity FCFS 640 None Perfect O(1) SSTF 236 Possible Poor O(n) SCAN 236 None Good O(n log n) C-SCAN 382 None Better O(n log n) LOOK ~200* None Good O(n log n) C-LOOK 322 None Best O(n log n)

*LOOK varies based on request distribution

items.title: Selection Guidelines
items.text: Scenario Recommended Light load SSTF (simple, good throughput) Heavy load SCAN / C-SCAN (less starvation) Real-time C-LOOK / LOOK (predictable) General purpose SSTF or LOOK (default)

items.title: Selection Factors
items.text: Factor Consideration Load Heavy → SCAN/C-SCAN; Light → SSTF Starvation tolerance Low → avoid SSTF Predictability Real-time → LOOK/C-LOOK Implementation Modular design for easy replacement

items.title: The Problem
items.text:
• Rotational latency ≈ Seek time (can be equally large)
  • OS cannot easily optimize because:
  • Modern disks don't expose physical block locations
  • Logical Block Address (LBA) ≠ physical sector

items.title: Solution: Controller-Based Scheduling
items.text:
OS → Batch of requests → Disk Controller
    ↓
Controller queues & schedules for:
  1. Seek time optimization
  2. Rotational latency optimization

items.title: Modern Approach
items.text: Layer Responsibility OS High-level scheduling (seek optimization) Disk Controller Low-level (rotational latency, NCQ)

items.title: NCQ (Native Command Queuing)
items.text:
• SATA feature: drive reorders commands internally
  • Optimizes both seek + rotational latency

items.title: Disk Formatting
items.text: Level Description Low-level Physical sectors/tracks (factory) Partitioning Logical divisions (MBR/GPT) High-level File system creation (mkfs)

items.title: Bad Block Handling
items.text: Method Description Spare sectors Reserved sectors replace bad ones Bad block list Maintained by controller/OS Sector slipping Shift sectors to skip bad ones

items.title: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks)
items.text: Level Description Redundancy RAID 0 Striping None RAID 1 Mirroring Full RAID 5 Striping + Parity 1 disk RAID 6 Striping + Dual Parity 2 disks RAID 10 Mirrored Stripes Full

items.title: 31.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. FCFS = simple, fair, poor performance
  2. SSTF = better throughput, starvation risk
  3. SCAN = elevator; no starvation; ends wait longer
  4. C-SCAN = uniform wait; return trip empty
  5. LOOK/C-LOOK = practical SCAN/C-SCAN (don't go to physical ends)
  6. Selection = SSTF/LOOK for default; SCAN/C-SCAN for heavy load
  7. Rotational latency = handled by disk controller (NCQ)
  8. Modular design = scheduling algorithm as separate module

items.title: 31.7 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer FCFS movement Sum of absolute differences in arrival order SSTF Minimum seek from current head; may starve SCAN Elevator; reverses at end; no starvation C-SCAN Circular; returns to start without service LOOK SCAN but reverses at last request, not disk end C-LOOK C-SCAN but jumps to first request, not cylinder 0 SSTF vs SCAN SSTF = better throughput, possible starvation SCAN vs C-SCAN C-SCAN = more uniform wait times Rotational latency Handled by disk controller (NCQ) Algorithm modularity Should be separate module for replaceability

items.title: Topic 32: RAID Structure
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.8 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 12 (Silberschatz Ch. 12, Stallings Ch. 13)

items.title: What is RAID?
items.text:
• RAID = Redundant Array of Independent (Inexpensive) Disks
  • Multiple disks working together as a single storage unit
  • Addresses: Performance + Reliability

items.title: Why RAID?
items.text: Problem RAID Solution Single large disk expensive Use multiple smaller disks Single disk failure = catastrophic Redundancy via redundancy Slow single-disk access Parallel I/O across disks Data loss on failure Redundancy (mirroring/parity)

items.title: RAID Goals
items.text: Goal Technique Large capacity Combine multiple disks Performance Striping (parallel I/O) Reliability Redundancy (mirroring/parity)

items.title: 32.1 Striping
items.text:
• Data split across multiple disks
  • Block-level striping (most common): Consecutive blocks on different disks
  • Bit-level striping: Bits spread across disks (rare)
Block 0 → Disk 0
Block 1 → Disk 1
Block 2 → Disk 2
Block 3 → Disk 3
Block 4 → Disk 0
...

items.title: Benefits of Striping
items.text: Benefit Description Parallel I/O Multiple disks read/write simultaneously Higher throughput Aggregate bandwidth of all disks Parallel requests Different blocks served by different disks

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Exact copy of data on two separate disks
  • RAID 1 = Mirroring

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text: Aspect Benefit Cost Read ✅ Parallel reads from both Write ❌ Write to both (slower) Reliability ✅ Complete redundancy 2× disk cost Rebuild ✅ Fast (copy from good disk)

items.title: MTTF (Mean Time To Failure)
items.text:
• Single disk MTTF: 100,000 hours
  • Array of N disks: MTTF_array = MTTF_disk / N
  • Example: 100 disks × 100,000 hrs = 1,000 hours (41.6 days)

items.title: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair)
items.text: • Time to replace failed disk + restore data

items.title: Data Loss Probability
items.text:
• Depends on: MTTF, MTTR, RAID level
  • Independent failures assumed (not power/correlated)

items.title: RAID 0: Striping (No Redundancy)
items.text: Aspect Detail Technique Block-level striping Redundancy ❌ None Capacity N × disk size Read/Write ✅ Fast (parallel) Failure Any disk loss = total data loss MTTF Lowest (1/N of single disk) Use Case Performance-critical, non-critical data

items.title: RAID 1: Mirroring (Shadowing)
items.text: Aspect Detail Technique Exact copy on 2+ disks Redundancy ✅ Full (100%) Capacity N/2 × disk size (50% usable) Read ✅ Parallel from both Write ❌ Both disks (slower) Cost Highest (2× disks) Rebuild Fast (copy from good disk)

items.title: RAID 4: Block Striping + Dedicated Parity
items.text: Aspect Detail Striping Block-level Parity Dedicated parity disk Write Penalty High (parity disk bottleneck) Read Fast (parallel data disks) Write Slow (parity disk bottleneck)

items.title: RAID 5: Block-Interleaved Distributed Parity
items.text: Aspect Detail Striping Block-level Parity Distributed across all disks Parity Distribution Rotates across disks Write Penalty ✅ No bottleneck (parallel) Failure Tolerance 1 disk Capacity (N-1) × disk size

items.title: RAID 5 Parity Layout (4 Disks)
items.text:
Block:     0    1    2    3
Disk 0:    D0   D1   D2   P3
Disk 1:    D4   D5   P2   D3
Disk 2:    D8   P1   D5   D6
Disk 3:    P0   D9   D10  D11
- Parity rotates across disks - No single parity bottleneck

items.title: Write Penalty
items.text: Operation Disk Accesses Read 1 (data) Write (small) 4 (read old data, read old parity, write new data, write new parity) Write (full stripe) N (optimal)

items.title: RAID 6: P+Q Dual Parity
items.text: Aspect Detail Parity Two independent parity schemes (P + Q) Failure Tolerance 2 disks Write Penalty Higher than RAID 5 (2 parities) Capacity (N-2) × disk size Use Case High reliability, large arrays

items.title: 32.5 RAID Level Comparison
items.text: Level Technique Redundancy Capacity Read Write Failure Tolerance RAID 0 Striping ❌ None N× ⚡ Fast ⚡ Fast 0 disks RAID 1 Mirroring ✅ Full (2×) N/2 ⚡ Parallel ⚠️ 2 writes N-1 disks RAID 4 Striping + Dedicated Parity Parity disk (N-1)× ⚡ Fast 🐢 Parity bottleneck 1 disk RAID 5 Striping + Distributed Parity Distributed Parity (N-1)× ⚡ Fast ⚡ Good (parallel) 1 disk RAID 6 Striping + Dual Parity P+Q Parity (N-2)× ⚡ Fast ⚠️ Dual parity calc 2 disks RAID 10 (1+0) Mirror + Stripe Mirror N/2 ⚡ Parallel ⚡ Fast N/2 disks

items.title: RAID 10 (1+0): Mirror then Stripe
items.text:
Mirror pairs → Stripe across pairs
Disk 1 ↔ Disk 2 (mirror)
Disk 3 ↔ Disk 4 (mirror)
Stripe across pairs

Failure: 1 disk lost → pair survives

items.title: RAID 01 (0+1): Stripe then Mirror
items.text:
Stripe first → Mirror the stripe
Stripe A ↔ Stripe B (mirror)

Failure: 1 disk lost → entire stripe fails

items.title: Comparison
items.text: Aspect RAID 10 (1+0) RAID 01 (0+1) Single Disk Failure Pair survives Entire stripe lost Rebuild Fast (copy from mirror) Slow (entire stripe) Reliability ✅ Better ⚠️ Worse

items.title: 32.6 RAID Level Comparison Summary
items.text: Level Redundancy Capacity Read Write Fail Tolerance Cost 0 None 100% ⚡⚡⚡ ⚡⚡⚡ 0 $ 1 Mirror 50% ⚡⚡ ⚡ N-1 $$$ 4 Dedicated Parity (N-1)/N ⚡⚡ 🐢 1 $$ 5 Distributed Parity (N-1)/N ⚡⚡ ⚡⚡ 1 $$ 6 Dual Parity (N-2)/N ⚡⚡ ⚡ 2 $$$ 10 Mirror+Stripe 50% ⚡⚡ ⚡⚡ N/2 $$$

items.title: Software RAID
items.text:
• OS manages RAID (Linux mdadm, Windows Storage Spaces)
  • CPU overhead for parity calc
  • Flexible, no special hardware

items.title: Hardware RAID
items.text:
• Dedicated controller with cache, battery backup
  • Offloads parity calculation
  • Transparent to OS
  • Better performance, battery-backed cache

items.title: 32.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. RAID 0 = Speed only, no redundancy
  2. RAID 1 = Mirroring; simple, expensive, fast reads
  3. RAID 4 = Dedicated parity (bottleneck)
  4. RAID 5 = Best balance; distributed parity; 1 disk failure
  5. RAID 6 = Dual parity; 2 disk failures; enterprise
  6. RAID 10 = Best performance + reliability; expensive
  7. RAID 0+1 vs 1+0 = 1+0 preferred (better failure handling)

items.title: 32.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer RAID 0 Striping, no redundancy RAID 1 Mirroring; 50% capacity; 2 writes RAID 4 vs 5 4 = dedicated parity (bottleneck); 5 = distributed RAID 5 write Read old data + old parity, write new data + new parity (4 I/Os) RAID 6 Dual parity (P+Q); tolerates 2 failures RAID 10 vs 01 10 = mirror then stripe (better); 01 = stripe then mirror RAID 5 capacity (N-1) × disk size RAID 6 capacity (N-2) × disk size RAID 10 capacity 50% (N/2)

items.title: Topic 33: OS Security — Program Threats
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.9 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 14-15 (Silberschatz Ch. 14, 15, Stallings Ch. 15)

items.title: Why Security Matters
items.text: OS manages valuable resources: - Programs & processes - Files & data - Memory & CPU - Network resources - User accounts & credentials

items.title: Security Breach Impact
items.text: Consequence Description Unauthorized Access Access to restricted data/systems Data Theft/Disclosure Confidential info exposed Data Modification Integrity violation Data Destruction Availability breach Resource Misuse Theft of service (CPU, storage) Service Disruption Denial of Service

items.title: 33.2 Security Violation Types
items.text: Violation Type Description CIA Triad Breach of Confidentiality Unauthorized reading/disclosure Confidentiality Breach of Integrity Unauthorized modification Integrity Breach of Availability Unauthorized destruction/disruption Availability Theft of Service Unauthorized resource use Availability/Integrity Denial of Service (DoS) Prevent legitimate access Availability

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Program Threat: Malicious/compromised program attempts unauthorized access, resource misuse, or system damage
  • Programs/processes = primary work mechanism → primary attack vector

items.title: Attacker Capabilities via Program Exploitation
items.text: Capability Description Unauthorized Data Access Read restricted files/data File Modification/Deletion Corrupt or destroy data Privilege Escalation Gain higher privileges (root/admin) Code Execution Run arbitrary malicious code System Disruption Crash, hang, resource exhaustion

items.title: Malware Categories
items.text: Threat Description Malware Malicious software to exploit/disable/damage Trojan Horse Appears legitimate, hides malicious function Spyware Secretly collects user/system info Ransomware Encrypts files, demands ransom Code Injection Inject unauthorized code into program Virus Self-replicating code attached to host Worm Self-replicating, spreads via network Trap Door/Back Door Hidden unauthorized access point

items.title: Malware
items.text: Aspect Description Definition Software designed to exploit, disable, damage, or gain unauthorized access Deception Appears legitimate while performing malicious actions Forms Trojan, Spyware, Ransomware, Virus, Worm

items.title: Trojan Horse
items.text: Characteristic Description Deception Appears legitimate, hides malicious payload Execution Runs with user's privileges Delivery User unknowingly installs/executes Damage Data theft, system modification, backdoor creation

items.title: Spyware
items.text: Aspect Description Purpose Secretly collect user/system information Targets Browsing, credentials, personal info, files Exfiltration Sends data to attacker without user knowledge Example Keylogger, screen scraper, credential harvester

items.title: Ransomware
items.text: Aspect Description Action Encrypts victim's files/data Demand Ransom payment for decryption key Impact Data inaccessible without key Payment Often cryptocurrency (untraceable)

items.title: Code Injection
items.text: Aspect Description Definition Insert unauthorized code into program execution Cause Poor input validation, insecure coding Impact Modify behavior, execute commands, access data, gain control

items.title: Buffer Overflow (Classic Example)
items.text:
Program: char buffer[64];
Input:    "A" × 100  (exceeds 64 bytes)
Result:   Overflow → overwrite return address → execute attacker's code
Step Description 1. Program allocates fixed buffer 2. Attacker supplies excess data 3. Overflow overwrites adjacent memory 4. Crafted input overwrites return address 5. Program jumps to attacker's code

items.title: Virus
items.text: Property Description Structure Code fragment embedded in legitimate program/file Replication Infects other programs/files Trigger Requires user action (execute infected file) Payload Modify/destroy files, corrupt programs, crash system, spread Virus Type Behavior Boot Sector Infects boot sector File Infector Attaches to executables Macro Infects documents (Word/Excel) Polymorphic Changes code to evade detection

items.title: Worm
items.text: Property Virus Worm Attachment Needs host program Standalone Spread User action required Automatic (network) Replication Infects files Self-replicates Propagation File sharing, media Network exploits Worm Impact Description Network Congestion Bandwidth consumption System Slowdown Resource consumption Service Disruption Overload services Secondary Payload Install additional malware

items.title: Trap Door / Back Door
items.text: Aspect Description Definition Hidden entry point bypassing authentication Origin Intentional (dev) or malicious (attacker) Risk Unauthorized system access Detection Code review, auditing, intrusion detection

items.title: Definition
items.text: A user or program should be given only the minimum privileges required to perform its task.

items.title: Privilege Limitation Dimensions
items.text: Dimension Application Scope What resources can be accessed Time How long access is granted

items.title: Implementation
items.text: Technique Description Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Privileges by role, not user Capabilities Fine-grained tokens for specific operations Sandboxing Isolate process with minimal privileges Dropping Privileges Drop root after initialization

items.title: System Threats
items.text: Threat Description Buffer Overflow Overwrite memory to execute code Race Condition Timing-dependent vulnerability Privilege Escalation Gain higher privileges Rootkit Hide malicious activity

items.title: Network Threats
items.text: Threat Description Eavesdropping Intercept network traffic Man-in-the-Middle Intercept/modify communications Replay Attack Re-send captured valid data Session Hijacking Take over authenticated session DDoS Distributed Denial of Service

items.title: Prevention
items.text: Mechanism Description Input Validation Sanitize all inputs Bounds Checking Prevent buffer overflows ASLR Address Space Layout Randomization DEP/NX Data Execution Prevention Stack Canaries Detect stack smashing

items.title: Detection
items.text: Mechanism Description Intrusion Detection (IDS) Monitor for suspicious activity Antivirus/Anti-malware Signature + heuristic scanning Audit Logs Track security events

items.title: Response
items.text: Action Description Quarantine Isolate compromised systems Patch Apply security updates Forensics Analyze breach

items.title: 33.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Security Goals = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability (CIA)
  2. Program Threats = Malware, Trojans, Spyware, Ransomware, Viruses, Worms, Code Injection
  3. Buffer Overflow = Classic code injection via input overflow
  4. Virus vs Worm = Virus needs host/user action; Worm = standalone + network spread
  5. Back Door = Hidden unauthorized access
  6. Least Privilege = Minimum necessary privileges only
  7. Defense = Input validation, ASLR, DEP, stack canaries, IDS

items.title: 33.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer CIA Triad Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability Virus vs Worm Virus needs host/user action; Worm = standalone + network Buffer Overflow Input exceeds buffer → overwrite return address → code execution Trojan Horse Legitimate appearance, hidden malicious function Ransomware Encrypts files, demands ransom for decryption key Spyware Secretly collects user data (keystrokes, credentials) Code Injection Unauthorized code execution via input validation flaw Buffer Overflow Exceeds buffer → overwrites return address → executes shellcode Least Privilege Minimum necessary privileges only Trap Door/Backdoor Hidden access bypassing authentication

items.title: Topic 34: System & Network Threats
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.10 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 14-15 (Silberschatz Ch. 14, 15, Stallings Ch. 15)

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• System Threat: Attack targeting system services, resources, or operating environment
  • Goals: Make resources unavailable, consume resources, gain unauthorized access, exploit weaknesses, disrupt operations

items.title: Common System Threats
items.text: Threat Description Denial-of-Service (DoS) Make system/service unavailable to legitimate users Port Scanning Probe network ports to find open services/entry points

items.title: Definition
items.text: • DoS Attack: Overwhelms system resources to make service unavailable to legitimate users

items.title: Resources Targeted
items.text: Resource Attack Method CPU Infinite loops, heavy computation requests Memory Memory allocation exhaustion (malloc bombs) Network Bandwidth Flood with packets (volumetric attacks) Connection Capacity SYN flood, connection table exhaustion Storage Disk fill (log filling, temp files)

items.title: DoS Attack Types
items.text: Type Description Volumetric Flood bandwidth (UDP flood, ICMP flood) Protocol Exploit protocol weaknesses (SYN flood, Ping of Death) Application Layer Target specific apps (HTTP flood, Slowloris) Distributed (DDoS) Multiple compromised systems (botnet)

items.title: DoS Mitigation
items.text: Defense Description Rate Limiting Throttle requests per IP SYN Cookies Prevent SYN flood Traffic Filtering Block malicious IPs CDN/Load Balancer Distribute traffic Resource Quotas Per-user/process limits

items.title: Definition
items.text: • Port Scanning: Systematically probe network ports to identify open services

items.title: Why Port Scanning?
items.text: Purpose Description Reconnaissance Find open services & entry points Vulnerability Assessment Identify vulnerable service versions Attack Planning Map attack surface

items.title: Common Ports
items.text: Port Service 21 FTP 22 SSH 23 Telnet 25 SMTP 53 DNS 80 HTTP 110 POP3 143 IMAP 443 HTTPS 3306 MySQL 3389 RDP

items.title: Port Scan Types
items.text: Scan Type Technique TCP Connect Full TCP handshake (SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK) SYN Scan Send SYN, analyze SYN/ACK (stealthier) FIN/XMAS/NULL Abnormal flag combinations UDP Scan Send UDP, check ICMP unreachable

items.title: Legitimate vs Malicious
items.text: Context Purpose Administrator Security auditing, troubleshooting Attacker Reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery

items.title: Definition
items.text: • Attacks exploiting vulnerabilities in network communication, protocols, or connected systems

items.title: Attacker Goals
items.text: Goal Description Intercept Communication Eavesdrop on traffic Steal Information Credentials, data, session tokens Impersonation Spoof identity, MITM Data Modification Alter transmitted data Service Disruption DoS, connection reset

items.title: 34.3 Common Network Threats
items.text: Threat Description IP Spoofing Forge source IP address Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Intercept/modify communication between parties Packet Sniffing Capture & analyze network packets Session Hijacking Take over authenticated session Replay Attack Re-send captured valid data DNS Spoofing/Poisoning Redirect to malicious sites

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Technique: Forge source IP address in packet headers
  • Purpose: Hide identity, impersonate trusted host, bypass IP-based filters

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
Attacker → Forged Packet (src=Trusted_IP) → Victim
Victim → Response → Trusted_IP (not attacker)

items.title: Uses
items.text: Purpose Description DoS Flood with spoofed packets Bypass Filters Bypass IP-based ACLs MITM Setup Impersonate trusted host Blind Spoofing Predict sequence numbers

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Attacker secretly positions between two communicating parties
  • Can intercept, read, modify, or inject messages
  • Parties believe they communicate directly

items.title: MITM Process
items.text:
Alice ←────────→ Attacker ←────────→ Bob
   (believes Bob)          (believes Alice)

items.title: Capabilities
items.text: Capability Description Intercept Read all communication Modify Alter messages in transit Inject Insert malicious data Impersonate Pretend to be each party to the other

items.title: MITM Requirements
items.text: Requirement Method Network Position Same LAN, compromised router, ARP spoofing Encryption Bypass SSL stripping, fake certificates Trust Establishment Fake certificates, CA compromise

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Packet Sniffing: Capture and analyze network packets in transit
  • Tool: Packet sniffer (software/hardware)

items.title: Dual Nature
items.text: Context Purpose Legitimate Network monitoring, troubleshooting, security analysis Malicious Capture sensitive data without authorization

items.title: Information Exposed (Unencrypted)
items.text: Data Type Examples Credentials Usernames, passwords (HTTP basic, FTP, Telnet) Network Info IP/MAC addresses, topology Session Data Cookies, session IDs, tokens Communication Email, chat, file transfers Any Unencrypted HTTP, FTP, SNMP, DNS

items.title: Tools
items.text: Tool Type Wireshark GUI analyzer tcpdump CLI capture Ettercap MITM + sniffing dsniff Password sniffing suite

items.title: 1. Firewalls
items.text: Type Description Packet Filter Rule-based (IP, port, protocol) Stateful Tracks connection state Application/Proxy Inspects application layer Next-Gen Deep packet inspection, IPS Function Description Block Unauthorized Deny unauthorized connections Allow Authorized Permit legitimate traffic Log/Alert Record suspicious activity

items.title: 2. Encryption
items.text: Aspect Description Purpose Convert readable → unreadable (ciphertext) Protection Prevent understanding of captured data Scope Data in transit (TLS/SSL, IPsec, SSH) Protocol Use Case TLS/SSL HTTPS, SMTPS, IMAPS IPsec VPN, site-to-site SSH Remote shell, SFTP DTLS UDP-based (VoIP, WebRTC)

items.title: 3. Authentication
items.text: Method Description Passwords Knowledge-based (weak alone) Certificates PKI, X.509, TLS Multi-Factor (MFA) Something you know + have + are Kerberos Ticket-based (Windows domain) OAuth/OIDC Delegated authorization

items.title: MFA Factors
items.text: Factor Example Knowledge Password, PIN Possession Phone, token, smart card Inherence Fingerprint, face, iris

items.title: 34.5 Additional Network Protections
items.text: Mechanism Purpose VPN Encrypted tunnel over public network VLAN Network segmentation IDS/IPS Detect/block attacks Honeypot Decoy to detect/analyze attacks NAC Network Access Control (device health check) Zero Trust Never trust, always verify

items.title: 34.5 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. DoS = Overwhelm resources (CPU, memory, bandwidth, connections)
  2. Port Scanning = Reconnaissance for open services
  3. IP Spoofing = Forge source IP to hide/impersonate
  4. MITM = Intercept/modify communication between parties
  5. Packet Sniffing = Capture unencrypted traffic
  6. Firewall = Filter traffic by rules
  7. Encryption = Protect data in transit (TLS, IPsec, SSH)
  8. Authentication = Verify identity (MFA > passwords)
  9. Encryption + Authentication = Defense in depth

items.title: 34.6 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer DoS Overwhelm resources to deny service DDoS Distributed (botnet) DoS Port Scan Probe open ports for services IP Spoofing Forge source IP address MITM Intercept/modify between two parties Packet Sniffing Capture packets; exposes unencrypted data Firewall Filter traffic by rules (packet/stateful/app) Encryption Protect data in transit (TLS, IPsec, SSH) MFA Multiple factors (know/have/are) VPN Encrypted tunnel over public net IDS/IPS Detect/block intrusions

items.title: Topic 35: Access Matrix & Implementation
items.text: Source: Lecture 4.11 (Unit 4) + Textbook Ch. 14 (Silberschatz Ch. 14, Stallings Ch. 14)

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Access Matrix = Protection model specifying who can access what and how
  • Rows = Domains (subjects/users/processes)
  • Columns = Objects (files, printers, memory, devices)
  • Cells = Access Rights (read, write, execute, print, delete)

items.title: Core Concept
items.text: Access Matrix = Function: Domain × Object → Set of Rights

items.title: Basic Structure
items.text: Object 1 Object 2 Object 3 Printer Domain 1 read read Domain 2 print Domain 3 read, write Domain 4 read, write read, write

items.title: Example from Slides
items.text: Domain F1 F2 F3 Printer D1 read read D2 print D3 read, write D4 read, write read, write

items.title: Key Rules
items.text: Rule Description Only allowed access Matrix defines exact permissions Strict control No implicit permissions OS decides Which domain process runs in; what rights granted

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Domain treated as an object
  • Switch = operation to change from domain Di → Dj

items.title: Switching Rule
items.text: Process can switch from Domain Di → Domain Dj only if switch right exists in Access Matrix

items.title: Example Switch Rights
items.text: From Domain Can Switch To D1 D2 D2 D3, D4 D4 D1

items.title: Additional Special Rights
items.text: Right Meaning copy Duplicate access rights to another domain owner Full control over object control Modify access rights of other domains

items.title: Problem
items.text:
• Complete matrix can be huge (Domains × Objects)
  • Most entries empty (sparse matrix)
  • Storing full matrix = memory inefficient

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Single table with all non-empty <Domain, Object, Rights> tuples
Domain Object Rights D1 F1 read D1 F3 read D2 Printer print D3 F2 read, write D4 F1 read, write D4 F3 read, write

items.title: Lookup Process
items.text:
1. Process requests access to object
  2. OS searches global table for <Domain, Object>
  3. If found → check rights → allow/deny

items.title: Limitations
items.text: Issue Impact Large table Memory inefficient for sparse matrices Slow lookup Search entire table (O(n)) Management Hard to group similar rights

items.title: 35.3 Access Control Lists (ACL) — Access List per Object
Structure
items.text:
• Each object maintains list of <Domain, Rights>
  • Format: Object → [(Domain, Rights), ...]

items.title: Example: File F1
items.text: F1 → [(D1, read), (D3, read, write), (D4, read, write)]

items.title: Lookup Process
items.text:
1. Process requests access to object
  2. OS checks object's ACL
  3. Finds requesting domain
  4. Checks rights → allow/deny

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Who can access? Easy to see all domains with access to object Modify permissions Easy to add/remove entries Default permissions Easy to set defaults

items.title: Limitation
items.text: Limitation Description Reverse query Hard to find "what objects can Domain D access?"

items.title: Example (F1 ACL)
items.text:
F1 → (D1, read), (D3, read/write), (D4, read/write)
→ D2 has NO access to F1

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Each domain maintains list of capabilities
  • Format: Domain → [(Object, Rights), ...]

items.title: Example: Domain D1
items.text: D1 → [(F1, read), (F2, read/write), (Printer, print)]

items.title: Lookup Process
items.text:
1. Process runs in Domain D
  2. OS checks D's capability list
  3. Finds requested object
  4. Checks rights → allow/deny

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Advantage Description Fast lookup Per-domain list; typically smaller Revocation Remove capability from list Delegation Copy capability to another domain

items.title: Comparison: ACL vs Capability
items.text: Aspect ACL (Per Object) Capability (Per Domain) Question "Who can access X?" "What can D access?" Lookup Check object's list Check domain's list Revocation Scan all ACLs Remove from domain's list Delegation Add to object's ACL Copy capability Space Good if few domains/object Good if few objects/domain

items.title: 35.4 Comparison of Implementation Methods
items.text: Method Structure Lookup Space Best For Global Table Single <D,O,R> table Search all entries O(n) Small systems ACL Per-object lists Search object's list Sparse Object-centric access Capability Per-domain lists Search domain's list Sparse Domain-centric access

items.title: Mechanism
items.text:
• Domain switching = operation on domain object
  • Switch Right required in Access Matrix

items.title: Implementation
items.text:
Access Matrix Cell (Di, Dj) contains "switch" right
→ Process in Di can switch to Dj

items.title: Protection
items.text:
• Only authorized switches allowed
  • Prevents unauthorized privilege escalation

items.title: 35.5 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Access Matrix = Domains × Objects → Rights
  2. Domain Switching = Requires switch right in matrix
  3. Global Table = Simple but memory inefficient
  4. ACL = Per-object lists; answers "who can access?"
  5. Capability List = Per-domain; answers "what can I access?"
  6. Choice = Depends on access patterns (object-centric vs domain-centric)

items.title: 35.5 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer Access Matrix Rows=Domains, Columns=Objects, Cells=Rights Domain Switching Requires switch right in matrix Global Table Single table of <D,O,R>; slow lookup ACL Per-object list; "who can access X?" Capability Per-domain list; "what can D access?" ACL vs Capability ACL = object-centric; Capability = domain-centric Global Table drawback Large, slow, hard to manage Capability advantage Fast lookup, easy revocation/delegation

items.title: Problem 1: Access Matrix Construction
items.text:
Domains: D1, D2, D3
Objects: F1, F2, Printer
Rights: D1→read F1, write F2; D2→read F1; D3→print
Draw matrix.

items.title: Problem 2: Domain Switching
items.text:
Matrix has: (D1,D2)=switch, (D2,D3)=switch
Process in D1 wants to reach D3.
Can it? How?

items.title: Problem 3: ACL vs Capability
items.text:
File F1 ACL: [(D1, r), (D2, rw)]
Domain D1 Capabilities: [(F1, r), (F2, r)]
Are these consistent?

items.title: Problem 4: Access Check
items.text:
Process in D3 requests write to F1.
ACL(F1) = [(D1,r), (D2,rw)]
Capability(D3) = [(F2,r)]
Result?

items.title: Problem 5: Implementation Choice
items.text:
System with 1000 domains, 10000 objects, sparse access.
ACL or Capability? Why?

path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.1 Access Control Fundamentals
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Access Control = Mechanism determining who can access what and how
  • OS uses protection mechanisms to control access to files, devices, objects
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Access Control Flow
items.text: User/Process → Access Request → Security Check → Allow/Deny
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Key Components
items.text: Component Role Subject User/Process/Domain requesting access Object Resource (file, device, memory) Operation Read, Write, Execute, Delete, etc. Policy Rules governing access
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.2 Revocation of Access Rights
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Definition
items.text:
• Revocation = Removing previously granted access rights
  • Required in dynamic protection systems where access changes over time
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Example
items.text:
Before Revocation:
Faculty → File F1 → Read + Write

After Revocation:
Faculty → File F1 → Read (Write removed)
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.2 Why Revocation is Needed
items.text: Reason Description Role Change User's responsibilities change No Longer Needed User no longer requires access Increased Restriction Resource becomes more sensitive Expiration Temporary access expires Admin Action Admin withdraws permissions
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.3 Types of Revocation
items.text: Classification Types Description Timing Immediate / Delayed Instant vs scheduled Scope Selective / General Specific user vs all users Extent Partial / Total Some rights vs all rights Duration Temporary / Permanent Time-limited vs permanent
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.3 Revocation Dimensions
items.text: Dimension Types Description Timing Immediate / Delayed Instant vs scheduled Scope Selective / General Specific user vs all users Extent Partial / Total Some rights vs all rights Duration Temporary / Permanent Time-limited vs forever
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.4 Revocation with ACL vs Capability
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: ACL (Access Control List) — Easy Revocation
items.text:
Aspect Description Mechanism Remove/modify entry in object's ACL Ease ✅ Straightforward Operations Supports all revocation types 
ACL(F1): [(D1, rw), (D2, r)]
→ Revoke D2 write: remove (D2, rw) or change to (D2, r)
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Capability List — Difficult Revocation
items.text: Challenge Description Distribution Capabilities scattered across domains Tracking Hard to locate all copies Revocation Must find & modify all copies
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.4 Capability Revocation Techniques
items.text: Technique Mechanism Pros Cons Reacquisition Capabilities expire; re-request on need Simple; automatic cleanup Overhead on re-request Back-Pointers Maintain pointers to all capability copies Complete revocation Space overhead; pointer maintenance Indirection Access via global table; invalidate table entry Centralized control Indirection overhead Keys Capability + key; change key to invalidate Granular control Key management overhead
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.5 Revocation Techniques Detail
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 1. Reacquisition (Expiration)
items.text:
Capability validity = T
After T → expire → must re-request
Revoked → expiration time = now
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 2. Back-Pointers
items.text:
Capability → [back-pointers to all holders]
Revocation → traverse pointers → invalidate all
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 3. Indirection (Global Table)
items.text:
Capability → Index in global table
Revocation → Delete/invalidate table entry
All capabilities pointing there → invalid
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 4. Keys
items.text:
Capability + Key
Revocation → Change key → Old capability invalid
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.5 Access Matrix Recap
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Structure
items.text: Object 1 Object 2 Object 3 Domain 1 read write Domain 2 read Domain 3 execute
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Components
items.text: Element Description Rows Domains (subjects/processes) Columns Objects (files, devices) Cell Access rights (read, write, execute, etc.)
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Example
items.text: F1 F2 F3 Printer D1 read read D2 print D3 read, write D4 read, write read, write
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.6 Domain Switching
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Rule
items.text: Process can switch Domain Di → Dj only if switch right exists in Access Matrix
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Example
items.text: From Can Switch To D1 D2 D2 D3, D4 D4 D1
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Special Rights
items.text: Right Meaning copy Duplicate rights to another domain owner Full control over object control Modify other domains' rights
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.6 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Concept
items.text:
• Permissions → Roles → Users
  • Role = job function (Admin, Faculty, Student)
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: RBAC Structure
items.text: Users → Roles → Permissions → Objects
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Example
items.text: Role Permissions Admin read, write, delete Faculty read, write Student read only
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: User Assignment
items.text:
User 1 → Faculty Role → read, write
User 2 → Student Role → read only
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Advantages
items.text: Benefit Description Simplicity Manage roles, not users Flexibility Change role → all users updated Security No direct permission assignment Scalability Handles large systems
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: Limitation
items.text: Issue Description Role Explosion Too many roles → complexity Design Effort Requires careful role engineering
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.7 Key Takeaways
items.text:
1. Access Control = Who → What → How (Subject, Object, Operation)
  2. Revocation = Remove granted rights; needed for dynamic systems
  3. Revocation Types = Immediate/Delayed, Selective/General, Partial/Total, Temporary/Permanent
  4. ACL = Easy revocation (modify object's list)
  5. Capability = Hard revocation (distributed copies)
  6. Revocation Techniques = Reacquisition, Back-pointers, Indirection, Keys
  7. RBAC = Permissions→Roles→Users; simplifies management
  8. Access Matrix = Domains × Objects → Rights
path: Topic 36: Access Control & Revocation of Access Rights

items.title: 36.8 Exam-Relevant MCQ Patterns
items.text: Question Answer Revocation Removing previously granted access Immediate vs Delayed Instant vs scheduled Selective vs General Specific user vs all users Partial vs Total Some rights vs all rights ACL Revocation Easy (modify object's list) Capability Revocation Hard (distributed copies) Reacquisition Expire capabilities, force re-request Back-Pointers Track all capability copies Indirection Global table; invalidate entry Keys Change key to invalidate RBAC Permissions→Roles→Users RBAC Benefit Simplify management; update role not users
